SDE-2 HLD Handbook

High-level design from first principles to SDE-2 interviews in 17 modules and 16 case studies, practice first: every lesson opens with a question to try, every flow diagram steps through, every case study asks before it tells, and a design tracker brings each design back for spaced review.

Start with Module 1: Systems and requirementsTry the decode drillsSee the interview framework
Phase 1: FoundationsPhase 2: ScalingPhase 3: DataPhase 4: AsyncPhase 5: ProductionCase studiesRings fill as you tick lessons studied, and as you design each case study.

Loading your progress.

How this handbook teaches

The goal is not to memorize 16 architectures. The goal is to look at a new prompt, name what makes it hard, and assemble a design from building blocks you understand well enough to defend. So the handbook asks you to think before it explains.

  • Try before you read. Every lesson opens with a short question. Answer it on paper first; getting it wrong is what makes the explanation stick.
  • Analogy, then mechanism, then trade-off. Each idea starts with what it solves and a plain analogy, then how it works, then what it costs. Depth sits in folded "Go deeper" sections.
  • Step through every flow. Diagrams with a step bar reveal one arrow at a time. Predict the next arrow before pressing Next. You should be able to redraw each one from memory.
  • Production notes. Green "In production" boxes show how the idea appears in real systems, including payments and data pipelines, so the handbook serves your day job, not only interviews.
  • Interview signals. Purple boxes say what interviewers listen for at SDE-2 (L4) and what an L5 answer adds.
  • One method everywhere. The decode method turns any prompt into pressures and building blocks in seven steps.
  • Live tools. Calculators for estimation and availability, a quorum explorer, a consistent hashing playground, and a token bucket simulator let you test intuitions with numbers.

How to study one module

  1. Clear the revision queue above at the start of each session: redesign those systems from a blank page.
  2. Do the warm-up quiz without reading anything. Note which questions you missed.
  3. For each lesson: answer the "Try it first" question, read the short part, step through the figure, then say out loud what problem the idea solves and when it fails.
  4. Open "Go deeper" only when a case study or your own question needs it.
  5. Do the self-check quiz at the end, then tick lessons as studied.
  6. Tick the mastery checklist only when each item is true with your notes closed.

How to practice a case study

  1. Set a 45-minute timer and design it yourself on paper or a whiteboard using the interview framework: requirements, estimates, API, data model, diagram, deep dives.
  2. Then open the case study and compare section by section. Answer each guided deep dive before revealing it.
  3. Set an honest status at the top of the page. The handbook schedules a review.
  4. Redesign it from memory when it comes due, faster each time. Then try the related practice prompts in the tracker.

Design statuses and the revision queue

Status Meaning Next review
Not started Not attempted Not scheduled
Could not design it You needed the solution for the core 2 days
Designed with hints You got there with a few peeks 4 days
Designed independently Full design in 45 minutes, trade-offs explained 10 days
Needs revision Did it before, but a redo went badly 1 day
Can teach it Designed it twice weeks apart, and can answer every follow-up 30 days

When a design comes up for review, redesign it without looking at notes, then set the new status or press "Reviewed, same status" to restart its timer.

Where your progress is saved

Lesson ticks, mastery checks, readiness checks, and design statuses save automatically to your account, privately: nobody else who opens this page sees them, and they follow you to other devices. The indicator in the top bar shows where the latest change went. If the page cannot reach your account (for example in a private window), it saves in this browser instead, and the tracker has a backup and restore box.

Scope

This handbook covers what general SDE-2 system design rounds test, in the depth they test it, plus the production knowledge a backend engineer uses daily. It deliberately leaves out: machine learning system design (feature stores and model serving appear only as boxes), cloud certification trivia, and research-level internals (Paxos proofs, CRDT algebra). Low-level design (classes and patterns) belongs to a separate LLD track.

Syllabus and prerequisite map

Seventeen modules in five phases, then sixteen case studies. The order follows dependencies: each phase uses ideas from the one before.

The map

Priority overview

Module Why it matters Interview weight Time

Total: about 45 hours of study, plus about 20 hours for the 16 case studies (45 minutes to design each, then about 30 minutes to compare and note what you missed).

How each module is organized

  • Warm-up quiz to expose what you do not know yet.
  • Lessons, each opening with a "Try it first" question, then what the idea solves, an analogy, the mechanism, and the trade-offs.
  • Figures that step through flows one arrow at a time.
  • Go deeper folds for details you need only sometimes.
  • In production notes and Interview signal notes.
  • Common mistakes, a self-check quiz, and a mastery checklist.

Case studies follow one format: try it first, requirements, estimates, API, data model, architecture figure, guided deep dives, failures, what a strong answer shows at L4 and L5, and follow-up questions.

Phase 1: FoundationsFoundation

Module 1: How a system is built

High-level design is deciding which boxes exist, how they talk, where the data lives, and what happens when load grows or a box dies. This module gives you the vocabulary and the habit of turning a vague product into numbers.

8 lessons3 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 1.1What high-level design is
  2. 1.2The building blocks
  3. 1.3Following one request end to end
  4. 1.4Functional and non-functional requirements
  5. 1.5Quality attributes and their trade-offs
  6. 1.6Growing a design from one box
  7. 1.7Common mistakes
  8. 1.8Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: what would you add?

Answer each in one line before reading. Reveal and compare. Misses tell you which lesson to read closely.

  1. A single server runs the app and the database. Deploys cause 2 minutes of downtime. What is the first change?
    Reveal

    Run 2+ app servers behind a load balancer and deploy one at a time (rolling deploy). The database moves to its own machine so app servers become replaceable.

  2. The home page is identical for everyone and the database CPU sits at 90%.
    Reveal

    Cache it. A cache (Redis, or a CDN for whole pages) serves the repeated read from memory, so the database only sees misses.

  3. Sending a welcome email makes sign-up take 3 seconds.
    Reveal

    Put the email on a queue and let a worker send it. The user's request returns as soon as the job is enqueued.

  4. Profile photos are stored on the app servers' disks. A new server has none of them.
    Reveal

    Store files in an object store (S3, GCS) and serve them through a CDN. App servers keep no local state.

  5. "The system must be fast." What should you ask?
    Reveal

    Fast for which action, at what percentile, at what load: for example "feed loads in under 200 ms at p99 for 10K requests per second".

1.1What high-level design is

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

You are asked to "design Instagram". Write the first three questions you would ask before drawing anything.

Reveal the answer

Good first questions narrow the scope and get numbers:

  1. Which features are in scope? (post photos, follow, feed; probably not stories, DMs, ads)
  2. How many users, and how active? (for example 500M daily active users, 2 posts per day each)
  3. What matters most? (feed latency, never losing a photo, how fresh the feed must be)

Drawing before asking is the most common reason candidates design the wrong system well.

What it is

A plan for a system at the level of components: services, data stores, caches, queues, and the network paths between them. It answers: where does each piece of data live, who reads and writes it, and what happens at 10x load or when a machine dies.

Analogy

City planning versus interior design. HLD decides where the roads, power station, and water tanks go and how big they must be. Low-level design (LLD) decides the rooms inside one building: classes, interfaces, and methods inside one service.

What you produce

A diagram of components and data flow, the API, the data model, back-of-the-envelope numbers, and the trade-offs you chose with the reason for each.

High-level design (HLD) Low-level design (LLD)
Unit Services, databases, queues, regions Classes, interfaces, methods
Questions Which database? Where is the cache? How do we shard? Which classes? Which design pattern? What are the method signatures?
Failure thinking Machine, network, region outages Exceptions, invalid states
Output Architecture diagram, data model, API, capacity estimates Class diagram, sequence diagram, code
In production

At work, HLD is the "design doc" stage: before a team builds a new pipeline (say, a statement-generation service), someone writes the components, data flow, failure handling, and capacity plan, and reviewers attack the trade-offs. The interview round is a compressed version of that review.

1.2The building blocks

Try it first2 minutes

Name the component you would reach for in each case: (a) many users read the same data, (b) work takes 30 seconds, (c) store 10 TB of videos, (d) spread requests across 20 servers.

Reveal the answer

(a) Cache. (b) Queue plus workers. (c) Object storage plus a CDN. (d) Load balancer. Most designs are these blocks, wired differently.

Almost every design is assembled from about a dozen blocks. Learn what each one is for, and you can read any architecture diagram.

Block Its job Typical technology Module
Client Sends requests, renders results Browser, mobile app, another service 2
DNS Turns a name into an IP address Route 53, Cloud DNS 2
CDN Serves static or cacheable content from servers near the user CloudFront, Akamai, Cloudflare 7
Load balancer Spreads requests across healthy servers NGINX, HAProxy, AWS ALB/NLB, Envoy 5
API gateway One front door: auth, rate limits, routing to services Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway 5, 14
App service Business logic; stateless so any copy can serve any request Spring Boot service on Kubernetes 5
Cache Keeps hot data in memory to cut latency and DB load Redis, Memcached 6
Database Durable source of truth PostgreSQL, MySQL, Cassandra, DynamoDB 8
Object storage Cheap, durable storage for files and blobs S3, GCS 7
Queue / log Decouples producers from consumers; absorbs bursts Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS 12
Workers Process background jobs from a queue Consumer services, batch jobs 12
Search index Full-text and faceted search Elasticsearch, OpenSearch 17

1.3Following one request end to end

Try it first3 minutes

A user opens a feed in the app. List every hop the request makes until the first byte comes back.

Reveal the answer

App resolves the domain (DNS, usually cached), opens a TCP + TLS connection to the load balancer, the LB forwards to one app server, the app server checks the cache, on a miss queries the database, builds the response, and sends it back the same way. Images on the page come separately from the CDN.

The rule this figure teaches: keep the synchronous path short. Everything the user waits for adds latency and is a place to fail. Move anything slow or non-essential (emails, thumbnails, analytics) to a queue.

Go deeper

Where the milliseconds go

A rough budget for one dynamic request within a region:

Hop Typical cost
DNS lookup 0 ms if cached, 20-120 ms if not
TCP + TLS 1.3 handshake 1-2 round trips; ~30-100 ms on mobile, ~1 ms inside a datacenter
Load balancer hop under 1 ms
Redis read ~0.5-1 ms over the network
Indexed SQL query 1-10 ms
Unindexed query on a large table seconds
Cross-region call 50-150 ms

Connection reuse (HTTP keep-alive, HTTP/2) removes the handshake cost from all but the first request, which is why clients and services keep long-lived connection pools.

1.4Functional and non-functional requirements

Try it first3 minutes

For a URL shortener, write two functional and three non-functional requirements. Put a number in every non-functional one.

Reveal the answer

Functional: create a short URL for a long URL; redirect a short URL to the long one. (Maybe: custom aliases, expiry, click counts.)

Non-functional: 100M new URLs per month; redirect latency under 50 ms at p99; 99.99% availability for redirects; short URLs never collide; links last at least 5 years.

Functional (FR)

What the system does, written as user actions: "a user can post a photo", "a user sees a feed of people they follow". Keep 3-5 core ones and say out loud what you are leaving out.

Non-functional (NFR)

How well it must do it, with numbers: scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability, security, cost. NFRs decide the architecture; FRs decide the API.

The NFR checklist to run through in every design:

Quality Question to ask Example answer
Scale How many users, requests per second, data per day? 100M DAU, 50K reads/s peak
Read/write ratio Read-heavy or write-heavy? 100:1 reads to writes
Latency Which action, at which percentile? Feed under 200 ms at p99
Availability How much downtime is acceptable? 99.99% (about 52 minutes a year)
Consistency Must every reader see the latest write immediately? Feed can lag 5 s; payments cannot
Durability Can we ever lose data? Never lose a confirmed payment
Security / compliance PII, payments, regions? Card data under PCI DSS; data stays in India
Cost Any budget or hardware limit? Storage dominates; use cold tiers
Key idea

Consistency and availability requirements are often different per feature. "Likes can be eventually consistent, but the account balance must be strongly consistent" is a better answer than one global choice.

1.5Quality attributes and their trade-offs

Try it first2 minutes

Why can't a system be maximally fast, cheap, always available, and always consistent at once? Pick one pair and explain the tension.

Reveal the answer

Example: consistency vs availability. To guarantee every read sees the latest write, replicas must coordinate; if the network between them breaks, a replica must either refuse requests (lose availability) or answer with possibly stale data (lose consistency). Another: latency vs cost, since lower latency needs more replicas, more cache memory, and servers closer to users.

Attribute Meaning Main tools
Scalability Handle more load by adding resources Stateless services, load balancing, caching, sharding, queues
Availability Fraction of time the system answers Redundancy, failover, health checks, multi-zone
Reliability Answers correctly, even with faults Retries, idempotency, replication, testing
Latency Time for one request Caching, CDN, indexes, fewer hops, async work
Throughput Requests or bytes per second Horizontal scaling, batching, partitioning
Consistency Readers agree on the latest value Single leader, quorums, consensus, transactions
Durability Confirmed data survives failures Replication, write-ahead logs, backups
Maintainability Easy to change and operate Clear boundaries, observability, automation

The trade-offs you will name in almost every design:

  • Consistency vs availability and latency. Strong consistency needs coordination, which costs round trips and can block during failures (Module 11).
  • Latency vs throughput. Batching raises throughput but makes each item wait (Kafka producer batching, DB group commit).
  • Read speed vs write speed. Indexes, caches, and denormalized copies make reads fast and writes slower or more complex.
  • Simplicity vs scale. A single PostgreSQL primary handles far more than most people assume. Shard only when numbers force you to.
Interview signal

Interviewers at L4 listen for trade-offs said out loud with a reason: "I'll use cache-aside with a 60 s TTL because the profile page tolerates a minute of staleness and reads outnumber writes 100 to 1." A list of technologies without the "because" scores low.

1.6Growing a design from one box

Try it first3 minutes

A system on one server is growing fast. In what order would you add: CDN, read replicas, load balancer, separate DB server, cache, sharding? Justify the first two.

Reveal the answer

A common order: separate DB server, then load balancer with 2+ app servers, then cache and read replicas, then CDN and queues, then sharding, then multi-region. Separate the DB first because it lets app servers become stateless and replaceable; add the LB next because it removes the single point of failure and enables zero-downtime deploys. Sharding comes late because it is the most expensive change to undo.

Stage Bottleneck it fixes
Separate DB App and DB fight for CPU and memory; one deploy kills both
LB + many app servers One app server is a single point of failure and a CPU ceiling
Cache + read replicas Database reads saturate the primary
CDN + queue Static bytes waste server bandwidth; slow tasks block requests
Sharding Writes or data size exceed one primary
Multi-region Region outages and far-away users
Watch out

Do not jump to stage 6 for a system with 1,000 users. Over-engineering is marked down just like under-engineering. Size the design to the numbers you estimated.

1.7Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Drawing before asking. Five minutes on requirements saves you from designing the wrong system.
  • Non-functional requirements without numbers. "Highly available" and "low latency" decide nothing; "99.99%" and "200 ms p99" decide a lot.
  • Stateful app servers. Sessions or files on local disk break load balancing and autoscaling. Keep state in a database, cache, or object store.
  • Putting slow work on the request path. Email, image processing, and fan-out belong on a queue.
  • One consistency choice for everything. Split by feature: money strong, counters and feeds eventual.
  • Technology names as answers. "Use Kafka" is not a design; say what problem it solves here and what it costs.

1.8Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons

If you miss one, reread the lesson it points to.

  1. What is the difference between availability and durability?
    Reveal

    Availability is whether the system answers right now. Durability is whether confirmed data survives failures. A system can be down (unavailable) without losing data (durable), or up while having lost data.

  2. Name three things that make an app server stateful, and where each should live instead.
    Reveal

    Sessions (Redis or a signed cookie/token), uploaded files (object storage), in-memory counters or caches that must be shared (Redis or the database).

  3. Why is "the system should be scalable" a weak requirement?
    Reveal

    It has no number. Say what grows (users, writes per second, data size) and to what level, so it can drive choices like sharding or caching.

  4. Give one example of the latency vs throughput trade-off.
    Reveal

    Batching: a Kafka producer waits a few milliseconds (linger) to send messages together, raising throughput but adding latency to each message.

  5. A design doc proposes sharding the database on day one for 5,000 users. What do you say?
    Reveal

    One well-indexed PostgreSQL primary with replicas handles this easily. Sharding adds cross-shard queries, rebalancing, and operational cost; defer it until estimates show writes or data size exceed one node.

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Module 2: Networking essentials

Every arrow in a diagram is a network call with a cost and a failure mode. This module covers the parts of networking that change design decisions: TCP vs UDP, DNS, HTTP versions, TLS, and how to push data to clients in real time.

8 lessons4 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 2.1Addresses, ports, and layers
  2. 2.2TCP and UDP
  3. 2.3DNS
  4. 2.4HTTP versions and TLS
  5. 2.5Real-time: polling, long polling, SSE, WebSockets
  6. 2.6RPC and gRPC
  7. 2.7Common mistakes
  8. 2.8Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: five quick calls

One line each, then reveal.

  1. A video call drops a packet. Should the app wait for it to be resent?
    Reveal

    No. A late video frame is useless, so video calls use UDP (or WebRTC over UDP) and skip lost packets. File transfers and APIs need every byte in order, so they use TCP.

  2. You change a DNS record to fail over to a new IP. Why do some users keep hitting the old IP for a while?
    Reveal

    Resolvers and clients cache the old answer until its TTL expires, and some ignore short TTLs. DNS failover is never instant.

  3. A chat app needs the server to push messages instantly to the phone. Which protocol?
    Reveal

    A persistent connection: WebSocket (two-way), or server-sent events if only the server pushes. Polling wastes requests and adds delay.

  4. Why do services keep connection pools instead of opening a connection per request?
    Reveal

    Each new TCP + TLS connection costs 2 round trips of handshakes plus CPU for crypto. Reusing connections removes that cost from every request after the first.

  5. Your gRPC service has 10 backends but one gets all the traffic. Why?
    Reveal

    gRPC uses long-lived HTTP/2 connections. An L4 load balancer balances connections, not requests, so one connection carries everything to one backend. Use an L7 (request-aware) load balancer or client-side balancing.

2.1Addresses, ports, and layers

Try it first2 minutes

A server runs PostgreSQL and a web app. How does a packet arriving at the machine know which program it is for?

Reveal the answer

By the destination port. The IP address identifies the machine; the port identifies the program on it: 443 for HTTPS, 5432 for PostgreSQL, 6379 for Redis, 9092 for Kafka.

Analogy

Shipping a parcel. The IP address is the building, the port is the apartment, TCP is a tracked courier that guarantees delivery in order, UDP is a postcard: cheap and fast, no tracking.

What you need

You do not need all 7 OSI layers in an interview. You need three: L3 network (IP: routing between machines), L4 transport (TCP or UDP: delivery between programs), and L7 application (HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket, DNS: the message format).

Why it matters

Load balancers are described by layer. An L4 balancer routes by IP and port without reading the request. An L7 balancer reads HTTP and can route by path, header, or cookie (Module 5).

Layer Protocols Unit Design impact
L7 Application HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket, DNS Request / message Routing by URL, auth, caching, retries
L4 Transport TCP, UDP, QUIC (over UDP) Segment / datagram Reliability, ordering, connection cost
L3 Network IP Packet Addressing, routing, cross-region latency

2.2TCP and UDP

Try it first2 minutes

Name two applications that should use UDP and two that must use TCP. What property decides it?

Reveal the answer

UDP: live video or voice calls, online games, DNS lookups, QUIC/HTTP/3 (which builds its own reliability on top). TCP: web APIs, database connections, file transfer, email. The deciding property: whether late data is still useful. If a retransmitted packet would arrive too late to matter, skip it (UDP); if every byte must arrive in order, use TCP.

TCP UDP
Connection Yes: 3-way handshake first No: just send
Delivery Guaranteed, retransmits lost segments Best effort, may lose packets
Order In order No ordering
Flow and congestion control Yes No (application decides)
Overhead Higher (handshake, acks, 20+ byte header) Lower (8 byte header)
Used for HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, databases, gRPC DNS, video calls, games, QUIC (HTTP/3)
Go deeper

Head-of-line blocking and why HTTP/3 moved to UDP

TCP delivers bytes in order. If one packet is lost, every later packet waits in the receive buffer until the lost one is retransmitted, even if those later packets belong to unrelated requests. This is head-of-line (HOL) blocking.

HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one TCP connection, so one lost packet stalls all of them. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, which is built on UDP and tracks each stream separately: a lost packet only stalls its own stream. QUIC also combines the transport and TLS handshakes into one round trip and keeps a connection alive when a phone switches from Wi-Fi to mobile data (connection IDs instead of IP and port).

2.3DNS

Try it first2 minutes

You type api.shop.com. Nothing is cached anywhere. Who answers, in what order?

Reveal the answer

Your OS asks a recursive resolver (your ISP's, or 8.8.8.8). The resolver asks a root server (which points to the .com servers), then a .com TLD server (which points to shop.com's name servers), then the authoritative server for shop.com, which returns the IP. Every answer is cached for its TTL, so the next lookup is usually instant.

Record Maps Example use
A / AAAA Name to IPv4 / IPv6 address api.shop.com -> 203.0.113.7
CNAME Name to another name www.shop.com -> shop.cdn-provider.net
MX Domain to mail servers Email routing
NS Domain to its authoritative name servers Delegation
TXT Free text Domain ownership checks, SPF for email

DNS is also a coarse load balancer:

  • Round-robin DNS: return several IPs; clients spread across them. No health awareness.
  • GeoDNS / latency-based routing: return the IP of the region closest to the user (Route 53 latency routing, Cloud DNS geolocation).
  • Failover routing: health-check a region and stop returning its IP when it fails.
Watch out

DNS changes propagate only as fast as caches expire. A TTL of 60 s helps, but some resolvers and clients cache longer. For fast failover, put a load balancer or anycast IP in front and fail over behind it; use DNS for slower, coarse moves.

2.4HTTP versions and TLS

Try it first2 minutes

A web page loads 80 small files from one domain. Why is it faster over HTTP/2 than HTTP/1.1?

Reveal the answer

HTTP/1.1 handles one request at a time per connection, so browsers open about 6 connections per domain and queue the rest. HTTP/2 multiplexes all 80 requests over one connection at once and compresses repeated headers.

HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3
Transport TCP TCP QUIC over UDP
Requests per connection One at a time (keep-alive reuses the connection) Many, multiplexed as streams Many, independent streams
Headers Plain text, repeated Binary, compressed (HPACK) Binary, compressed (QPACK)
HOL blocking Per connection At the TCP level Only per stream
Handshake for new HTTPS TCP + TLS: 2 round trips Same 1 round trip (0 on resumption)

TLS (the S in HTTPS) gives three things: encryption (nobody can read the traffic), integrity (nobody can modify it), and authentication (the certificate proves the server is really shop.com). TLS 1.3 needs one round trip; TLS 1.2 needed two.

In production

Most systems terminate TLS at the load balancer or gateway: the LB holds the certificate, decrypts, and forwards to services over the private network. PCI DSS requires strong encryption for card data over public networks, and many teams also encrypt inside the private network to reduce risk: traffic is re-encrypted to the service, or services talk with mutual TLS (mTLS), where both sides present certificates. A service mesh (Module 14) automates mTLS between services.

2.5Real-time: polling, long polling, SSE, WebSockets

Try it first3 minutes

Pick a mechanism for each: (a) live sports score shown on a web page, (b) multiplayer chat, (c) checking whether a report export has finished, roughly every 30 s.

Reveal the answer

(a) Server-sent events: only the server pushes, works over plain HTTP, auto-reconnects. (b) WebSocket: both sides send frequently. (c) Plain polling is fine: rare checks, simple, cacheable, no long-lived connections to manage.

Mechanism Direction How it works Use when
Short polling Client pulls Request every N seconds Updates are rare and delay is fine
Long polling Client pulls, server holds Server keeps the request open until data or timeout, client re-requests Need push but cannot use WebSocket or SSE
Server-sent events (SSE) Server to client One HTTP response that stays open and streams text/event-stream events; browser auto-reconnects with the last event ID Feeds, notifications, live scores, LLM token streaming
WebSocket Both directions HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket, server answers 101, then frames flow both ways over the same TCP connection Chat, collaborative editing, games

Scaling persistent connections

Each WebSocket is a long-lived connection pinned to one server. Two problems follow: the load balancer must keep each client on its server for the life of the connection, and a message for Bob must reach the specific server holding Bob's connection.

Go deeper

Operating WebSocket fleets

  • Capacity: one tuned server can hold tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of mostly idle connections; memory per connection and file descriptor limits decide the number.
  • Heartbeats: send ping/pong every 20-60 s so you detect dead connections and keep NAT and load balancer idle timeouts from cutting them.
  • Deploys: draining a gateway disconnects its clients. Clients must reconnect with backoff and jitter, or every client reconnects at once (a thundering herd).
  • Missed messages: a reconnecting client asks for messages after the last ID it saw; the server reads them from storage. The connection is a delivery optimization, never the source of truth.

2.6RPC and gRPC

Try it first2 minutes

Two internal services exchange 50,000 small requests per second. Why might they use gRPC instead of JSON over HTTP?

Reveal the answer

gRPC sends compact binary Protocol Buffers instead of JSON text (smaller, faster to parse), multiplexes calls over HTTP/2, generates typed client and server code from one .proto contract, and supports streaming and deadlines natively.

  • gRPC = Protocol Buffers (schema and binary encoding) + HTTP/2 (transport). Four call types: unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional streaming.
  • Strengths: performance, strict contracts, code generation in many languages, deadlines that propagate across calls.
  • Costs: not human-readable, browsers need a gRPC-Web proxy, and long-lived HTTP/2 connections need L7 or client-side load balancing.
  • Typical split: REST/JSON for public and browser-facing APIs, gRPC between internal services. API styles are compared in Module 3.
Note

A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and acts for them (TLS termination, compression, caching, routing): NGINX, Envoy. A forward proxy sits in front of clients and acts for them (egress control, corporate filtering). Load balancers and API gateways are specialized reverse proxies.

Interview signal

Interviewers rarely ask about TCP flags, but they do expect you to pick the right client-server channel and say why: "SSE for the live score because only the server pushes", "WebSockets for chat with a registry so any server can route to the user's connection", "gRPC between internal services, behind an L7 balancer".

2.7Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Ignoring connection setup cost. New TCP + TLS per request adds 2 round trips. Pool and reuse connections.
  • Expecting instant DNS failover. Cached answers outlive TTL changes; fail over behind a stable IP when speed matters.
  • WebSockets for everything. If only the server pushes, SSE is simpler. If updates are rare, polling is simpler.
  • Treating the socket as storage. Messages sent while a client was disconnected must come from a database on reconnect.
  • L4 load balancing for gRPC. Connections, not requests, get balanced, so load piles onto a few backends.
  • Saying "UDP is unreliable, so never use it". It is the right choice when late data is worthless.

2.8Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What does TLS provide besides encryption?
    Reveal

    Integrity (tampering is detected) and authentication (the certificate proves the server's identity; with mTLS, the client's too).

  2. Why does HTTP/2 still suffer from head-of-line blocking, and what fixes it?
    Reveal

    All streams share one TCP connection, and TCP delivers in order, so one lost packet stalls every stream. HTTP/3 over QUIC recovers loss per stream.

  3. A client reconnects its WebSocket after 2 minutes offline. How does it get the messages it missed?
    Reveal

    It sends the last message ID (or timestamp) it received; the server queries durable storage for newer messages and sends them, then resumes live delivery.

  4. What is the difference between GeoDNS and an anycast IP?
    Reveal

    GeoDNS returns different IPs based on where the resolver is. Anycast announces the same IP from many locations and lets internet routing deliver packets to the nearest one. Anycast reacts faster because it does not depend on DNS caches.

  5. When is plain polling the best choice?
    Reveal

    When updates are infrequent and a delay of one interval is acceptable, for example checking a long export job every 30 s. It is simple, stateless, and cache-friendly.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Module 3: API design

The API is the contract between your system and everything that calls it. A good one makes retries safe, pages stable, and changes backward compatible. In an interview it is the bridge from requirements to architecture.

9 lessons3 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 3.1Resources, methods, and status codes
  2. 3.2Designing the API for a feature
  3. 3.3Pagination
  4. 3.4Idempotency keys and safe retries
  5. 3.5REST, gRPC, and GraphQL
  6. 3.6Versioning, errors, and evolution
  7. 3.7Async APIs and webhooks
  8. 3.8Common mistakes
  9. 3.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: name the right choice

One line each.

  1. Which HTTP status for a successful POST that created an order?
    Reveal

    201 Created, with a Location header pointing at the new order (for example /orders/123).

  2. A client retries POST /payments after a timeout. What prevents a double charge?
    Reveal

    An idempotency key: the client sends a unique key per logical payment; the server stores the first result under that key and returns it for any retry.

  3. Page 2 of a feed shows a post that was already on page 1. What pagination bug is this?
    Reveal

    Offset pagination. A new item was inserted at the top, shifting everything down one position. Cursor (keyset) pagination fixes it.

  4. Generating a report takes 2 minutes. What should POST /reports return?
    Reveal

    202 Accepted with a job ID or status URL. The client polls the status resource or gets a webhook when it is done.

  5. You need to rename a JSON field used by mobile apps you cannot force-update. What do you do?
    Reveal

    Add the new field, keep sending the old one, and remove it only after usage drops to zero, or ship the change in a new API version.

3.1Resources, methods, and status codes

Try it first2 minutes

Which of these can a client safely retry without side effects: GET /users/7, PUT /users/7 {name: "A"}, POST /orders, DELETE /orders/9?

Reveal the answer

GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent: repeating them leaves the server in the same state as doing them once (PUT sets the same value, a second DELETE finds nothing to delete). POST is not: each call may create a new order. That is why POST needs an idempotency key for safe retries.

Idea

REST models the system as resources (nouns, each with a URL) and uses the standard HTTP methods (verbs) on them. GET /users/7/orders lists Alice's orders; POST /users/7/orders creates one.

Analogy

A library catalog. Every book has a shelf address (URL). You look a book up (GET), replace its record (PUT), fix one field (PATCH), add a new book (POST), or remove one (DELETE). The verbs are the same for every shelf.

Method Purpose Safe (no change) Idempotent
GET Read a resource or list Yes Yes
POST Create, or run an action No No
PUT Replace a resource fully No Yes
PATCH Change some fields No Not guaranteed
DELETE Remove a resource No Yes
Code Meaning Typical use
200 / 201 / 204 OK / Created / No content Read, create, delete
202 Accepted for later processing Async jobs
301 / 302 Moved permanently / temporarily Redirects (URL shortener!)
304 Not modified Conditional GET with ETag
400 / 422 Malformed / semantically invalid request Validation errors
401 / 403 Not authenticated / not allowed Missing token / wrong permissions
404 / 409 Not found / conflict with current state Duplicate unique key, version conflict
412 Precondition failed If-Match ETag no longer current
429 Too many requests Rate limited; send Retry-After
500 / 502 / 503 / 504 Server error / bad upstream / overloaded / upstream timeout Retry 502, 503, 504 with backoff

3.2Designing the API for a feature

Try it first3 minutes

Write the endpoints for a photo app: upload a photo, get a user's photos, like a photo, get the home feed.

Reveal the answer

POST /v1/photos -> 201 {photo_id, upload_url} GET /v1/users/{user_id}/photos?cursor=...&limit=20 PUT /v1/photos/{photo_id}/likes/me -> 204 (idempotent like) DELETE /v1/photos/{photo_id}/likes/me -> 204 (unlike) GET /v1/feed?cursor=...&limit=20 Making "like" a PUT on a sub-resource makes it naturally idempotent: liking twice is still one like. The upload returns a presigned URL so the bytes go straight to object storage (Module 7).

Rules that keep an API clean:

  • Nouns in paths, verbs in methods: POST /orders, not POST /createOrder. For actions that are not CRUD, use a sub-resource: POST /orders/9/cancel.
  • The user comes from the auth token, not from the body: GET /feed, not GET /feed?user_id=7. Otherwise anyone can read anyone's feed.
  • Every list is paginated and has a maximum page size.
  • Return what the client needs next: IDs, a cursor, a status URL.
  • Use IDs that do not leak information: random or time-ordered IDs, not sequential ones that reveal your order count (Module 17).
Interview signal

In an interview, write 3-5 endpoints with method, path, key parameters, and response, then move on. Ten minutes on API details is too long; zero minutes means the interviewer cannot see how clients use your system.

3.3Pagination

Try it first2 minutes

Why does LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000 get slower as users scroll, even with an index?

Reveal the answer

The database must still walk past the first 100,000 rows before returning 20. Cost grows with the offset. Keyset pagination (WHERE id < last_seen_id ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20) jumps straight to the right place with the index, so every page costs the same.

Offset (?page=3) Cursor / keyset (?cursor=abc)
Jump to page N Yes No, only next or previous
Cost of deep pages Grows with offset Constant with an index
Stable under inserts and deletes No: duplicates and skips Yes
Use for Admin tables, small data Feeds, timelines, any large or live list

The cursor is usually an opaque, encoded value of the sort key, for example base64 of (created_at, id). Include the ID as a tie-breaker so rows with equal timestamps are not skipped.

3.4Idempotency keys and safe retries

Try it first3 minutes

A payment request times out. The client does not know whether the charge happened. Design the server behavior so the client can always retry safely.

Reveal the answer

The client generates a unique key per logical operation (a UUID) and sends it in an Idempotency-Key header. The server records the key before doing the work (with a unique constraint), stores the final response under it, and on any request with a key it has already finished, returns the stored response without redoing the work. If the first request is still in progress, the retry gets 409 Conflict (or waits) instead of starting a second charge.

Go deeper

Implementing idempotency correctly

  • Key scope: unique per client (or account) plus key, so two merchants can use the same string.
  • Atomic claim: INSERT ... (key, status='in_progress') with a unique constraint. The loser of a race sees the conflict and does not start the work.
  • Same key, different body: compare a hash of the request; if it differs, return 422. Otherwise a buggy client could reuse a key for a different payment.
  • Store the outcome, including failures that are final (a declined card), so the retry gets the same answer.
  • Expiry: keep keys long enough to cover realistic retries. Stripe, for example, documents keeping them for at least 24 hours.
  • Downstream calls: pass an idempotency key on to the card network or PSP too, so your own retries cannot double-charge.
In production

The same pattern protects any "do it exactly once" effect: sending a notification, creating a loan account, posting a ledger entry. A unique constraint on a business key ((merchant_id, idempotency_key) or (event_id)) in the database is the most reliable guard, more reliable than a Redis TTL key, because it is atomic with the write and survives restarts.

3.5REST, gRPC, and GraphQL

Try it first2 minutes

A mobile home screen needs data from 6 services. With REST it makes 6 calls over a slow network. Name two ways to fix this.

Reveal the answer

(1) A backend-for-frontend or aggregation endpoint: one call to a server that fans out to the 6 services over the fast internal network. (2) GraphQL: the client sends one query describing exactly the fields it needs and the GraphQL server resolves them.

REST (JSON over HTTP) gRPC GraphQL
Shape Resources and verbs Typed procedures from a .proto contract One endpoint; client sends a query for exact fields
Payload JSON text Protocol Buffers, binary JSON
Strengths Simple, universal, HTTP caching works Fast, typed, streaming, code generation No over-fetching, one round trip for nested data
Weaknesses Over- and under-fetching, many calls Needs HTTP/2, browsers need a proxy HTTP caching is harder, N+1 resolvers, query cost control
Best for Public APIs, web and mobile Internal service-to-service Rich clients with varied data needs
Note

N+1 in GraphQL: a query for 50 posts and each post's author can trigger 1 query for posts plus 50 for authors. Batch with a DataLoader (collect IDs, one WHERE id IN (...) query). Protect the server with query depth and cost limits.

3.6Versioning, errors, and evolution

Try it first2 minutes

Which of these changes break existing clients: adding a new optional response field, removing a field, making an optional request field required, adding a new endpoint?

Reveal the answer

Breaking: removing a field and making an optional request field required. Safe (additive): a new optional response field and a new endpoint. Clients should ignore fields they do not know (the tolerant reader rule), which is what makes additive changes safe.

  • Version in the path (/v1/orders) is the most common and easiest to route; header-based versioning keeps URLs stable but is less visible.
  • Prefer additive change inside a version; create v2 only for breaking changes, and run both until clients migrate.
  • One error format everywhere: an HTTP status plus a body like {"error": {"code": "card_declined", "message": "...", "request_id": "..."}}. The machine-readable code lets clients branch; the request ID lets support find logs.
  • Tell clients about limits: 429 with Retry-After, and headers for the current quota.
  • Optimistic concurrency: return an ETag (a version); clients send If-Match on updates; the server returns 412 if someone else changed it first.

3.7Async APIs and webhooks

Try it first2 minutes

Your API calls a partner whose response takes up to 5 minutes. How do you avoid holding the HTTP request open?

Reveal the answer

Return 202 Accepted immediately with a status URL; a worker does the slow call. The client either polls the status URL or registers a webhook URL that you call when the job finishes.

Webhooks are the server calling the client. To make them reliable:

  • Sign every payload: an HMAC-SHA256 of the body plus a timestamp, using a shared secret. The receiver recomputes it and rejects stale timestamps to stop replays.
  • Retry with backoff on non-2xx responses, for hours or days, and give the receiver a way to fetch missed events.
  • Receivers must be idempotent: the same event can arrive twice. Deduplicate by event ID.
  • Receivers should answer fast: store the event, return 200, process asynchronously.

3.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Verbs in URLs (/getUser) and actions that hide side effects behind GET.
  • Taking the user ID from the request body for "my" resources instead of from the auth token.
  • Unbounded lists with no pagination or page-size cap.
  • Offset pagination for feeds, which duplicates and skips items and slows down on deep pages.
  • Retrying POST without an idempotency key, which turns network timeouts into duplicate orders or charges.
  • Breaking changes without a new version, and clients that crash on unknown fields.

3.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Why is PUT /photos/9/likes/me a better "like" endpoint than POST /photos/9/like?
    Reveal

    PUT on a sub-resource is idempotent: liking twice leaves one like. The POST version would need extra dedup logic for retries.

  2. What should a cursor contain for a feed sorted by time?
    Reveal

    The sort key of the last item seen plus a unique tie-breaker, for example (created_at, post_id), encoded so clients treat it as opaque.

  3. Two requests with the same idempotency key arrive at the same time. What stops both from charging?
    Reveal

    An atomic claim: inserting the key with a unique constraint (or a conditional write) before doing the work. Only one insert succeeds; the other gets a conflict and waits or returns 409.

  4. When would you choose gRPC over REST?
    Reveal

    For internal service-to-service calls with high volume, strict contracts, or streaming, where binary encoding, code generation, and HTTP/2 multiplexing pay off.

  5. How does a webhook receiver know a request really came from the sender?
    Reveal

    It verifies the signature: HMAC of the payload (and timestamp) with the shared secret must match the signature header, and the timestamp must be recent.

Module 4: Back-of-the-envelope estimation

A two-minute estimate decides whether you need one database or fifty, whether the cache fits in memory, and whether you need a CDN. The skill is not precision; it is getting the order of magnitude right and saying what it implies.

8 lessons1 figures1 guided designs6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 4.1Why estimate at all
  2. 4.2Numbers to remember
  3. 4.3Estimating traffic
  4. 4.4Estimating storage
  5. 4.5Bandwidth, cache, and servers
  6. 4.6Little's Law and utilization
  7. 4.7Common mistakes
  8. 4.8Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: estimate in your head

Round hard. Within 2x is good enough.

  1. 1 million requests per day is about how many per second?
    Reveal

    About 12 per second (1,000,000 / 86,400). Remember it: 1M/day is roughly 10/s.

  2. 100M users each upload one 200 KB photo per day. Storage per day?
    Reveal

    100M x 200 KB = 20 TB per day, about 7 PB per year before replication.

  3. A service peaks at 30,000 requests/s and one server handles 2,000. How many servers?
    Reveal

    15 at peak, so run about 20 or more to survive losing a zone and to absorb spikes.

  4. Can 50M user profiles of 2 KB each fit in one Redis node's memory?
    Reveal

    50M x 2 KB = 100 GB. That fits on one large machine, but it is near the limit; shard it across a few nodes for headroom and failover.

  5. Which is faster: a network round trip inside a datacenter or a random read from an SSD?
    Reveal

    The SSD random read (tens of microseconds) is faster than a datacenter round trip (about half a millisecond). Both are about 1,000 times slower than reading memory.

4.1Why estimate at all

Try it first2 minutes

An interviewer says "1 billion URLs shortened per month, each read 100 times". Without computing exact numbers, what two design decisions might these numbers change?

Reveal the answer

(1) Storage and sharding: 1B new rows a month is 12B a year, too many to keep comfortably in one relational node for years, so plan for a horizontally scalable store or sharding. (2) Caching: about 40,000 reads per second on average is read-heavy enough that a cache in front of the database is clearly worth it.

What it decides

How many servers, whether data fits in one database or needs sharding, whether hot data fits in a cache, whether bandwidth needs a CDN, and which component is the bottleneck.

Analogy

Planning a wedding. You do not count grains of rice; you estimate guests x plates x cost per plate to decide between a hall for 100 and one for 1,000. The precision only has to be good enough to pick the hall.

How to do it

Write the formula, round every number to one significant figure, keep units visible, and state the implication out loud: "40K reads/s, so we need a cache."

4.2Numbers to remember

Try it first2 minutes

How many bytes is: a 64-bit timestamp, a UUID stored in binary, a 140-character ASCII message, a typical row for a user profile?

Reveal the answer

8 bytes; 16 bytes (36 as a text string); 140 bytes; a few hundred bytes to about 1 KB. These small sizes add up when multiplied by billions of rows.

Power Approx value Unit
2^10 1 thousand (10^3) KB
2^20 1 million (10^6) MB
2^30 1 billion (10^9) GB
2^40 1 trillion (10^12) TB
2^50 1 quadrillion (10^15) PB
Time and rates Value
Seconds in a day 86,400, round to 10^5
Seconds in a month / year about 2.5 million / about 30 million
1M requests per day about 12 per second
1B requests per day about 12,000 per second
Typical sizes Value
int / long / timestamp 4 / 8 / 8 bytes
UUID 16 bytes binary, 36 as text
URL about 100 bytes
Short post or tweet with metadata about 300 bytes to 1 KB
Compressed photo about 200 KB (thumbnail 20 KB, full 1-3 MB)
1 minute of HD video at 5 Mbps about 40 MB

Rough capacity per node

These are planning numbers for simple operations on modern hardware. Real numbers depend on payload size, query shape, and tuning, so say "roughly" and move on.

Component Rough capacity per node
Stateless API server 1,000-10,000 requests/s for light requests
PostgreSQL / MySQL primary Thousands to low tens of thousands of simple indexed queries/s; fewer writes
Redis Around 100,000 simple ops/s, more with pipelining
Kafka broker Hundreds of MB/s of messages
Cassandra node Thousands to tens of thousands of writes/s
Network card 10-25 Gbps, about 1-3 GB/s
Server memory / SSD 64-512 GB RAM, several TB of SSD

4.3Estimating traffic

Try it first2 minutes

50M daily active users each open the app 10 times a day and each open loads a feed. Average and peak feed QPS?

Reveal the answer

50M x 10 = 500M feed loads a day. 500M / 10^5 is about 5,000/s on average (exactly 5,787). Peak is commonly 2-3x the average, so plan for about 15,000/s, more if traffic spikes around events.

The formula: QPS = daily active users x actions per user per day / 86,400. Then:

  • Split reads and writes. They usually scale differently and hit different components. A 100:1 read-to-write ratio points at caching and read replicas; write-heavy points at partitioning, queues, and append-friendly storage.
  • Peak vs average. Use 2-3x for normal daily peaks; 10x or more for flash sales, ticket launches, or live events.
  • Fan-out multiplies. One post to 1,000 followers is 1 write request but 1,000 feed updates if you precompute feeds (Case study 4).

4.4Estimating storage

Try it first2 minutes

A chat app stores 20B messages a day at about 100 bytes each, for 5 years, with 3 replicas. Total storage?

Reveal the answer

20B x 100 B = 2 TB per day. x 365 x 5 = about 3.65 PB. x 3 replicas = about 11 PB. That number tells you this needs a horizontally scalable store (Cassandra, HBase, or sharded SQL) and probably cheaper storage tiers for old messages.

Storage = new items per day x size x retention days x replication. Then say what it implies:

  • Single-digit TB and a few thousand writes/s: one well-provisioned relational primary with replicas is usually fine.
  • Tens of TB, or writes beyond what one primary handles: partition the data (Module 10).
  • Large binary objects (photos, video): never in the database. Object storage holds the bytes; the database holds metadata and the object key (Module 7).
  • Indexes add space: often 20-100% on top of the raw data.

4.5Bandwidth, cache, and servers

Try it first2 minutes

Readers fetch 10,000 images per second at 200 KB each. Egress bandwidth? What does that imply?

Reveal the answer

10,000 x 200 KB = 2 GB/s, about 16 Gbps. That would saturate the network of several servers and cost a lot in egress, so put a CDN in front: most bytes then come from edge caches near users.

  • Bandwidth = QPS x response size. Gbps = GB/s x 8.
  • Cache size: many systems follow an 80/20 shape, where about 20% of items get about 80% of reads. Caching 20% of a day's read volume is a common first estimate and usually an overestimate, since repeated reads hit the same items.
  • Servers = peak QPS / QPS per server, then add headroom (run at 50-70% of capacity) and redundancy (survive losing one zone).
Estimation calculatorPrefilled with a URL shortener. Change any input; every output shows its formula.

Rounding rule: 1 day = 86,400 s, about 10^5. Use these numbers to decide things (shard or not, cache fits or not, how many servers), not to be precise.

Guided designEstimate a photo-sharing app200M daily users, 0.1 uploads and 50 views per user per day
  1. 1
    Upload and view QPS

    Compute the average and peak for both.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Uploads: 200M x 0.1 = 20M per day, about 230/s on average and about 700/s at 3x peak. Views: 200M x 50 = 10B per day, about 115,000/s on average and about 350,000/s at peak. Reads outnumber writes 500 to 1.

  2. 2
    Photo storage

    Assume about 2 MB stored per photo across all sizes. Per day and per year?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    20M x 2 MB = 40 TB per day, about 15 PB per year. Object storage handles durability internally (replication or erasure coding), so do not multiply by 3 here; do say it is the dominant cost and old photos can move to colder, cheaper tiers.

  3. 3
    Metadata storage

    About 1 KB per photo row (owner, caption, time, object key, counts).

    Write your answer, then reveal

    20M x 1 KB = 20 GB per day, about 7 TB per year. Too big for one node over several years, but small compared with the images, so a sharded relational store or a wide-column store works.

  4. 4
    Egress

    Views fetch a 200 KB display size. What bandwidth, and what does it mean?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    115,000/s x 200 KB = 23 GB/s on average, about 180 Gbps. Only a CDN can serve this economically; origin servers should see only cache misses.

  5. 5
    What the numbers decide

    Summarize the design consequences in three bullets.

    Write your answer, then reveal
    • Bytes go to object storage plus a CDN; uploads go straight to storage with presigned URLs.
    • Reads dominate: cache metadata and precompute or cache feeds.
    • Metadata needs partitioning; pick a shard key such as user_id (Module 10).
In production

Capacity planning at work uses the same arithmetic with measured inputs: take today's peak QPS from dashboards, apply the growth forecast and a safety factor, divide by per-instance throughput from a load test, and add enough redundancy to lose a zone. Re-run it before every big launch or sale.

Interview signal

Spend about 5 minutes on estimates and never leave a number without its consequence. Interviewers care far less about the exact figure than about whether it changes your design: sharding or not, cache or not, CDN or not.

4.6Little's Law and utilization

Try it first2 minutes

A service handles 2,000 requests/s and each request holds a database connection for 50 ms. How many connections are busy at any moment? What happens if the database slows to 200 ms per query?

Reveal the answer

Busy connections = throughput x time held = 2,000 x 0.05 s = 100. At 200 ms it becomes 400: the same traffic now needs 4x the connections, which is how a slow dependency exhausts pools and threads in services that call it.

  • Little's Law: items in a system = arrival rate x time each item spends in it (L = lambda x W). It holds for any stable system, so it sizes thread pools, connection pools, and consumer counts. Consumers needed = message rate x processing time per message (5,000 msg/s x 20 ms = 100 concurrent consumers).
  • Utilization drives queueing: as a server nears 100% busy, waiting time explodes. In a simple single-server queue, average wait is about service time x rho / (1 - rho), where rho is utilization:
Utilization Wait relative to service time
50% 1x
80% 4x
90% 9x
95% 19x

That curve is why capacity plans target 50-70% utilization at peak, and why latency spikes long before CPU reaches 100%.

4.7Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • False precision. "115,740.74 QPS" wastes time. Say "about 120K".
  • Dropping units. Mixing bits and bytes (Gbps vs GB/s) or KB and MB produces errors of 8x or 1,000x.
  • Forgetting peaks. Capacity is sized for the peak, not the average.
  • Estimating without a conclusion. Every number should end in "so we need..." or "so one node is enough".
  • Storing blobs in the database because the storage math was skipped.
  • Ignoring replication and indexes when sizing databases.

4.8Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. 300M daily users each post 2 messages of 1 KB. Daily storage and write QPS?
    Reveal

    600M messages x 1 KB = 600 GB per day; 600M / 86,400 is about 7,000 writes/s on average, about 20,000 at peak.

  2. Convert 2 GB/s to Gbps.
    Reveal

    16 Gbps (multiply bytes by 8).

  3. Your estimate says 4 TB of hot data and 2,000 writes/s. Do you shard on day one?
    Reveal

    Not necessarily. One strong primary with replicas can handle this; plan the shard key now so you can split later, and shard when growth projections cross one node's limits.

  4. Why add headroom on top of peak QPS / per-server QPS?
    Reveal

    Servers degrade near full utilization (queueing makes latency spike), and you must survive losing a zone or a deploy taking servers out.

  5. Read QPS is 200K/s, read size 10 KB. What is the bandwidth, and where should the reads go?
    Reveal

    2 GB/s (16 Gbps). Serve from cache and, if the content is public, a CDN; the database should see only misses.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Decode a design prompt

Every design prompt hides one or two dominant pressures: read-heavy, write-heavy, fan-out, real time, big files, money, location, spikes. Name the pressure and the building blocks follow. This page starts with six drills, then gives the method and the signal table they use.

On this page

  1. Six drills
  2. The method
  3. Signals and the blocks they point to
  4. Quick reflex quiz

Six drills

Do each drill in about 5 minutes on paper. Answer each step before revealing it. The goal is speed at spotting what matters, not a full design.

Guided designDrill 1: a pastebinUsers paste text up to 1 MB and share a link; links expire
  1. 1
    Users and core actions

    Who uses it, and what are the two or three actions?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Anyone creates a paste (write) and anyone with the link reads it (read). Optional: expiry, private pastes, syntax highlighting.

  2. 2
    Dominant pressure

    Read-heavy or write-heavy? What is unusual?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Read-heavy (each paste read many times), and the payload is a blob up to 1 MB. Expiry adds cleanup work.

  3. 3
    Building blocks

    Which blocks follow from that?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Object storage for paste bodies, a small metadata store (key, owner, expiry, object key), unique short keys (Module 17), cache plus CDN for hot pastes, a background job or TTL to delete expired pastes.

  4. 4
    The one hard problem

    What will the interviewer push on?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Key generation without collisions, and serving popular pastes cheaply (CDN with correct cache headers). It is the URL shortener plus blobs.

Guided designDrill 2: live comments on a sports stream2M viewers watch one match; comments should appear within 2 seconds
  1. 1
    Users and core actions

    What happens, and how often?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Viewers post comments (maybe 5,000/s at peaks) and every viewer sees new comments in near real time.

  2. 2
    Dominant pressure

    What is the multiplier?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Fan-out in real time: one comment must reach up to 2M open connections. Writes are modest; delivery is huge.

  3. 3
    Building blocks

    Which blocks?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    WebSocket or SSE gateways holding connections, pub/sub to fan messages to all gateways, sampling or batching (send the latest 20 comments per second, not all), a comment store for history, rate limits and moderation.

  4. 4
    The one hard problem

    Where does it break?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Pushing every comment to every viewer is impossible at peak; the answer is to batch and sample per viewer and to fan out through a tree of gateways.

Guided designDrill 3: a payment API for merchantsMerchants charge cards through your API; no double charges
  1. 1
    Users and core actions

    Who calls it and what must happen?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Merchant servers create payments; you call card networks or processors; merchants get results and webhooks.

  2. 2
    Dominant pressure

    Speed or correctness?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Correctness: exactly-once effects across unreliable networks, an auditable ledger, and partners that time out. Volume is moderate.

  3. 3
    Building blocks

    Which blocks?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Idempotency keys, a relational ledger (double entry), a payment state machine, outbox to publish events, retries with backoff to the processor, webhooks with signatures, daily reconciliation.

  4. 4
    The one hard problem

    What will be probed?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A timeout from the processor: did the charge happen? Answer with idempotent retries using the processor's idempotency key, status queries, and reconciliation.

Guided designDrill 4: nearby gymsUsers see gyms within 5 km, sorted by distance; 1M gyms, data changes rarely
  1. 1
    Dominant pressure

    What kind of query is this?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A read-heavy geospatial query over mostly static data.

  2. 2
    Building blocks

    Which blocks?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A geospatial index (geohash or quadtree, or PostGIS or Elasticsearch geo queries), read replicas or an in-memory index per region, caching of popular areas, a separate service for gym details.

  3. 3
    The one hard problem

    What detail matters?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Cell edges: query the user's cell plus neighbors, then filter by exact distance; choose cell precision from the radius.

Guided designDrill 5: a flash sale100K users try to buy 1,000 discounted phones at 12:00
  1. 1
    Dominant pressure

    Name two.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A huge spike at a known moment, and strict inventory correctness (no overselling).

  2. 2
    Building blocks

    Which blocks?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A waiting room or queue to admit users at a controlled rate, pre-scaled stateless tiers, inventory decremented atomically (a conditional update in the DB, or an atomic Redis counter reconciled with the DB), reservation with a payment timeout, CDN for static pages.

  3. 3
    The one hard problem

    What will be probed?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Preventing oversell under contention while keeping the database alive: atomic decrements, reservations that expire, and admission control in front.

Guided designDrill 6: a metrics platform100K servers send 200 metrics every 10 seconds; dashboards and alerts
  1. 1
    Dominant pressure

    Read-heavy or write-heavy?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Write-heavy: 100K x 200 / 10 = 2M data points per second, append-only, time-ordered.

  2. 2
    Building blocks

    Which blocks?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A buffer (Kafka), a time-series store (or wide-column with time buckets), downsampling (raw for days, 1-minute rollups for months), an alert evaluator, a query layer with caching for dashboards.

  3. 3
    The one hard problem

    What will be probed?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Cardinality (unique label combinations), storage cost and retention tiers, and keeping ingestion working when the query side is overloaded.

The method

Use this sequence on every prompt. It is the same order as the interview framework, compressed to what drives decisions.

Step Ask yourself Output
1. Users and actions Who uses it? What are the 3-5 core actions? What is out of scope? Functional requirements
2. Numbers How many users, actions per day, read/write ratio, data size, peak? QPS, storage, bandwidth (Module 4)
3. Qualities Latency target, availability, consistency per action, durability, compliance Non-functional requirements
4. Dominant pressure Which one or two pressures from the table below dominate? One sentence: "This is a read-heavy fan-out problem"
5. Blocks Which building blocks answer those pressures? High-level diagram
6. Hard problem Where will it break at 10x? What fails first? 2-3 deep dives
7. Trade-offs What did you give up, and why is it acceptable? Spoken trade-offs

Signals and the blocks they point to

Signal in the prompt or numbers Pressure Reach for
Same data read far more than written Read-heavy Cache-aside, read replicas, CDN, denormalized read models
Writes in the tens of thousands per second, append-only Write-heavy Kafka buffer, LSM / wide-column store, partitioning, batching
One action must reach many users (followers, viewers) Fan-out Fan-out on write or read (hybrid), pub/sub, feed cache
"Instantly", "live", chat, presence Real time WebSocket or SSE gateways, pub/sub, connection registry
Photos, video, files, documents Large objects Object storage, presigned uploads, CDN, async processing
Money, inventory, seats, "never twice" Strong correctness Relational DB transactions, conditional updates, idempotency keys, outbox, reconciliation
Users worldwide, low latency everywhere Geo-distribution CDN, geo-routing, regional replicas, data residency
Known spike moment (sale, launch, match) Spiky load Queue, waiting room, pre-scaling, load shedding
Text search, filters, relevance Query flexibility Inverted index (Elasticsearch) fed by CDC
"Near me", maps, drivers Location Geohash, quadtree, S2 or H3, in-memory grid for moving objects
Counts, top-K, trending, unique visitors Aggregation Stream processing, sharded counters, count-min sketch, HyperLogLog
Steps across services that must all happen or be undone Workflow Saga with orchestrator, state machine, compensations
Run at a time in the future, repeatedly Scheduling Time-bucketed job store, leases, idempotent jobs
Must be ordered (per account, per chat) Ordering Partition by that key; single writer per key
Reports over everything Analytics Columnar warehouse fed by CDC or batch export
IDs across many servers Coordination-free IDs Snowflake or UUIDv7
Key idea

Say the pressure out loud before drawing: "This is read-heavy with a hot-key problem for viral links, so the core is a cache in front of a key-value store." Interviewers score the reasoning, and the rest of your design becomes a consequence of it.

Quick reflex quiz

Self-checkName the dominant pressure

One line each. Then check which blocks follow.

  1. "Design Google Docs."
    Reveal

    Real-time collaboration with concurrent edits to the same object: ordering and merging (OT or CRDT), per-document session servers, WebSockets (Case study 16).

  2. "Design YouTube."
    Reveal

    Large objects and read-heavy delivery: upload and transcoding pipeline, object storage, CDN with adaptive bitrate (Case study 9).

  3. "Design a ride-hailing service."
    Reveal

    Location plus real time: frequent location updates of moving drivers, geo index in memory, matching, and a trip state machine (Case study 11).

  4. "Design Ticketmaster."
    Reveal

    Spiky load plus strong correctness: waiting room, seat holds with expiry, atomic reservation (Case study 12).

  5. "Design a web crawler."
    Reveal

    Write-heavy distributed work with politeness constraints: URL frontier, dedup with Bloom filters and content hashes, per-host rate limits (Case study 8).

  6. "Design a notification system."
    Reveal

    Fan-out and reliability across channels: queues per channel, retries, dedup, user preferences, rate limits (Case study 6).
