Phase 2: Scaling the stateless tierCore

Module 5: Scaling and load balancing

Most systems scale by running many identical, stateless copies of a service behind a load balancer. This module covers why statelessness matters, how load balancers pick a server, how to remove single points of failure, and how autoscaling keeps up with demand.

9 lessons4 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 5.1Vertical and horizontal scaling
  2. 5.2Stateless services
  3. 5.3Load balancers: L4 and L7
  4. 5.4Choosing a server: algorithms and health checks
  5. 5.5Removing single points of failure
  6. 5.6API gateways and reverse proxies
  7. 5.7Autoscaling
  8. 5.8Common mistakes
  9. 5.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Your app stores user sessions in server memory. What breaks when you add a second server behind a load balancer?
    Reveal

    A user logged in on server 1 may be sent to server 2, which has no session, so they appear logged out. Move sessions to a shared store (Redis) or use signed tokens.

  2. Requests vary from 5 ms to 5 s. Why can round robin overload one server?
    Reveal

    Round robin counts requests, not work. A server stuck with several 5 s requests keeps receiving its turn. Least connections or least outstanding requests adapts to actual load.

  3. Your single load balancer dies. What happens, and how do you prevent it?
    Reveal

    Everything behind it is unreachable. Run load balancers redundantly (managed LBs span zones; self-run ones use an active-passive pair with a floating IP).

  4. Autoscaling adds servers when CPU passes 70%. Traffic doubles in 30 seconds. Why do users still see errors?
    Reveal

    New instances take minutes to boot and warm up. Scaling reacts after demand rises, so keep headroom, scale on a leading metric, or pre-scale for known events.

  5. When is buying a bigger machine the right answer?
    Reveal

    When it is cheaper than the complexity of distributing: databases that are hard to shard, small systems, or a quick fix while you redesign. It has a ceiling and keeps a single point of failure.

5.1Vertical and horizontal scaling

Try it first2 minutes

A database server at 90% CPU. Option A: move to a machine with 4x the cores. Option B: add 3 more database servers. What does each cost you?

Reveal the answer

A (vertical) is simple: no code change, no distributed data. But it has a hardware ceiling, gets expensive at the top end, and is still one machine that can fail. B (horizontal) scales further and survives failures, but the data must be replicated or partitioned, which brings consistency and routing problems (Modules 9 and 10).

Vertical (scale up) Horizontal (scale out)
How Bigger CPU, more RAM, faster disk More machines
Code changes None Service must be stateless, or data must be partitioned
Ceiling The biggest machine you can buy Practically none
Failure Still a single machine Survives losing nodes
Cost curve Rises steeply at the high end Roughly linear
Good for Databases early on, quick fixes Stateless services, large data, high availability
Key idea

Stateless services scale horizontally almost for free. Stateful systems (databases, caches, queues) are where scaling gets hard, which is why most of this handbook is about data.

5.2Stateless services

Try it first2 minutes

List every place a typical web server might keep state between requests.

Reveal the answer

In-memory sessions, local file uploads, in-process caches, scheduled jobs that run on "the" server, WebSocket connections, and local counters (for example a rate limit counted in memory). Each one breaks when requests for the same user land on different servers.

Idea

A stateless service keeps nothing between requests that another copy would need. Any instance can serve any request, so the load balancer can send traffic anywhere and you can add, remove, or replace instances freely.

Analogy

A bank with many tellers. Any teller can serve you because your account lives in the bank's central ledger, not in one teller's notebook.

Where state goes

Sessions in Redis or in a signed token (JWT) carried by the client; files in object storage; shared caches in Redis; durable data in the database; scheduled jobs in a distributed scheduler with a lock (Case study 14).

Sticky sessions (the LB keeps sending a user to the same server, by cookie or IP hash) is a shortcut that keeps state on servers. It works, but load becomes uneven, and when that server dies its users lose their sessions. Prefer external state; use stickiness only as an optimization (for example to keep a warm local cache), never for correctness.

5.3Load balancers: L4 and L7

Try it first2 minutes

You want /api/* to go to API servers and /images/* to go to image servers behind one domain. Which kind of load balancer can do that, and why?

Reveal the answer

An L7 (application) load balancer. Routing by URL path requires reading the HTTP request, which means terminating TLS and parsing HTTP. An L4 load balancer only sees IP addresses and ports.

L4 (transport) L7 (application)
Sees IP, port, TCP/UDP Full HTTP: path, headers, cookies
Balances Connections Individual requests
Features Very fast, protocol-agnostic, preserves client connection Path and header routing, TLS termination, retries, compression, auth hooks, WebSocket upgrade
Examples AWS NLB, Google TCP/UDP LB, LVS, HAProxy in TCP mode AWS ALB, NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy in HTTP mode
Pick when Non-HTTP traffic, extreme throughput, pass-through TLS Web and API traffic, microservice routing, gRPC

5.4Choosing a server: algorithms and health checks

Try it first2 minutes

Three servers have 4, 9, and 2 requests in flight. Where does round robin send the next request if it is server B's turn? Where should it go?

Reveal the answer

Round robin sends it to B because it is B's turn, even though B is the busiest. It should go to C, which has the fewest requests in flight. That is what least connections (or least outstanding requests) does.

Algorithm How it picks Good for Watch out
Round robin Next server in order Uniform, short requests Ignores load and server size
Weighted round robin In order, more turns for bigger servers Mixed hardware, canary at 5% Weights are static
Least connections / least requests Fewest in flight Uneven request durations Needs accurate counts
Power of two choices Pick 2 at random, use the less loaded Many LB nodes with partial information Slightly less exact, avoids herding
IP hash / consistent hash Hash of client IP or a key Session affinity, cache locality Uneven if keys are skewed
Least response time Lowest recent latency Latency-sensitive traffic Can oscillate

Health checks keep traffic away from broken servers:

  • Active: the LB calls /health every few seconds and removes a server after N failures, adding it back after M successes.
  • Passive (outlier detection): the LB watches real traffic and ejects servers that return too many errors or time out.
  • Readiness vs liveness (Kubernetes): failing readiness takes a pod out of the load balancer (it is warming up or overloaded); failing liveness restarts it (it is stuck). A health endpoint that checks the database can take every pod out at once when the database blips, so keep readiness checks about the instance itself.
  • Connection draining: on deploy or scale-in, stop sending new requests to an instance and let in-flight ones finish before killing it.

5.5Removing single points of failure

Try it first2 minutes

You have 10 app servers behind one load balancer and one database. List the single points of failure and a fix for each.

Reveal the answer

The load balancer (run redundant LB nodes across zones or use a managed LB), the database (a standby replica with automatic failover), the zone or datacenter they all sit in (spread across availability zones), and DNS or the certificate if managed by hand (use managed DNS, automate renewals).

  • Redundancy at every tier: at least N+1 instances, spread across availability zones (separate power and network within a region).
  • Load balancers themselves: cloud LBs are already distributed across zones. Self-run ones use an active-passive pair sharing a virtual IP (keepalived/VRRP): if the active one stops sending heartbeats, the passive one takes the IP.
  • Across regions: GeoDNS or anycast sends users to the nearest healthy region (global server load balancing). Region failover also needs the data to be there (Module 15).
  • Availability multiplies: two components in series, each 99.9%, give about 99.8%. Two redundant copies in parallel, each 99.9%, give about 99.9999% if their failures are independent. Module 15 has a calculator.

5.6API gateways and reverse proxies

Try it first2 minutes

Ten microservices each implement their own authentication, rate limiting, and request logging. What is the problem, and where should that logic live?

Reveal the answer

Duplicated, inconsistent cross-cutting logic: one service forgets a check, versions drift, and fixing a bug means 10 deploys. Put it in an API gateway (the single front door) and keep services focused on business logic.

An API gateway is an L7 reverse proxy with API features: authentication and token validation, rate limiting and quotas, routing to services, request and response transformation, TLS termination, request IDs, and sometimes response caching or aggregation. Examples: Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway, Envoy-based gateways.

  • A backend for frontend (BFF) is a gateway per client type (web, iOS, partner API) that shapes responses for that client.
  • Keep the gateway thin. Business logic in the gateway turns it into a bottleneck every team must change.
  • The gateway is on every request, so it must be redundant and fast, and it must fail predictably (Module 15).

5.7Autoscaling

Try it first2 minutes

Why is "scale out when CPU is above 70% for 5 minutes" too slow for a flash sale that starts at 12:00 sharp?

Reveal the answer

Demand jumps in seconds; the metric needs 5 minutes to trigger, and new instances need minutes to start and warm caches. Pre-scale before the known event (scheduled scaling), keep headroom, and put a queue or waiting room in front of the hottest path (Case study 12).

  • Scale on a metric that tracks load: CPU, requests per instance, queue length (best for workers), or p99 latency.
  • Target tracking: "keep average CPU near 60%" adds and removes instances to hold the target.
  • Cooldowns and limits: avoid flapping (adding and removing repeatedly); set a maximum so a bug or attack cannot scale you into a huge bill.
  • Scale-in carefully: drain connections and finish in-flight jobs before terminating.
  • Scheduled or predictive scaling for daily peaks and known events.
  • Remember the dependencies: doubling app servers doubles the connections to the database. Scale the bottleneck, not just the easy tier.
In production

On Kubernetes, a Service plus an Ingress or Gateway gives you L4 and L7 balancing, readiness probes decide which pods receive traffic, and the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales on CPU or custom metrics such as queue lag. Size database connection pools so that max pods x pool size stays under the database's connection limit, or put PgBouncer in between.

Interview signal

Say "stateless services behind a load balancer, spread across zones" early in every design, then spend your time on the stateful parts. Interviewers check that you remove single points of failure without being asked.

5.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Sessions, files, or counters in server memory, then adding a load balancer and wondering why users get logged out.
  • Health checks that call the database: one database blip removes every instance from the load balancer.
  • A single load balancer, NAT gateway, or database in a design that claims high availability.
  • Round robin for very uneven request costs.
  • Autoscaling the app tier into a database connection storm. Use connection pooling (PgBouncer) and size pools to the database's limit.
  • Business logic in the API gateway.

5.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Why is an L7 load balancer needed for gRPC services?
    Reveal

    gRPC multiplexes many calls over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection. An L4 LB pins the whole connection to one backend; an L7 LB balances individual calls.

  2. What is the difference between readiness and liveness checks?
    Reveal

    Readiness decides whether the instance gets traffic (out of the LB while starting or overloaded). Liveness decides whether it is restarted (stuck or deadlocked).

  3. Two components in series each have 99.9% availability. What is the combined availability?
    Reveal

    0.999 x 0.999 = about 99.8%. Series chains lose availability with every component.

  4. What problem does "power of two choices" solve?
    Reveal

    With many load balancer nodes each picking the globally least-loaded server, they all pick the same one and overload it (herding). Picking the better of two random servers spreads load well with little coordination.

  5. When are sticky sessions acceptable?
    Reveal

    As a performance optimization (cache locality, a WebSocket that must stay on one server) when losing the stickiness does not break correctness, because the real state lives elsewhere.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Module 6: Caching

A cache keeps a copy of hot data somewhere faster than its source. It is the cheapest way to cut latency and database load, and the easiest way to serve wrong data. This module covers where to cache, how to read and write through a cache, how to keep it fresh, and how caches fail.

9 lessons4 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 6.1Why caching works
  2. 6.2Where to cache
  3. 6.3Reading and writing through a cache
  4. 6.4Invalidation and consistency
  5. 6.5Eviction
  6. 6.6When caches fail
  7. 6.7Redis essentials
  8. 6.8Common mistakes
  9. 6.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Reads are 100K/s. Cache hit ratio goes from 90% to 99%. What happens to database read load?
    Reveal

    It drops 10x, from 10K/s to 1K/s. The miss rate, not the hit rate, decides database load.

  2. After updating a user's name in the database, should you update the cached value or delete it?
    Reveal

    Usually delete it. The next read reloads the current value. Updating the cache from the writer races with other writers and can leave an older value in the cache.

  3. A popular key expires and 5,000 requests miss at once. What is this called and what is one fix?
    Reveal

    A cache stampede (thundering herd). Fix: let one request reload the key while the others wait or get the stale value (single-flight), or refresh hot keys before they expire.

  4. Attackers request random IDs that do not exist, so every request misses the cache and hits the database. Fix?
    Reveal

    Cache negative results (an empty marker with a short TTL) and reject impossible IDs early, for example with a Bloom filter of valid IDs.

  5. Why put a small in-process cache in front of Redis for a few extremely hot keys?
    Reveal

    One Redis node holds each key, so a very hot key overloads that one node. A local copy on every app server spreads the load, at the cost of a few seconds of staleness.

6.1Why caching works

Try it first2 minutes

A page needs a database query that takes 20 ms; a Redis read takes 1 ms. With a 95% hit ratio, what is the average latency? What is it at 80%?

Reveal the answer

Average = hit x 1 ms + miss x (1 ms + 20 ms). At 95%: 0.95 x 1 + 0.05 x 21 = about 2 ms. At 80%: 0.8 x 1 + 0.2 x 21 = about 5 ms. Small changes in hit ratio move both latency and database load a lot.

Idea

Access patterns are skewed: a small fraction of items gets most of the reads (popular products, celebrity profiles, today's posts). Keep those in memory and most requests never reach the slow store.

Analogy

A chef keeps salt, oil, and onions on the counter and everything else in the storeroom. The counter is small but serves most reaches. Deciding what earns counter space and when to throw out stale items is the whole art.

Cost

Every cache is a second copy of the data, so it can be stale. Caching is a trade of freshness for speed; decide per piece of data how stale is acceptable.

  • Hit ratio = hits / (hits + misses). Database load = miss ratio x read QPS.
  • Cache data that is read often, changes rarely, and is expensive to compute or fetch.
  • Do not cache data that must be exactly current for correctness (an account balance used to approve a payment) unless the cache is part of a consistent design.

6.2Where to cache

Try it first2 minutes

For each, pick a cache layer: (a) product images, (b) a user's session, (c) a currency-rate table used in every request, (d) the rendered public home page.

Reveal the answer

(a) CDN. (b) Distributed cache (Redis). (c) In-process cache on each server, refreshed every minute: tiny, read constantly, tolerates a little staleness. (d) CDN or reverse proxy cache, with a short TTL.

Layer Holds Freshness control
Browser / app Static files, API responses with cache headers Cache-Control, ETag; you cannot purge it
CDN Static assets, public pages, video segments TTL plus purge API (Module 7)
Reverse proxy Whole responses TTL, purge
In-process Tiny, very hot, mostly static data Short TTL; each server has its own copy
Distributed (Redis, Memcached) Objects, sessions, computed results, counters TTL plus explicit delete; shared by all servers
Database buffer pool Pages of tables and indexes Automatic; always consistent

6.3Reading and writing through a cache

Try it first3 minutes

Writes must be fast, and losing the last second of writes on a crash is acceptable. Reads are mostly of data written recently. Which write pattern fits?

Reveal the answer

Write-behind (write-back): write to the cache, return immediately, and flush to the database asynchronously in batches. Fast writes and recent data is already cached, at the cost of possible loss if the cache dies before flushing. Counters, view counts, and analytics events fit; payments do not.

Pattern Read Write Strengths Weaknesses
Cache-aside (lazy loading) App reads cache; on miss reads DB and fills cache App writes DB, then deletes cache key Simple; cache holds only what is read; cache failure is survivable First read after a write misses; stale-set races (below)
Read-through App reads only the cache; the cache loads from DB on miss Usually combined with one of the write patterns Loading logic in one place Cache must know how to load
Write-through Cache is always populated for written keys Write goes to cache and DB synchronously Reads after writes are fresh Slower writes; caches data that may never be read
Write-behind (write-back) As above Write to cache; flush to DB asynchronously Very fast writes, batching Data loss if the cache fails before the flush; harder consistency
Write-around Filled on read miss Write straight to DB, skip the cache Avoids filling the cache with write-once data Reads right after writes miss
Key idea

Default answer for most read-heavy services: cache-aside with a TTL, delete on write. Mention write-through when reads right after writes must be fast, and write-behind only when you can tolerate loss.

6.4Invalidation and consistency

Try it first3 minutes

With cache-aside, a writer updates the database and deletes the key. How can the cache still end up holding the old value?

Reveal the answer

A reader missed the cache and read the old value from the database just before the write. It then paused (GC, slow network). Meanwhile the writer updated the database and deleted the key. The reader wakes up and sets the old value into the cache, where it stays until the TTL expires.

Ways to bound or remove staleness, from simplest:

  1. Always set a TTL. It is the safety net that limits any bug or race to N seconds.
  2. Delete, do not update, on write. Two concurrent writers updating the cache can apply in the wrong order; a delete cannot.
  3. Delayed double delete: delete, then delete again a short time later, to catch a racing reader. Cheap, not a guarantee.
  4. Versioned values: store a version with the value and only overwrite with a newer version (a conditional set or Lua script).
  5. Leases: on a miss the cache hands the reader a token; a delete invalidates outstanding tokens, so the late set is rejected. Facebook's memcache uses this.
  6. Invalidate from the database's change log (CDC, Module 13): a consumer reads committed changes and deletes affected keys, so no write path can forget.
In production

"How stale is acceptable?" is a product question. A profile picture can be 5 minutes old; a card's available credit limit shown before a purchase should come from the source of truth or from a cache updated in the same flow. Write the staleness budget next to each cached item in the design doc.

6.5Eviction

Try it first2 minutes

A cache has room for 1 million items and receives a nightly batch job that scans 50 million items once. Why can LRU behave badly here, and what helps?

Reveal the answer

The scan touches 50M items once each, and LRU evicts the genuinely hot items to make room for items that will never be read again (cache pollution). LFU-style policies keep frequently used items, and many systems skip the cache for bulk scans entirely (write-around, or a separate connection that bypasses caching).

Policy Evicts Good for
LRU (least recently used) Item not used for the longest time Most workloads with recency
LFU (least frequently used) Item used least often Stable popularity; resists one-off scans
FIFO Oldest inserted Simple, rarely best
TTL-based Items past their expiry first Time-bound data
Random Any item Cheap; surprisingly decent

In Redis, maxmemory caps memory and maxmemory-policy picks the policy: allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for a pure cache, volatile-* variants to evict only keys that have a TTL. The default is noeviction, which returns errors on writes when memory is full, the right choice when Redis holds data you cannot lose. Redis approximates LRU and LFU by sampling keys, which is cheap and close enough.

6.6When caches fail

Try it first2 minutes

At midnight, a deploy flushes the whole cache. Within seconds the database is at 100% CPU and timing out. Name the problem and two fixes.

Reveal the answer

A cold cache (and a cache avalanche): every request misses at once. Fixes: warm the cache before taking traffic (preload hot keys), roll out gradually so only part of the fleet is cold, and rate-limit or queue requests to the database so it degrades rather than collapses.

Problem What happens Fixes
Stampede (thundering herd) A hot key expires; thousands of requests miss together and all query the DB Single-flight per key; a short lock so one request rebuilds; serve stale while one refreshes; refresh hot keys early (probabilistic early expiry)
Avalanche Many keys expire at the same moment, or the cache restarts Add random jitter to TTLs; warm up; replicate the cache; circuit-break DB calls
Penetration Requests for keys that do not exist always miss Cache "not found" with a short TTL; Bloom filter of valid keys; validate input
Hot key One key gets a huge share of traffic and saturates its node In-process cache for that key; replicate it under several keys (k#1..k#N) and read a random copy
Big key One value is megabytes (a huge list); slow to read and move Split it; paginate; store large blobs elsewhere

6.7Redis essentials

Try it first2 minutes

Which Redis structure fits each: (a) a game leaderboard, (b) a set of users online now, (c) unique visitor count of about 100M IDs using little memory, (d) a per-user object with 10 fields.

Reveal the answer

(a) Sorted set (ZADD, ZRANGE ... REV, ZREVRANK). (b) Set, or keys with TTL refreshed by heartbeats. (c) HyperLogLog (about 12 KB per counter, under 1% standard error). (d) Hash.

Structure Use it for
String Cached objects, counters (INCR), locks (SET key val NX PX 30000)
Hash Objects with fields, updated field by field
List Queues, recent items (LPUSH + LTRIM)
Set Membership, tags, unique items
Sorted set Leaderboards, rankings, time-ordered feeds, sliding-window rate limits
Stream Append-only log with consumer groups (light Kafka-like use)
HyperLogLog Approximate unique counts
Bitmap Daily active flags per user ID
Geo Nearby search by radius

How Redis behaves, in the points interviews probe:

  • Commands execute on one thread, so each command is atomic. Multi-step logic made atomic with MULTI/EXEC or a Lua script (used for rate limiters, Case study 2). Newer versions use extra threads for network I/O, but command execution stays single-threaded.
  • Persistence is optional: RDB snapshots (periodic, may lose minutes) and AOF (append-only log, typically fsync every second, so up to about a second of loss).
  • Replication is asynchronous: a failover can lose recently acknowledged writes. Redis Sentinel automates failover for a primary and its replicas.
  • Redis Cluster shards keys over 16,384 hash slots (CRC16(key) mod 16384). Multi-key commands work only within one slot; a hash tag like {user:7}:cart forces related keys into the same slot.
  • Valkey is the open-source, Redis-compatible fork that many managed cache services now offer; everything here applies to it.
  • Memcached is the simpler alternative: multithreaded, strings only, no persistence or replication, sharded by the client. Fine for pure caching; Redis wins when you need data structures.
Watch out

Do not treat Redis as a database of record unless you have designed for its durability model (AOF with fsync, replicas, and an accepted loss window). As a cache, design so a full Redis loss is survivable: slower, not wrong.

Interview signal

For every cache you add, state four things: what is cached and its key, the pattern (usually cache-aside), the TTL and staleness budget, and what happens on a miss storm or cache outage. That checklist covers most caching follow-ups.

6.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • No TTL. Every bug and race then lives forever.
  • Updating the cache on write instead of deleting, so concurrent writes leave old values.
  • Caching without a staleness budget for each data type.
  • Forgetting the cold start: a flushed cache or new region sends full load to the database.
  • One huge hot key on one Redis node with no local cache or key replication.
  • Assuming the cache is always up. If Redis is down, the service should degrade (read from the DB with a rate limit), not crash.
  • Caching personalized responses in a shared CDN without varying the cache key by user: one user's data served to another.

6.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Why does cache-aside delete the key on write instead of setting the new value?
    Reveal

    Setting from the write path races with other writers and with readers repopulating old values; deleting forces the next read to load the current committed value.

  2. Write-through vs write-behind: which can lose data, and when?
    Reveal

    Write-behind. Writes are acknowledged after reaching the cache; if the cache fails before flushing to the database, those writes are lost.

  3. How do you stop a stampede on a hot key?
    Reveal

    Let one caller rebuild (single-flight or a short lock) while others wait or serve the stale value; refresh before expiry; add jitter to TTLs.

  4. In Redis Cluster, why might MGET user:1 user:2 fail, and how do you fix it?
    Reveal

    The keys may hash to different slots on different nodes. Use a hash tag so related keys share a slot, or fetch them separately.

  5. Your service must survive a total Redis outage. What does the design need?
    Reveal

    Timeouts and a circuit breaker on cache calls, a fallback to the database protected by rate limits or load shedding, and no data that exists only in Redis.

Mastery checklist

Module 7: CDN and object storage

Files, images, video, backups, and exports do not belong in your database or on your app servers. They live in object storage and reach users through a CDN. This module covers the storage types, direct uploads with presigned URLs, how CDNs cache, and how to control cost and freshness.

7 lessons2 figures5 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 7.1Block, file, and object storage
  2. 7.2Uploads and downloads with presigned URLs
  3. 7.3How a CDN works
  4. 7.4Serving images and video
  5. 7.5Cost, retention, and security
  6. 7.6Common mistakes
  7. 7.7Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Where do you store 5 PB of user photos, and where do you store the photo's caption and owner?
    Reveal

    Bytes in object storage (S3, GCS); metadata (owner, caption, object key, status) in a database. Never put large blobs in the database.

  2. A 2 GB video upload through your API servers ties up threads and bandwidth. Better design?
    Reveal

    The API returns a presigned URL and the client uploads straight to object storage, in parts, so it can resume. Your servers only handle small metadata requests.

  3. You deploy new CSS but users still get the old file from the CDN for a day. How do you avoid this next time?
    Reveal

    Put a content hash or version in the file name (app.3f9a1c.css) and cache it for a year. A new deploy references a new file name, so nothing needs purging.

  4. Private documents must be downloadable through the CDN only by their owner. How?
    Reveal

    Signed URLs (or signed cookies): the app issues a short-lived URL with a signature that the CDN verifies before serving.

  5. Why does a CDN help even for content that cannot be cached?
    Reveal

    Users terminate TCP and TLS at a nearby edge (fewer long round trips), and the edge keeps warm, optimized connections to your origin.

7.1Block, file, and object storage

Try it first2 minutes

Match each to a storage type: (a) a PostgreSQL data directory, (b) a shared folder that several servers mount, (c) 100 million user-uploaded images.

Reveal the answer

(a) Block storage (a disk volume, like EBS or a local NVMe SSD): low latency, random writes. (b) File storage (NFS, EFS, Filestore): a shared file system with directories. (c) Object storage (S3, GCS): cheap, durable, effectively unlimited, accessed by key over HTTP.

Block File Object
Looks like A raw disk A shared folder tree A huge key-value store of files
Access Mounted by one server, random reads and writes Mounted by many servers via NFS/SMB HTTP API: PUT, GET, DELETE by key
Latency Lowest (sub-millisecond) Low Higher (tens of milliseconds to first byte)
Scale and cost Limited per volume, priciest per GB Medium Effectively unlimited, cheapest per GB
Typical use Databases, OS disks Legacy apps, shared configs Images, video, backups, logs, data lakes

What to know about object storage (S3 as the example):

  • Flat namespace: a bucket holds objects under keys like photos/2026/10/abc.jpg; the slashes are just characters, not real directories.
  • Objects are replaced whole: no in-place edits. To change a file, write a new version. S3 also supports conditional writes (If-None-Match: * to create only if absent, If-Match for compare-and-swap), useful for simple locks and manifests.
  • Very durable: S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability by storing data redundantly across multiple facilities.
  • Strong read-after-write consistency for S3 since 2020: after a successful PUT, reads see the new object.
  • Storage classes and lifecycle rules: move objects to cheaper infrequent-access or archive tiers after N days, and delete them after the retention period.
  • Versioning and object lock protect against accidental deletes and support write-once retention for compliance.

7.2Uploads and downloads with presigned URLs

Try it first3 minutes

Design photo upload so that app servers never handle the image bytes, the photo is resized after upload, and the app knows when it is ready.

Reveal the answer
  1. Client asks the API to start an upload; API creates a metadata row with status = pending and returns a presigned PUT URL for a specific key.
  2. Client PUTs the bytes directly to object storage.
  3. Storage emits an "object created" event to a queue; a worker validates, scans, and generates sizes.
  4. Worker updates metadata to ready with the keys of each size; the client polls or receives a push.
  • A presigned URL is a normal storage URL plus a signature and expiry, created with the server's credentials. Whoever holds it can do exactly one thing (PUT this key, or GET this key) until it expires.
  • Large files go in parts (S3 multipart upload, GCS resumable upload): each part is retried on its own, and parts can upload in parallel.
  • Validate after upload, not before: check type, size, and malware in the worker, since the client controls the bytes.
  • Downloads of private files use presigned GET URLs or CDN signed URLs, so authorization stays in your API while bytes flow from storage or the CDN.

7.3How a CDN works

Try it first2 minutes

A user in Mumbai fetches an image stored in a US region. Without a CDN each request costs about 250 ms of round trips. What does a CDN change for the first request and for the next one?

Reveal the answer

The first request goes to the nearby Mumbai edge, which misses and fetches from the origin (still slow, but the TLS handshake ended nearby). The edge caches the image; the next request from anyone near Mumbai is served in about 10-20 ms without touching the origin.

Pull CDN Push CDN
How content arrives Edge fetches from origin on the first miss You upload content to the CDN ahead of time
Good for Most websites and APIs; long-tail content Large, predictable files (game patches, software releases)
Downside First request per edge is slow You manage what is where; storage costs

Controlling what the CDN caches:

  • Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable for versioned static files (hash in the file name). They never need purging.
  • s-maxage sets the TTL for shared caches (the CDN) separately from browsers.
  • no-cache means "store it, but revalidate before each use" (with ETag / If-None-Match, a 304 is cheap). no-store means "never store it", for sensitive responses.
  • Cache key: by default the URL. Adding headers or cookies to the key (for language or device) splits the cache; never cache per-user responses under a shared key.
  • Purge / invalidation removes content early, but takes time to reach all edges. Versioned URLs avoid needing it.
  • Stale-while-revalidate: serve the cached copy while fetching a fresh one in the background.
In production

CDNs do more than cache: TLS termination near users, DDoS absorption, a web application firewall (WAF), bot filtering, image resizing at the edge, and edge functions. For an API, a CDN in front often cuts latency even at a 0% cache hit rate because the long-haul connection to origin is kept warm.

7.4Serving images and video

Try it first2 minutes

An app shows each photo at 4 sizes. Should you resize at upload time or on request?

Reveal the answer

Both are valid. Pre-generating at upload (in the worker) makes reads simple and fast and costs storage for every size. Resizing on request at the edge (an image CDN or a resize service behind the CDN, cached after the first hit) saves storage and supports new sizes without reprocessing, but the first request per size is slow. Common choice: pre-generate the few standard sizes, resize on demand for rare ones.

  • Images: store the original; serve resized, compressed variants (WebP or AVIF where supported) from the CDN.
  • Video: transcode each upload into several resolutions and bitrates and cut each into short segments (2-10 s). A manifest lists the variants; the player switches quality per segment based on bandwidth. This is adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS or MPEG-DASH), and every segment is a cacheable CDN object. Case study 9 designs the full pipeline.

7.5Cost, retention, and security

Try it first2 minutes

Regulation requires keeping statement files for 7 years, but users only open files from the last 3 months. How do you keep the cost low?

Reveal the answer

A lifecycle policy: keep recent files in the standard tier, move them to an infrequent-access tier after about 90 days and to an archive tier after a year, and delete after 7 years. Add object lock (write-once) if regulation requires that files cannot be altered or deleted early.

  • Storage tiers trade retrieval speed and fees for a lower monthly price. Archive tiers can take minutes to hours to restore.
  • Egress is often the biggest bill. Serving through a CDN reduces origin egress; keep compute in the same region as the bucket.
  • Encrypt at rest with keys from a key management service (server-side encryption with KMS); restrict buckets to private and grant access through presigned URLs and IAM roles, never public listing.
  • Checksums (MD5 or CRC) on upload detect corruption; store them in metadata for later verification.
Interview signal

Whenever a design involves files, say three things without being asked: bytes go to object storage and never through your API servers (presigned URLs), metadata goes to a database, and reads go through a CDN with versioned URLs. Then spend your time on processing and cost.

7.6Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Blobs in the database or on app server disks.
  • Uploading through your API servers instead of directly to storage.
  • Trusting the client's file type and size without validating after upload.
  • Overwriting files at the same URL and relying on CDN purges; use versioned names.
  • Caching personalized or private content at a shared CDN key.
  • Public buckets for convenience.
  • Ignoring egress and tiering, which dominate storage cost at scale.

7.7Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What exactly does a presigned URL grant?
    Reveal

    One operation (for example PUT or GET) on one object key until an expiry time, authorized by a signature made with the server's credentials.

  2. Pull vs push CDN: which suits a news site with millions of articles?
    Reveal

    Pull. The CDN fetches articles on demand and caches the popular ones; pushing millions of rarely read pages ahead of time is wasteful.

  3. What does an origin shield protect against?
    Reveal

    Many edge locations missing on the same object at the same time and each fetching it from the origin. The shield collapses them into one origin fetch.

  4. Difference between no-cache and no-store?
    Reveal

    no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation before use. no-store forbids storing at all.

  5. How does adaptive bitrate streaming fit a CDN well?
    Reveal

    Video is split into small segment files per quality level, each a normal cacheable object, so the CDN serves them like any static file and the player picks quality per segment.

Module 8: Databases and data models

The database is usually the hardest part of a design to change and the first to become a bottleneck. This module covers transactions and isolation, locking, indexes, how storage engines trade read speed for write speed, the NoSQL families, and how to choose.

10 lessons5 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 8.1Relational databases and ACID
  2. 8.2Isolation levels and anomalies
  3. 8.3Locking: pessimistic and optimistic
  4. 8.4Indexes
  5. 8.5Storage engines: B-trees and LSM trees
  6. 8.6The NoSQL families
  7. 8.7Choosing a database
  8. 8.8Data modeling for scale
  9. 8.9Common mistakes
  10. 8.10Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Two users buy the last item at the same moment and both succeed. Name the bug and one fix.
    Reveal

    A race on read-modify-write (lost update / oversell). Fix with an atomic conditional update: UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0, and treat 0 rows updated as sold out.

  2. Why does adding an index make writes slower?
    Reveal

    Every insert, update, or delete must also update each index on the table. Reads get faster; writes do more work.

  3. Which storage engine design is better for very write-heavy workloads such as event logs?
    Reveal

    An LSM tree (Cassandra, RocksDB): writes are sequential appends to a log and memory, flushed in batches. B-trees (PostgreSQL, MySQL) update pages in place, which costs more random I/O per write.

  4. You need "all orders by customer, newest first" and "monthly revenue by city across 2 billion orders". Same database?
    Reveal

    Usually not. The first is OLTP (row store with an index on customer and time). The second is OLAP (a columnar warehouse such as BigQuery, Redshift, or ClickHouse), fed from the OLTP database.

  5. When is a document database a better fit than SQL?
    Reveal

    When data is naturally a self-contained aggregate read and written as a whole (a product with variable attributes, a user's settings) and you rarely join across aggregates.

8.1Relational databases and ACID

Try it first2 minutes

A transfer moves 500 from account A to B: debit A, credit B. The server crashes between the two statements. What should the database guarantee, and which ACID letter is that?

Reveal the answer

Atomicity: either both changes commit or neither does. After the crash, recovery rolls back the partial transaction, so money is neither lost nor created. Durability then guarantees that once the commit is acknowledged, it survives the crash.

Idea

Data in tables of rows and columns with a fixed schema, related by keys and combined with joins. SQL lets you ask new questions without redesigning storage.

Analogy

A well-run accounts office with ledgers that cross-reference each other. Every entry follows the format, and a transaction either makes all its ledger entries or none.

Default

For most new systems, PostgreSQL or MySQL is the right default until numbers or access patterns say otherwise. They scale further than most people expect, especially with replicas, caching, and good indexes.

Letter Guarantee How databases provide it
Atomicity All statements in a transaction commit, or none do Undo/redo logs; rollback on failure
Consistency Constraints and invariants hold before and after (unique keys, foreign keys, checks) Constraints plus correct application logic
Isolation Concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work, to the chosen level Locks or multi-version concurrency control (MVCC)
Durability A committed transaction survives crashes Write-ahead log flushed to disk before commit is acknowledged; replicas
Note

"Consistency" in ACID means "invariants hold". It is a different idea from "consistency" in CAP (every reader sees the latest write, Module 11). Interviewers like to check that you keep them apart.

8.2Isolation levels and anomalies

Try it first3 minutes

Two on-call doctors both open the app. Each checks "at least 2 doctors on call?" (yes), then marks themselves off call. Both commits succeed. Now nobody is on call. No row was written by both. Which anomaly is this, and which isolation level prevents it?

Reveal the answer

Write skew: each transaction read the same condition, then wrote a different row, and together they broke the rule. Snapshot isolation (PostgreSQL "repeatable read") allows it. Serializable prevents it, or you can lock the rows you read (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or move the rule into a single row you both update.

Anomaly What goes wrong
Dirty read Reading another transaction's uncommitted change, which may roll back
Non-repeatable read (read skew) Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values
Phantom Re-running a query and getting new rows that another transaction inserted
Lost update Two read-modify-write cycles overwrite each other
Write skew Two transactions read overlapping data, then write different rows, breaking an invariant together
Level Prevents Still allows Notes
Read committed Dirty reads and writes Non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates, write skew Default in PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server
Repeatable read / snapshot isolation Above plus non-repeatable reads Write skew (and, depending on engine, some phantoms or lost updates) Default in MySQL InnoDB. PostgreSQL's version is snapshot isolation and aborts one of two concurrent updates to the same row
Serializable All of the above Nothing; the result equals some serial order PostgreSQL uses serializable snapshot isolation (aborts conflicting transactions, so clients must retry)
Key idea

In design interviews, say which operations need protection and how: "Booking a seat uses a conditional update on the seat row, so two buyers cannot both win." That is more convincing than naming an isolation level for the whole database.

8.3Locking: pessimistic and optimistic

Try it first2 minutes

Ten workers poll a jobs table for pending jobs. How do you make each job go to exactly one worker without workers blocking each other?

Reveal the answer

SELECT ... FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, then mark them running in the same transaction. Each worker locks a different set of rows and skips rows already locked by others.

Pessimistic locking Optimistic concurrency control
Idea Lock the row before changing it; others wait Read a version; write only if the version is unchanged
SQL SELECT ... FOR UPDATE UPDATE ... SET v = v + 1 WHERE id = ? AND v = ? (0 rows = conflict, retry)
Best when Conflicts are frequent; the critical section is short Conflicts are rare; many readers
Risks Waiting, deadlocks, locks held across slow calls Retry storms under heavy contention
  • Never hold a database lock across a network call to another service; a slow call then blocks everyone.
  • Deadlocks happen when two transactions lock rows in opposite orders. Lock in a consistent order (for example by ID) and keep transactions short. Databases detect deadlocks and abort one transaction.
  • SKIP LOCKED turns a table into a simple work queue; NOWAIT fails immediately instead of waiting.

8.4Indexes

Try it first2 minutes

A table has an index on (customer_id, created_at). Which queries can use it efficiently: (a) WHERE customer_id = 5 ORDER BY created_at DESC, (b) WHERE created_at > yesterday, (c) WHERE customer_id = 5 AND created_at > yesterday?

Reveal the answer

(a) and (c) can: the index is sorted by customer, then time, so it seeks to customer 5 and reads in time order. (b) cannot seek efficiently, because created_at is the second column; rows for one time range are spread across every customer. This is the leftmost prefix rule.

  • B+tree index: sorted; supports equality, ranges, ORDER BY, and prefix matches. The default in relational databases.
  • Composite index (a, b, c): usable for a, a, b, and a, b, c. Put equality columns first, then the range or sort column.
  • Covering index: contains every column the query needs, so the table itself is not read (INCLUDE columns in PostgreSQL).
  • Partial index: indexes only rows matching a condition (WHERE status = 'pending'), small and fast for hot subsets.
  • Hash index: equality only. Inverted index: word to documents, for full-text search (Module 17). Geospatial index: R-tree, geohash (Module 17).
  • Cost: every index slows writes and uses space. Index for your actual queries; check them with EXPLAIN.

8.5Storage engines: B-trees and LSM trees

Try it first2 minutes

An IoT platform writes 500,000 sensor readings per second and reads them rarely. Why might a B-tree database struggle, and what design handles it better?

Reveal the answer

A B-tree updates pages in place, so each insert can cause random page writes, plus WAL writes and page splits. At very high write rates that random I/O becomes the limit. An LSM tree buffers writes in memory and a sequential log, then writes large sorted files sequentially, giving much higher write throughput.

B-tree (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) LSM tree (Cassandra, RocksDB, HBase, ScyllaDB)
Writes Update pages in place, plus WAL Append to WAL and memtable; flush sorted files
Reads One path down the tree Check memtable, then files newest to oldest; Bloom filters skip files
Strength Predictable reads, range queries, transactions Very high write throughput, good compression
Cost Random writes, page splits, fragmentation Read amplification, compaction uses I/O and CPU in the background

8.6The NoSQL families

Try it first3 minutes

Pick a family for each: (a) chat messages per conversation, 10B per day; (b) a product catalog with different attributes per category; (c) "friends of friends who like jazz"; (d) CPU metrics every 10 s from 100K servers; (e) session lookup by token.

Reveal the answer

(a) Wide-column (Cassandra, HBase, Bigtable), partitioned by conversation and sorted by time. (b) Document (MongoDB) or JSON columns in PostgreSQL. (c) Graph (Neo4j). (d) Time-series (Prometheus, InfluxDB, TimescaleDB). (e) Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB).

Family Data model Strengths Limits Examples
Key-value Key to opaque value Simplest, fastest, scales by key No queries by value Redis, DynamoDB, Riak
Document Key to JSON-like document with indexes Flexible schema, whole aggregates in one read Joins across documents are weak MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore
Wide-column Partition key to sorted rows of columns Huge write volume, time-ordered data per key, multi-datacenter Must design tables per query; limited secondary indexes Cassandra, HBase, Bigtable, ScyllaDB
Graph Nodes and edges Multi-hop relationship queries Hard to shard; niche Neo4j, Neptune
Time-series Timestamped measurements Fast append, downsampling, retention Narrow use Prometheus, InfluxDB, TimescaleDB
Search Inverted index over documents Full-text, relevance, facets Not a source of truth; near real-time Elasticsearch, OpenSearch
Columnar (OLAP) Columns stored separately Scans and aggregates over billions of rows Slow single-row writes and lookups BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, ClickHouse
Distributed SQL SQL tables sharded and replicated with consensus SQL and transactions at horizontal scale Higher write latency; cost Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, TiDB

8.7Choosing a database

Try it first3 minutes

Payments ledger, 5,000 writes/s, must never lose or double-apply an entry, needs joins for reporting. Which database, and what would push you to something else later?

Reveal the answer

A relational database (PostgreSQL or MySQL) with strong constraints and transactions; it handles 5,000 writes/s on good hardware, especially with batching. Push factors: sustained write growth beyond one primary (shard by account, or move to distributed SQL such as Spanner or CockroachDB) or global multi-region writes. Reporting goes to a warehouse fed by change data capture, not to the primary.

Questions that decide the choice:

  1. What are the access patterns? Lookups by key, range scans by time, ad hoc queries, joins, full-text, graph traversals.
  2. Do you need multi-row transactions? Money, inventory, bookings: yes. Likes, views, logs: rarely.
  3. What is the read/write ratio and volume? Write-heavy at huge scale favors LSM-based wide-column stores.
  4. How big will it get? Single-digit TB and a few thousand writes/s: one relational primary plus replicas. Tens of TB or more writes: partitioning or a natively distributed store.
  5. What consistency does each feature need? (Module 11)
  6. What does the team already run well? Operational experience is a real requirement.
Myth Reality
"SQL does not scale" Sharded MySQL runs some of the largest sites; distributed SQL scales writes horizontally
"NoSQL has no schema" The schema moves into the application and the queries; you still must design it
"NoSQL has no transactions" DynamoDB and MongoDB offer multi-item transactions, with limits
"Pick one database" Most systems use several: OLTP, cache, search, warehouse, each fed from the source of truth

8.8Data modeling for scale

Try it first2 minutes

A feed page shows each post with the author's name and avatar. Joining posts to users on every read is slow at scale. What are your options?

Reveal the answer

Denormalize: copy the author's name and avatar URL into the post (or the feed entry), accepting that a name change must update or tolerate old copies. Or cache user profiles and join in the application from the cache. Both trade write complexity or staleness for fast reads.

  • Normalize for correctness (one place to update) when writes and consistency matter. Denormalize for read speed when reads dominate and slight staleness is acceptable.
  • Model by access pattern for NoSQL: list the queries first, then design one table (or key layout) per query.
  • Keep transactions inside one partition where possible: put data that changes together under the same partition key (Module 10).
  • Separate OLTP and OLAP: the transactional database serves the product; a warehouse fed by change data capture or batch export serves analytics.
  • Soft deletes and audit trails: append-only history tables (who changed what, when) are often required in regulated domains.
In production

In financial systems, the common pattern is a relational database as the system of record (ledgers, accounts, state machines enforced with constraints), Kafka for events, Redis for hot reads and rate limits, a search engine for support tooling, and a warehouse for regulatory reports. Each copy is derived from the system of record and can be rebuilt from it.

Interview signal

Name the store per data type with a reason, write the primary key and main index, and say how the hottest query is served. "PostgreSQL because bookings need transactions; index on (event_id, seat_id)" scores better than a list of databases.

8.9Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Read-modify-write without protection for counters, stock, balances, and seats.
  • Choosing NoSQL "for scale" for a workload that needs joins and transactions and fits in one PostgreSQL.
  • No index for the main query, or an index whose column order does not match it.
  • Indexing everything, slowing every write.
  • Holding row locks across remote calls.
  • Running analytics on the primary, slowing the product.
  • Mixing up ACID consistency and CAP consistency.

8.10Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Which isolation level stops write skew, and what must clients do when using it in PostgreSQL?
    Reveal

    Serializable. PostgreSQL may abort a transaction with a serialization failure, so clients must retry it.

  2. How does optimistic concurrency detect a conflict?
    Reveal

    The update includes the version it read (WHERE id = ? AND version = ?). If someone else updated first, the version changed, 0 rows are updated, and the client retries or reports a conflict.

  3. Why do LSM trees need compaction?
    Reveal

    Flushes create many overlapping sorted files; reads would check more and more files, and deleted or overwritten data would never be reclaimed. Compaction merges files, drops obsolete versions, and keeps reads fast.

  4. Why can't a Cassandra table efficiently answer a query that does not include the partition key?
    Reveal

    The partition key decides which nodes hold the data. Without it, the query must ask every node and scan, so you design another table keyed for that query.

  5. What is a covering index?
    Reveal

    An index that contains all columns a query needs, so the database answers from the index alone without reading the table rows.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Module 9: Replication

Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines, so the system survives failures, serves more reads, and sits closer to users. The price is that copies can disagree. This module covers leader-based, multi-leader, and leaderless replication, lag, failover, and quorums.

9 lessons6 figures5 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 9.1Why replicate
  2. 9.2Single-leader replication
  3. 9.3Synchronous and asynchronous replication
  4. 9.4Replication lag and what users see
  5. 9.5Failover
  6. 9.6Multi-leader replication
  7. 9.7Leaderless replication and quorums
  8. 9.8Common mistakes
  9. 9.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Why replicate a database at all? Give three reasons.
    Reveal

    Availability (survive a machine or zone failure), read scaling (spread reads over followers), and lower latency (copies near users). Also durability: data survives the loss of one disk.

  2. A user edits their profile, refreshes, and sees the old version. What happened?
    Reveal

    The write went to the leader, the read went to a follower that had not received it yet (replication lag). The read-your-writes guarantee was broken.

  3. With asynchronous replication, the leader crashes right after acknowledging a write. What can happen to that write?
    Reveal

    It can be lost: the new leader (a follower) may never have received it.

  4. Two network halves each believe they have the leader and both accept writes. What is this called?
    Reveal

    Split brain. Prevent it with majority-based election (only the side with a majority can elect a leader) and fencing tokens that reject writes from an old leader.

  5. N = 3 replicas, writes wait for 2, reads ask 2. Will a read see the latest successful write?
    Reveal

    Usually: R + W = 4 > N = 3, so with a strict quorum and no concurrent writes, every read set overlaps the write set in at least one replica. It is not a strict guarantee (sloppy quorums, concurrent or partially failed writes, and clock-based conflict resolution can still return stale data), as the end of this module explains.

9.1Why replicate

Try it first2 minutes

Your database is the only copy, on one machine in one zone. List what replication fixes and what new problem it creates.

Reveal the answer

Fixes: machine or disk loss (durability), downtime while the machine is replaced (availability), read capacity limits (followers serve reads), and distance to far users (copies in other regions). New problem: the copies can disagree for a while, so readers may see stale data, and failover can lose or duplicate writes.

Idea

Keep the same data on several nodes. Every change is shipped from one copy to the others, usually as a log of changes.

Analogy

A head office and branch offices with copies of the same customer register. Changes are mailed to the branches; a branch that has not received today's mail answers with yesterday's data.

Three shapes

Single-leader (one node takes writes), multi-leader (several nodes take writes and sync with each other), leaderless (clients write to several nodes directly, using quorums).

9.2Single-leader replication

Try it first2 minutes

Reads are 95% of traffic and the leader's CPU is at 90%. What does adding two followers change, and what does it not change?

Reveal the answer

Reads can move to the followers, so leader load drops sharply. Writes still all go through the single leader, so write capacity does not change; for that you need partitioning (Module 10).

  • How changes ship: the leader sends its write-ahead log or a logical change stream (PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL binlog). Followers apply changes in the same order.
  • Read scaling: add followers for read-heavy workloads. Each extra follower adds load on the leader to ship the log, and all of them lag a little.
  • Used by: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, MongoDB replica sets, Redis, Kafka partitions (each partition has a leader).

9.3Synchronous and asynchronous replication

Try it first2 minutes

For a payments ledger in one region, would you wait for all followers to confirm each commit? Why or why not?

Reveal the answer

Not all: the slowest or a failed follower would block every commit. A common choice is semi-synchronous: wait for one follower (ideally in another zone) to confirm, then acknowledge. A confirmed write then exists on two machines, while the other followers catch up asynchronously.

Mode Leader acknowledges after Durability on leader crash Latency and availability
Synchronous (all) Every follower stored the write No loss Slowest; one dead follower blocks writes
Semi-synchronous At least one follower stored it No loss if that follower takes over Small added latency; tolerates other followers failing
Asynchronous Only its own log Recent writes can be lost Fastest; followers can lag far behind

Consensus-based systems (Module 11) generalize this: a write commits once a majority stores it, which tolerates a minority of slow or failed nodes without losing acknowledged writes.

9.4Replication lag and what users see

Try it first2 minutes

A user posts a comment and is redirected to the post page, served by a follower 3 seconds behind. Their comment is missing. Give two fixes.

Reveal the answer

(1) Read-your-writes: route this user's reads of the post to the leader for a short time after they write (for example 10 s), or until the follower has replayed past the write's log position. (2) Show the comment from the client's own state (optimistic UI) while the server catches up. Also possible: pin the user to a follower that is known to be caught up.

Guarantee Broken when Typical fix
Read-your-writes You do not see your own recent write Read your own data from the leader for a while; or wait until the replica passes your write's log position
Monotonic reads A later read shows older data than an earlier read (time goes backwards) Pin each user to one replica (hash of user ID)
Consistent prefix You see an answer before the question it replies to Keep causally related writes in the same partition; or track causal dependencies
In production

Lag is normally milliseconds, but it spikes during bulk jobs, large migrations, or long-running queries on followers. Monitor replication lag as a first-class metric and stop routing reads to followers beyond a threshold.

9.5Failover

Try it first3 minutes

The leader stops responding. List the steps of an automatic failover and one way each step can go wrong.

Reveal the answer
  1. Detect failure, usually by missed heartbeats or timeouts. Too short a timeout causes needless failovers during GC pauses or load spikes; too long means a long outage.
  2. Choose a new leader, ideally the most up-to-date follower, by election or by a coordinator. A lagging follower loses writes.
  3. Reconfigure: clients and the remaining followers switch to the new leader. If the old leader comes back still believing it leads, there are two leaders (split brain).
  • Lost writes: with async replication, acknowledged writes on the old leader that never reached the new one are gone. Their IDs may even be reused, which corrupts other systems that saw them.
  • Split brain: prevent it by requiring a majority to elect a leader (a 3-node or 5-node cluster) and by fencing: each leader term has a higher epoch number, and storage or downstream systems reject requests carrying an older epoch.
  • Use battle-tested tooling: Patroni (PostgreSQL, using etcd for consensus), managed databases with automatic failover (RDS Multi-AZ, Cloud SQL HA), Redis Sentinel. Do not hand-roll failover.
  • RPO and RTO (Module 15) describe the result: how much data you can lose (RPO) and how long recovery takes (RTO).

9.6Multi-leader replication

Try it first2 minutes

Users in India and the US both edit the same shared document title at the same moment, each writing to their local region's leader. What must the system decide, and what are the options?

Reveal the answer

It must resolve a write conflict. Options: last-write-wins by timestamp (simple, silently drops one edit), merge both values (show both, or app-specific merge), keep both as siblings for the user to resolve, or use a CRDT that merges automatically. Best of all is avoiding conflicts by routing each document to one home leader.

  • Use when: multiple regions each need low-latency writes, clients work offline (each device is a "leader" that syncs later), or collaborative editing.
  • Conflict resolution:
  • Last write wins (LWW): keep the value with the highest timestamp. Simple, but loses data, and clock skew can pick the "wrong" winner.
  • Application merge: union of shopping cart items, max of counters, flag for manual resolution.
  • CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types): counters, sets, and text types designed so concurrent updates always merge to the same result (Case study 16).
  • Avoid conflicts: give each record a home region and send all its writes there.
  • Cost: much harder to reason about; avoid unless the requirement truly needs it.

9.7Leaderless replication and quorums

Try it first3 minutes

A key is stored on 3 replicas. You want writes to survive one replica being down, and reads to always see the latest successful write. Choose W and R.

Reveal the answer

W = 2 and R = 2. A write succeeds with one replica down (2 of 3 acknowledge), a read succeeds with one replica down, and R + W = 4 > 3 guarantees the read set overlaps the write set. W = 3 would block writes when any replica is down; R = 1 with W = 2 could read the one replica that missed the write.

Quorum explorerPick N replicas, W write acks, and R read replies. Colored boxes show the worst case: writes on the left, reads on the right.

Dynamo-style stores (Cassandra, Riak, the original Dynamo; ScyllaDB) let the client write to and read from several replicas directly:

  • N replicas per key, W acknowledgments required for a write, R replies required for a read. R + W > N means reads and writes overlap. Common choice: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 (Cassandra's QUORUM).
  • Tunable: W = 1, R = 1 for speed with possible staleness; W = N for reads that only need one replica but writes that fail when any node is down.
  • Read repair: when a read sees a stale replica, it writes the newer value back to it.
  • Anti-entropy: a background process compares replicas using Merkle trees (hash trees over key ranges) and copies only the ranges that differ.
  • Hinted handoff: if a target replica is down, another node stores the write with a "hint" and delivers it when the replica returns. With a sloppy quorum, those stand-in nodes count toward W, which keeps writes available but weakens the overlap guarantee.
  • Conflicts still happen with concurrent writes; stores use LWW timestamps (Cassandra) or version vectors and siblings (Riak).
Watch out

R + W > N does not make a leaderless store linearizable. Concurrent writes, sloppy quorums, and partial failures can still produce surprising reads. Say "quorums give overlap, which makes stale reads much less likely," and use a consensus-based system when you need strict guarantees.

Interview signal

When you add replicas, interviewers often probe the read-after-write case. Have the answer ready: route a user's own reads to the leader for a short window or until the replica passes the write's log position.

9.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Assuming followers are up to date, then reading your own write from one.
  • Ignoring lost writes in async failover for data that must never be lost.
  • Two-node clusters with automatic failover: no majority is possible, so split brain is likely. Use 3 or 5 voters.
  • Multi-leader "for availability" without a conflict strategy.
  • Quoting R + W > N as strong consistency.
  • Reporting and backups on the leader instead of a dedicated follower.

9.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. How does a follower know it has caught up to a client's write?
    Reveal

    The leader returns the log position (LSN) of the write; the client or router sends it with later reads, and a follower serves the read only once it has replayed past that position.

  2. Why do consensus clusters use an odd number of nodes?
    Reveal

    A majority of 3 is 2 and of 4 is 3, so a 4th node adds cost without tolerating more failures (both tolerate 1). 5 nodes tolerate 2.

  3. What is a fencing token and who checks it?
    Reveal

    A number that increases with every new leader (or lock holder). The resource being written (storage, a downstream service) remembers the highest token seen and rejects requests with lower ones.

  4. When is multi-leader replication worth its complexity?
    Reveal

    When several regions need low-latency local writes, or clients must work offline and sync later, and the data model has a clear conflict strategy.

  5. What do Merkle trees do in anti-entropy?
    Reveal

    They summarize key ranges as hashes, so two replicas compare a few hashes from the root down and transfer only the ranges whose hashes differ.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.
