Module 10: Partitioning and consistent hashing

When data or writes outgrow one machine, you split the data into partitions (shards) on different nodes. The hard parts are choosing the key, keeping load even, moving data when nodes change, and answering queries that span partitions. Consistent hashing is the tool that makes adding and removing nodes cheap.

9 lessons5 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 10.1Why partition
  2. 10.2Choosing a partition key
  3. 10.3Range and hash partitioning
  4. 10.4Consistent hashing
  5. 10.5Hot spots and skew
  6. 10.6Rebalancing and request routing
  7. 10.7Queries across partitions
  8. 10.8Common mistakes
  9. 10.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Replication vs partitioning: which one increases write capacity?
    Reveal

    Partitioning. Replication copies all data to every replica, so every replica still handles every write; partitioning gives each node a different subset of writes.

  2. You shard orders by order_date. Why is that a bad shard key for writes?
    Reveal

    All new orders have today's date, so every write lands on the newest shard (a hot partition) while the others sit idle.

  3. You shard with hash(key) mod 4 and add a fifth server. Roughly what fraction of keys must move?
    Reveal

    About 80% (N/(N+1)). That is why plain mod N is replaced by consistent hashing or a fixed number of slots.

  4. A celebrity's account gets 1,000x the traffic of others and overloads one shard. One fix?
    Reveal

    Split that hot key: append a suffix (celeb#0..#9) to spread writes across shards and combine on read, and cache the hot reads.

  5. How do you find all orders for a product when orders are sharded by customer?
    Reveal

    Either ask every shard and merge the results (scatter-gather), or maintain a global secondary index (or a separate table) partitioned by product ID.

10.1Why partition

Try it first2 minutes

A table grows by 200 GB a month and takes 30,000 writes/s. Replicas are already in place. Why do replicas not help, and what does?

Reveal the answer

Replicas copy every write, so each still takes 30,000 writes/s and stores all the data. Splitting the table across, say, 10 shards gives each one about 3,000 writes/s and a tenth of the data. In practice you combine both: partition for scale, replicate each partition for availability.

Idea

Split the dataset by a partition key so each node owns a subset. Requests for a key go only to the node that owns it.

Analogy

A library too big for one building is split across branches by the first letter of the author's name. Each branch handles its own books and visitors. Picking the split rule well decides whether one branch has a queue out the door.

Combined with replication

Each partition is itself replicated, and each node holds leaders for some partitions and followers for others, so load and failures spread evenly.

10.2Choosing a partition key

Try it first3 minutes

For each, pick a partition key and name one risk: (a) chat messages, (b) a multi-tenant SaaS where one customer is 30% of traffic, (c) IoT readings queried by device and time.

Reveal the answer

(a) conversation_id: messages of one chat stay together and in order; risk: a huge group chat becomes a hot partition. (b) tenant_id: keeps a tenant's data together for queries and isolation; risk: the giant tenant overloads its shard, so give it dedicated shards or sub-partition by (tenant_id, user_id). (c) device_id (possibly with a time bucket like (device_id, day)): spreads load across devices, keeps one device's readings ordered; risk: unbounded partitions without the time bucket.

A good partition key:

  1. Has many distinct values (high cardinality), so data can spread across many nodes.
  2. Spreads load evenly, both data size and request rate. Watch for skew: a few very hot keys.
  3. Matches the main access pattern, so common queries hit one partition. The key you always know at query time (user ID, conversation ID) is usually the right one.
  4. Keeps things that must change together in one partition, so transactions stay local (an account and its ledger entries).
Key idea

The partition key is the hardest decision to change later. In an interview, say the key, why it fits the main query, and what happens with the hottest key.

10.3Range and hash partitioning

Try it first2 minutes

You need "all events between 10:00 and 10:05" quickly. Would you partition by range of timestamp or by hash of event ID? What does each cost?

Reveal the answer

Range by time makes that query hit one or two partitions, but all current writes go to the newest partition (hot). Hash by event ID spreads writes evenly, but the time-range query must ask every partition. A common compromise: partition by hash of a source ID (spread writes), and inside each partition sort by time (fast per-source ranges); or use time buckets plus a hash prefix.

Range partitioning Hash partitioning
Rule Key ranges (A-F, G-M; or by date) hash(key) decides the partition
Range queries Efficient Must query all partitions
Load balance Risk of hot ranges (sequential keys, popular letters, "today") Even, unless single keys are hot
Used by HBase, Bigtable, Spanner, MongoDB range sharding Cassandra, DynamoDB, Redis Cluster, MongoDB hashed sharding

Compound keys get both: Cassandra hashes the partition key to pick the node, then sorts rows inside the partition by clustering columns. PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), created_at) spreads users evenly and keeps each user's rows in time order (Module 8).

10.4Consistent hashing

Try it first3 minutes

With hash(key) mod N, why does adding one node move almost every key? What property do we want instead?

Reveal the answer

The partition depends on N itself: change N and almost every key's remainder changes, so about N/(N+1) of keys move. We want adding or removing one node to move only about 1/N of the keys: just the share the new node takes over or the departing node held.

How it works:

  1. Hash both nodes and keys onto the same circle of hash values (for example 0 to 2^32 - 1).
  2. A key belongs to the first node clockwise from its position.
  3. Adding a node takes keys only from its clockwise neighbor; removing a node gives its keys to its neighbor. About K/N keys move (K keys, N nodes).
  4. Virtual nodes: each physical node is placed at many points (for example 100-256). This evens out the arcs, spreads a failed node's load across all others instead of one neighbor, and lets bigger machines take more points.
  5. Replication on the ring: store each key on the next N distinct physical nodes clockwise (Dynamo, Cassandra).
Consistent hashing playground300 keys on a ring. Add or remove nodes and change virtual nodes per server; compare how many keys move with hash mod N.
Note

Not every system uses a ring. Redis Cluster uses 16,384 fixed hash slots assigned to nodes; Kafka uses a fixed number of partitions per topic; Elasticsearch fixes the number of primary shards per index. Fixed slots achieve the same goal: adding a node moves whole slots, not individual keys, and the key-to-slot mapping never changes. Related algorithms: rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing and Google's jump consistent hash.

10.5Hot spots and skew

Try it first2 minutes

A "like" counter for one viral post gets 200,000 increments per second, all to one key on one shard. How do you spread it?

Reveal the answer

Shard the counter itself: write increments to post:9:likes#0 to #15 chosen at random, so 16 keys (on different shards) share the load, and sum them on read (or periodically aggregate into the main counter). Reads of the total can be cached for a second. Batching increments in memory and flushing every second also cuts writes.

  • Hot keys: celebrities, viral items, a dominant tenant. Fixes: key salting (add a suffix to spread writes, merge on read), caching hot reads, dedicated partitions for known giants.
  • Hot ranges: sequential IDs or timestamps in range partitioning. Fixes: hash prefix, random or time-ordered-but-spread IDs, time buckets combined with another key.
  • Skewed sizes: one partition grows far larger (a huge group chat). Fixes: split by (key, bucket) such as month, cap partition size.
In production

Hash a time-ordered ID and you lose locality; use random IDs as a primary key in a B-tree and you scatter inserts across the index. Many teams use time-ordered IDs (UUIDv7, Snowflake) as the primary key inside a shard and hash a different field, such as the user ID, to pick the shard.

10.6Rebalancing and request routing

Try it first2 minutes

You started with 4 shards on 4 machines and now need 6 machines. If you had created 64 logical partitions on day one, how would growing to 6 machines work?

Reveal the answer

Move whole logical partitions: each of the 6 machines takes about 10-11 of the 64. The key-to-partition mapping never changes; only the partition-to-machine assignment does. That is far easier than re-splitting data, which is why many systems create many more partitions than nodes up front.

Strategy How Used by
Fixed number of partitions Create many partitions up front; move whole partitions between nodes Kafka, Redis Cluster slots, Elasticsearch, Riak
Dynamic splitting Split a partition when it grows too big; merge small ones HBase, Bigtable, DynamoDB, MongoDB
Consistent hashing with virtual nodes Nodes join the ring and take arcs Cassandra, Dynamo, many caches

How a request finds the right node:

  1. Any node forwards: the client contacts any node, which forwards to the owner (Cassandra coordinator).
  2. Routing tier: a proxy that knows the map (Vitess VTGate for MySQL, MongoDB mongos, a Redis proxy).
  3. Partition-aware clients: the client library caches the map and goes straight to the owner (Redis Cluster clients follow MOVED redirects, Kafka clients fetch metadata).

The map itself lives in a coordination service (ZooKeeper, etcd) or is spread by gossip, and moving data happens in the background, throttled so it does not overload the cluster.

10.7Queries across partitions

Try it first2 minutes

Users are sharded by user_id. Support staff need "find user by email". What are your options?

Reveal the answer

(1) Scatter-gather: ask every shard and merge; fine if rare and shards are few. (2) A global lookup table email -> user_id, itself partitioned by email, kept in sync on every user change. (3) Send user records to a search index (Elasticsearch) and query that. For a frequent, latency-sensitive query, use (2).

Local index (per partition) Global index (partitioned by term)
Write cost Cheap: same partition as the row A write may touch another partition's index; often updated asynchronously
Read cost Scatter-gather to all partitions Read one index partition
Freshness Immediate Can lag
Examples Cassandra secondary indexes, Elasticsearch (per shard), MongoDB DynamoDB global secondary indexes

Cross-partition joins and transactions are expensive: avoid them through key choice and denormalization, run them in batch or analytics systems, or use a store that supports distributed transactions (Spanner, CockroachDB) and accept the latency. Patterns such as sagas (Module 13) coordinate multi-partition business operations.

Interview signal

Always name the partition key, why it matches the main query, and what the hottest key looks like. Then say how you would rebalance. This is one of the most common deep dives at L4.

10.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Sharding too early when one node plus replicas would do.
  • A low-cardinality or monotonic shard key (country, status, date).
  • Plain mod N for anything that will grow.
  • Ignoring the hottest key: every key choice has a worst case; name it.
  • Frequent scatter-gather queries on the hot path.
  • Cross-shard transactions by default, instead of keeping related data on one shard.

10.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Why do virtual nodes improve consistent hashing?
    Reveal

    With one point per node, arcs are uneven and a failed node's load lands on one neighbor. Many points per node even out arc sizes and spread a failed node's keys across all remaining nodes.

  2. When adding the 11th node to a 10-node consistent-hashing cluster, about what fraction of keys moves?
    Reveal

    About 1/11 of the keys, the share the new node takes over.

  3. How does Redis Cluster map a key to a node?
    Reveal

    CRC16(key) mod 16384 gives a hash slot; each node owns a set of slots. Moving slots between nodes rebalances without changing the key-to-slot mapping.

  4. What is a partition key vs a clustering key in Cassandra?
    Reveal

    The partition key is hashed to choose the nodes that store the row; clustering keys sort rows within that partition, enabling ordered range reads inside it.

  5. Global secondary index reads are fast. What is the trade-off?
    Reveal

    Writes become more expensive or the index lags, because updating a row may require updating an index partition on another node, often asynchronously.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Module 11: Consistency, CAP, and consensus

Once data has copies, you must decide what readers are allowed to see and what the system does when nodes cannot talk. This module gives precise meanings for consistency models, CAP and PACELC, explains how consensus (Raft) makes many machines agree, and covers locks, fencing, and clocks.

8 lessons5 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 11.1Consistency models
  2. 11.2The CAP theorem
  3. 11.3PACELC: the trade-off when nothing is broken
  4. 11.4Consensus and Raft
  5. 11.5Coordination services, leases, and locks
  6. 11.6Time, clocks, and ordering
  7. 11.7Common mistakes
  8. 11.8Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. "CAP means you pick any two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance." What is wrong with this?
    Reveal

    Partitions are not optional in a distributed system; they happen. CAP says that during a partition you must choose between consistency (refuse some requests) and availability (answer, possibly with stale data).

  2. Why do etcd and ZooKeeper clusters usually have 3 or 5 nodes?
    Reveal

    They need a majority to agree. 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2. Even sizes add cost without adding tolerance.

  3. A service holds a Redis lock with a 30 s expiry, pauses for 40 s in garbage collection, then writes. What can go wrong?
    Reveal

    The lock expired; another client acquired it and is writing too. Both write. A fencing token checked by the storage prevents the stale holder's write.

  4. Two servers order events by their wall-clock timestamps. Why is that unsafe?
    Reveal

    Clocks drift and jump (NTP corrections), so a later event can carry an earlier timestamp. Use a single sequencer, logical clocks, or a consensus log for ordering.

  5. Which needs strong consistency: a "like" count, a username uniqueness check, a news feed, a bank transfer?
    Reveal

    Username uniqueness and the bank transfer. Like counts and feeds can be eventually consistent.

11.1Consistency models

Try it first2 minutes

You update your profile photo in India. A friend in the US refreshes 1 second later and sees the old photo; 5 seconds later they see the new one. Which consistency model allows this, and which would forbid it?

Reveal the answer

Eventual consistency allows it: replicas converge after a delay. Linearizability (strong consistency) forbids it: once your write completed, every later read anywhere must return the new photo. Paying for linearizability across continents would add tens to hundreds of milliseconds to every write or read.

Model Guarantee Example need
Linearizable (strong) The system behaves like a single copy: after a write completes, every later read sees it (or something newer) Unique usernames, leader election, account balance checks, seat booking
Causal If B depends on A (a reply to a post), everyone sees A before B; unrelated writes can appear in any order Comment threads, chat
Session guarantees Read your own writes; never go back in time within a session (Module 9) Profile edits, settings
Eventual If writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value Like counts, view counts, feeds, DNS, caches
Key idea

Choose per operation, not per system. "Placing an order is strongly consistent; the order history page reads from a replica and can lag a second" is a strong design statement.

11.2The CAP theorem

Try it first3 minutes

A network partition splits two replicas of an inventory database. A customer on side B wants to buy the last unit, which may already have been sold on side A. What are the system's two choices?

Reveal the answer

Consistency (CP): side B refuses or delays the purchase because it cannot confirm the latest stock; no oversell, but some customers get errors. Availability (AP): side B accepts the order using its possibly stale stock; customers are served, but the shop may oversell and must reconcile later (refund, backorder).

  • C (in CAP) = linearizability. A = every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response. P = the system keeps working despite lost messages between nodes.
  • Since partitions happen, the real choice is CP or AP during a partition:
  • CP: refuse or time out some requests to avoid stale or conflicting data (etcd, ZooKeeper, HBase, Spanner, a single-leader SQL database whose minority side cannot accept writes).
  • AP: keep answering and reconcile later (Cassandra and DynamoDB with eventual reads, DNS, multi-leader setups, most caches).
  • Many systems are tunable: Cassandra with QUORUM reads and writes behaves much more like CP than with ONE.

11.3PACELC: the trade-off when nothing is broken

Try it first2 minutes

No partition is happening. Why might a system still choose to return slightly stale data?

Reveal the answer

Latency. Guaranteeing the latest value means coordinating with other replicas (a quorum or the leader), possibly in other zones or regions, on every request. Reading the nearest replica is faster. That trade-off exists all the time, not only during partitions.

PACELC: if there is a Partition, choose A or C; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.

System (default settings) During partition Normal operation
Cassandra, DynamoDB (eventually consistent reads) Available Low latency
Spanner, etcd, HBase Consistent Consistent (pays latency)
ZooKeeper Consistent for writes Writes linearizable; reads served locally and may be stale unless the client calls sync() first
MongoDB, Cassandra with quorums Depends on read and write concern settings Depends

11.4Consensus and Raft

Try it first3 minutes

Five machines must agree on which one is the leader, even if two crash and the network delays messages. Why is "the node with the lowest ID that is alive is the leader" not enough?

Reveal the answer

Nodes cannot reliably tell "dead" from "slow" or "cut off". Two groups that cannot see each other would each pick their own lowest ID and both act as leader (split brain). Consensus protocols fix this with majorities: a leader needs votes from more than half the nodes, and two majorities of the same cluster always overlap, so two leaders cannot both win the same term.

What consensus gives you: a group of nodes agrees on one ordered log of decisions, even when a minority crash or messages are delayed. Everything built on it (leader election, locks, configuration, metadata) inherits that agreement.

Raft in five points:

  1. Roles: one leader, the rest followers. Followers that hear no heartbeat within a randomized timeout become candidates.
  2. Election: a candidate increments the term, votes for itself, and asks others. A node grants at most one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own. A majority wins.
  3. Log replication: clients send writes to the leader, which appends them and sends them to followers.
  4. Commit: an entry is committed once stored on a majority; then it is applied and acknowledged. Committed entries are never lost, because any future leader must have them to win a majority vote.
  5. Fault tolerance: 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f failures. Writes stop if a majority is unavailable (CP).

Paxos solves the same problem; Raft was designed to be easier to understand. Where you meet them: etcd (Raft, the store behind Kubernetes), ZooKeeper (ZAB), Consul (Raft), Kafka KRaft metadata (Raft), CockroachDB and TiKV (Raft per data range), Spanner (Paxos per split).

Watch out

Do not implement consensus in an interview or at work. Say "store the leader lease and configuration in etcd or ZooKeeper" and explain what you get: linearizable writes, leases, watches, and majority-based fault tolerance.

11.5Coordination services, leases, and locks

Try it first2 minutes

Ten instances of a scheduler run, but each job must be triggered by only one. How do you choose which instance runs jobs, and what happens if it dies?

Reveal the answer

Leader election through a coordination service: each instance tries to create a lease-backed key (an etcd lease or a ZooKeeper ephemeral node). The one that succeeds is leader and keeps renewing the lease. If it dies, the lease expires and another instance takes over. Jobs should still be idempotent, because a paused old leader might run a job once more before it notices.

Coordination services (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul) give small key-value storage with linearizable writes (etcd reads are linearizable by default; ZooKeeper reads can be slightly stale unless preceded by sync()), plus:

  • Leases / ephemeral nodes: keys that disappear when the client stops renewing, for leader election and membership.
  • Watches: notifications when a key changes, for configuration and service discovery.
  • Monotonic revision numbers: usable as fencing tokens.

Distributed locks come in two kinds:

Efficiency lock Correctness lock
Purpose Avoid duplicate work (two workers sending the same report) Prevent corruption (two writers to one account)
If it fails occasionally Some wasted work Data corruption
Good enough Redis SET key value NX PX 30000, released with a check-and-delete script Consensus-backed lock (etcd, ZooKeeper) plus fencing tokens, or a database constraint
In production

The simplest correct lock is often the database you already have: a unique constraint, a conditional update (UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'pending'), SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or PostgreSQL advisory locks. They are atomic with the data change. A Redis lock in front of a database write still leaves a window where both can write; the database check closes it.

11.6Time, clocks, and ordering

Try it first2 minutes

Two replicas accept writes to the same shopping cart while disconnected. Later, last-write-wins by timestamp keeps one cart and drops the other. Why is this a problem even if the clocks are perfect?

Reveal the answer

Both writes were made without knowing about each other (they are concurrent). Picking the later one silently discards a real user action (an added item). The system needs to detect concurrency and merge (union the carts), which timestamps cannot tell you but version vectors can.

  • Wall clocks drift and jump: NTP keeps servers within milliseconds usually, but not reliably, and corrections can move time backwards. Never use wall-clock time alone to order events across machines or to decide which write wins when it matters.
  • Monotonic clocks measure durations on one machine (timeouts, latency); use them for "how long", never for "when".
  • Lamport clocks: a counter incremented on every event and set to max(local, received) + 1 on every message. They give a total order consistent with causality, but cannot tell you whether two events were concurrent.
  • Vector clocks / version vectors: one counter per node. Compare two vectors: if one is greater or equal in every slot, it happened after; otherwise the events were concurrent and need merging (Riak, Dynamo).
  • Hybrid logical clocks: physical time plus a logical counter; close to wall time and causally safe (CockroachDB, YugabyteDB).
  • TrueTime (Google Spanner): GPS and atomic clocks give a time interval with a known error bound of a few milliseconds; Spanner waits out that uncertainty before committing, which gives globally consistent ordering of transactions.
Interview signal

Avoid reciting CAP. Instead, state per feature what happens during a partition: "bookings refuse writes on the minority side; the event page serves cached data." That shows you understand the trade-off, not just the acronym.

11.7Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • "Pick two of three" for CAP, or calling a single-node database "CA" as if it never meets a partition.
  • One consistency level for the whole system.
  • Hand-rolled leader election with heartbeats and lowest-ID rules.
  • Redis locks for correctness without fencing or a database-level guard.
  • Ordering events by wall-clock time across machines, or last-write-wins where losing writes matters.
  • Even-sized consensus clusters, or spreading a 3-node cluster so one zone holds 2 nodes and its failure loses the majority.

11.8Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Why can two Raft leaders never both commit entries in the same term?
    Reveal

    Winning a term requires votes from a majority, and each node votes at most once per term. Two majorities of one cluster always share a node, so only one candidate can win a given term.

  2. What happens to writes in a 5-node Raft cluster when 3 nodes are down?
    Reveal

    They stop. No majority (3 of 5) is reachable, so nothing can commit. The system chooses consistency over availability.

  3. Linearizable vs eventual consistency for a ticket booking system's seat inventory?
    Reveal

    Linearizable (or an equivalent atomic conditional update on one leader), because two buyers must never both get the same seat.

  4. What does a vector clock tell you that a Lamport clock does not?
    Reveal

    Whether two events are concurrent. Lamport clocks order everything, even events that did not influence each other.

  5. Why does PACELC matter more day to day than CAP?
    Reveal

    Partitions are rare, but the latency cost of consistency is paid on every request. Most design choices are about latency versus consistency in normal operation.

Module 12: Queues and streams

Messaging lets one part of a system hand work or events to another without waiting. It absorbs bursts, isolates failures, and lets many consumers react to one event. This module covers queues, pub/sub, and logs, Kafka's model, delivery guarantees, retries and dead letters, and stream processing.

10 lessons5 figures7 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 12.1Why asynchronous messaging
  2. 12.2Queue, pub/sub, and log
  3. 12.3How Kafka works
  4. 12.4Delivery guarantees
  5. 12.5Ordering and parallelism
  6. 12.6Failures: retries, dead letters, and backpressure
  7. 12.7Choosing a broker
  8. 12.8Stream processing
  9. 12.9Common mistakes
  10. 12.10Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. An order service calls email, inventory, and analytics services synchronously. Analytics is slow, so checkout is slow. Fix?
    Reveal

    Publish an OrderPlaced event to a topic. Email, inventory, and analytics each consume it at their own pace; checkout returns after the publish.

  2. Kafka: a topic has 6 partitions and a consumer group has 10 consumers. How many consumers are busy?
    Reveal
    1. In a classic consumer group each partition is read by at most one consumer, so 4 consumers sit idle. (Kafka's newer share groups, below, are the exception.)
  3. You need all events for one order processed in order. What decides that in Kafka?
    Reveal

    The message key. Use order_id as the key so all events for an order go to the same partition, which is ordered.

  4. A consumer processes a payment, then crashes before committing its offset. What happens on restart?
    Reveal

    It reprocesses the same message (at-least-once delivery). The handler must be idempotent, for example by recording processed message IDs.

  5. One malformed message makes the consumer throw every time and blocks the partition. What do you do?
    Reveal

    Retry a few times with backoff, then move it to a dead-letter queue and continue. Alert so a human can inspect and replay it.

12.1Why asynchronous messaging

Try it first2 minutes

A flash sale sends 50,000 orders per second for 2 minutes; the payment processor handles 5,000/s. What does a queue in between change?

Reveal the answer

The queue absorbs the burst: orders are accepted and stored durably, and payment workers drain them at 5,000/s for about 20 minutes. Without the queue, 90% of requests would fail or time out. The cost: payments complete later, so the user sees "order received, confirming payment" rather than an instant result.

Idea

The producer writes a message to a durable broker and moves on. Consumers read and process it when they can. Producer and consumer no longer need to be up, fast, or even known to each other at the same time.

Analogy

A restaurant ticket rail. Waiters clip orders to the rail and go back to customers; cooks take tickets as they free up. A rush makes the rail longer, not the waiters slower, and a new station (desserts) can read the same tickets.

What you gain

Decoupling, burst absorption (load leveling), retries without the caller waiting, fan-out to many consumers, and a replayable history of events.

What you pay

Eventual consistency (the effect happens later), duplicate and out-of-order handling, an extra system to operate, and harder debugging across asynchronous hops.

Commands vs events: a command asks for something to happen ("SendEmail", one intended handler). An event states that something happened ("OrderPlaced", any number of listeners). Events keep producers unaware of who reacts, which is what makes adding a new consumer free.

12.2Queue, pub/sub, and log

Try it first2 minutes

You want 20 workers to share resize jobs, and separately you want email, search, and audit to each receive every new-user event. Which messaging shape fits each?

Reveal the answer

Resize jobs: a work queue with competing consumers; each job goes to exactly one worker. New-user events: publish-subscribe; every subscriber gets its own copy. A Kafka topic can do both: one consumer group of 20 workers shares partitions, and each of email, search, and audit is its own consumer group.

Work queue Pub/sub Log (stream)
Delivery One consumer per message Every subscriber gets a copy Every consumer group reads all; each tracks an offset
After consumption Message deleted Deleted per subscriber Kept for the retention period
Replay No Usually no (some managed services can seek back, such as Google Pub/Sub) Yes: reset the offset
Ordering Mostly FIFO, weakened by parallel consumers and retries Per subscriber, often unordered Strict within a partition
Examples RabbitMQ queues, SQS SNS, Google Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ fanout exchange Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar, Redis Streams

12.3How Kafka works

Try it first3 minutes

A topic has 3 partitions. Group A has 2 consumers, group B has 1. Draw who reads which partition. Then group A adds a third consumer: what changes?

Reveal the answer

Group A: consumer 1 reads two partitions, consumer 2 reads one. Group B: its one consumer reads all three. Adding a third consumer to group A triggers a rebalance and each of its consumers gets one partition. Group B is unaffected; groups are independent.

  • Topic = named stream, split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log; each message has an offset.
  • Key decides partition: hash(key) mod partitions. Same key, same partition, so per-key order is preserved. No key: spread across partitions.
  • Consumer groups: within a classic consumer group, each partition goes to one consumer, so parallelism is capped by the partition count. Different groups are independent readers.
  • Share groups ("queues for Kafka", production-ready since Kafka 4.2 in 2026): many consumers read the same partition and acknowledge records one by one, like a work queue. More consumers than partitions becomes useful, but per-key ordering is lost.
  • Offsets: consumers commit the offset they have processed; on restart they resume from it. Retention is time- or size-based (days, often), not "until read".
  • Replication: each partition has a leader and followers on other brokers. The in-sync replica (ISR) set holds followers that are caught up. With acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2 (replication factor 3), an acknowledged write exists on at least 2 brokers.
  • Log compaction: optionally keep only the latest message per key, turning a topic into a durable changelog (current state per key).
  • Metadata: modern Kafka (4.0 onward) manages cluster metadata with its own Raft quorum (KRaft) instead of ZooKeeper.
Interview signal

Interviewers often ask "how many partitions?" Answer from throughput: if one consumer handles 2,000 msg/s and the peak is 40,000 msg/s, you need at least 20 partitions; choose more (say 32-64) for growth, since adding partitions later changes key-to-partition mapping and breaks per-key ordering during the change.

Go deeper

Event schemas and evolution

Producers and consumers deploy independently and events live for days or forever in the log, so event formats must change without breaking readers.

  • Use a schema (Avro, Protobuf, or JSON Schema) and a schema registry that checks every new version for compatibility before producers can publish it.
  • Compatibility modes: backward (consumers on the new schema can read old events; the usual default), forward (consumers on the old schema can read new events), full (both).
  • Safe changes: add optional fields with defaults; stop writing a field before removing it. Unsafe: renaming or retyping fields, reusing Protobuf field numbers, making optional fields required.
  • Breaking change: publish a new event version (or topic), run both while consumers migrate, then retire the old one.

12.4Delivery guarantees

Try it first2 minutes

Which do you choose for (a) click analytics, (b) sending a payment instruction to a bank: at-most-once or at-least-once? What extra work does each need?

Reveal the answer

(a) Either works; at-least-once with approximate dedup is common, and losing a few clicks is acceptable. (b) At-least-once plus idempotency: never lose the instruction, and make duplicates harmless with an idempotency key the bank honors and a processed-messages table on your side.

Guarantee How Risk Use for
At-most-once Commit (ack) before processing; no retries Lost messages Metrics where loss is fine
At-least-once Process, then commit; retry on failure Duplicates The default for almost everything
Exactly-once (effectively-once) At-least-once delivery plus idempotent or transactional processing Complexity Money, inventory, counts that must be exact

How exactly-once is really achieved:

  • Idempotent consumers: store the message ID (or a business key) with a unique constraint in the same database transaction as the effect. A duplicate hits the constraint and is skipped.
  • Kafka idempotent producer: the broker drops duplicate sends caused by producer retries (enabled by default in recent versions).
  • Kafka transactions: a read-process-write job (consume from one topic, produce to another) commits its output messages and its input offsets atomically; readers use read_committed. This is exactly-once within Kafka; side effects in external systems still need idempotency.
  • Stream processors (Flink) checkpoint state and offsets together and use transactional sinks for end-to-end exactly-once.
Key idea

Say it plainly in interviews: "Delivery is at-least-once; processing is idempotent, so the effect happens exactly once."

12.5Ordering and parallelism

Try it first2 minutes

Account events Deposit 100 then Withdraw 80 must apply in order. Yet you need 50 consumers in parallel. How?

Reveal the answer

Partition by account ID. All events of one account land in one partition and are processed in order by one consumer, while 50+ partitions spread different accounts across 50 consumers. Order is guaranteed per account, not globally, and that is all the business needs.

  • Global order and parallelism conflict. Pick the narrowest unit that must be ordered (per account, per order, per chat) and use it as the key.
  • Retries break order: if message 5 goes to a retry topic while message 6 succeeds, they apply out of order. For strict per-key order, retry in place (blocking that partition) or park all later messages of the same key.
  • Hot keys cap throughput: one key's messages are processed by one consumer. Split keys if needed (Module 10).
  • Rebalances move partitions between consumers and can cause reprocessing of uncommitted messages; the newer consumer rebalance protocol (Kafka 4.0 onward) rebalances incrementally instead of pausing the whole group. Keep processing idempotent and commit regularly.

12.6Failures: retries, dead letters, and backpressure

Try it first2 minutes

A downstream API is down for 10 minutes. Your consumer retries each message immediately, forever. What happens to the consumer and to the API?

Reveal the answer

The consumer spins on one message, so the whole partition stalls behind it (head-of-line blocking), and the constant retries hammer the API, possibly slowing its recovery. Use exponential backoff, a bounded number of attempts, delay or retry topics, a circuit breaker, and a dead-letter queue.

  • Transient vs permanent errors: retry timeouts and 503s; send validation errors and malformed payloads straight to the dead-letter queue (DLQ).
  • Backoff with jitter, and a cap on attempts.
  • DLQ is not a trash can: alert on it, show the error, and build a replay tool.
  • Backpressure: when consumers fall behind, consumer lag (latest offset minus committed offset) grows. Monitor it, autoscale consumers on it (up to the partition count), and slow or shed producers if the backlog would exceed retention.
  • Visibility timeout (SQS): a received message is hidden for N seconds; if not deleted in time, it reappears for another consumer. Set it longer than processing time.

12.7Choosing a broker

Try it first2 minutes

Pick: (a) background jobs for a small team on AWS, (b) an event backbone where 10 teams consume the same order events and analytics replays last week, (c) complex routing of tasks by type and priority.

Reveal the answer

(a) SQS: fully managed, simple, scales automatically. (b) Kafka (or a managed equivalent such as Confluent, MSK, Kinesis, or Pub/Sub): durable log, many independent consumer groups, replay. (c) RabbitMQ: exchanges and routing keys, priorities, per-message acknowledgments.

Kafka RabbitMQ SQS Google Pub/Sub
Model Partitioned log Broker with exchanges and queues Managed queue Managed pub/sub
Retention and replay Days or forever; replay by offset Until acknowledged (streams add replay) Up to 14 days, no replay Configurable retention, seek to time
Ordering Per partition Per queue (single consumer) FIFO queues: per message group Per ordering key
Throughput Very high High Very high (standard queues) Very high
Strengths Event backbone, many consumers, stream processing Flexible routing, priorities, low latency tasks Zero operations Global, zero operations

12.8Stream processing

Try it first3 minutes

You count payments per minute. A phone was offline and sends a payment that happened at 10:01 at 10:07. Which minute should it count in, and how long should you wait for late events?

Reveal the answer

It belongs to 10:01 by event time (when it happened), not 10:07 (processing time). A watermark says "events up to time T have probably arrived"; the 10:01 window closes when the watermark passes 10:01 plus an allowed lateness. Events later than that are dropped, sent to a side output, or trigger a correction.

  • Stream processors (Apache Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming, Google Dataflow) run continuous jobs: filter, enrich, join, aggregate over windows, with state that is checkpointed so a crash resumes without losing or double-counting.
  • Event time vs processing time: use event time for correctness, with watermarks to bound waiting.
  • Windows: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping: per-minute counts), sliding (overlapping: last 5 minutes, updated every minute), session (activity bursts separated by gaps).
  • Batch vs stream: batch (Spark, MapReduce, SQL on a warehouse) processes a bounded dataset, simpler and cheaper for daily reports; streaming gives results in seconds. The Lambda architecture runs both and merges them; Kappa uses one streaming pipeline and replays the log to recompute.
In production

In payments and fintech, Kafka plus Flink is a common backbone: transaction events flow through Kafka; Flink jobs compute running aggregates, detect fraud patterns within windows, route records by status, and write results to databases and alerting systems. Side outputs catch records that fail parsing so one bad record does not stop the pipeline.

Go deeper

Batch processing and data lakes

  • Batch model: MapReduce splits work into map (transform each record), shuffle (group by key across machines), and reduce (aggregate each group). Spark generalizes this into a graph of transformations kept in memory where possible.
  • Data lake: raw and processed data in object storage in columnar files (Parquet or ORC), laid out by partition such as events/dt=2026-10-17/, so queries skip irrelevant days.
  • Table formats (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Apache Hudi) add atomic commits, schema evolution, and time travel on top of those files, so many engines (Spark, Trino, Flink, BigQuery) can read and write the same tables safely.
  • Backfills: when a bug is fixed, rerun the job over the affected partitions. Make outputs idempotent by overwriting whole partitions (write to a new location, then swap), never appending.
  • Batch or stream? Batch for daily reports, model training data, and exact recomputation; streaming when results are needed within seconds. Many systems run both (Case study 15).

12.9Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Assuming exactly-once delivery and writing non-idempotent consumers.
  • More consumers than partitions in a classic consumer group, expecting more throughput (use more partitions, or share groups if you do not need per-key order).
  • No message key when per-entity order matters, or a low-cardinality key that creates hot partitions.
  • Infinite immediate retries that block a partition and hammer a sick dependency.
  • Dead-letter queues nobody watches.
  • Publishing an event outside the database transaction that made the change, so a crash leaves them inconsistent (use the outbox pattern, Module 13).
  • Using a queue where the caller needs the answer now, then building a slow request-reply over it.

12.10Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What limits consumer parallelism in a Kafka consumer group?
    Reveal

    The number of partitions, for a classic consumer group: each partition is assigned to at most one consumer in the group. Share groups (Kafka 4.2+) lift this limit at the cost of per-key ordering.

  2. What do acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2 together guarantee?
    Reveal

    A write is acknowledged only after it is stored on at least 2 in-sync replicas, so losing one broker cannot lose acknowledged data.

  3. How does an idempotent consumer make at-least-once delivery safe?
    Reveal

    It records each processed message ID (or business key) with a unique constraint, atomically with the side effect. A redelivered message is detected and skipped.

  4. What is consumer lag and why alert on it?
    Reveal

    The gap between the newest offset and the consumer's committed offset. Growing lag means consumers cannot keep up; if it exceeds retention, data is lost.

  5. Event time vs processing time: which do you use for "transactions per minute" and why?
    Reveal

    Event time, so late or delayed events count in the minute they actually happened; watermarks decide how long to wait.

Module 13: Distributed transactions and data integrity

When one business action spans several services or databases, there is no single transaction to roll back. This module covers why two-phase commit is rarely used between services, how sagas and compensations replace it, how the outbox pattern keeps data and events in sync, and how idempotency, event sourcing, CQRS, and reconciliation keep data correct.

10 lessons5 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 13.1Why cross-service transactions are hard
  2. 13.2Two-phase commit
  3. 13.3Sagas
  4. 13.4Transactional outbox and change data capture
  5. 13.5Idempotency everywhere
  6. 13.6Event sourcing
  7. 13.7CQRS
  8. 13.8Reconciliation
  9. 13.9Common mistakes
  10. 13.10Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. The order service saves an order, then publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka. It crashes between the two. What is broken?
    Reveal

    The order exists but the event was never published, so nothing downstream happens. Writing to two systems without a shared transaction is the dual-write problem.

  2. Why not use a distributed transaction (two-phase commit) across the order, payment, and inventory services?
    Reveal

    2PC locks resources until every participant votes and the coordinator decides; if the coordinator fails, participants block. It couples service availability and is often unsupported by brokers and third-party APIs.

  3. A saga charged the card but shipping failed permanently. What does the saga do?
    Reveal

    Run compensating actions in reverse order: refund the payment, release the inventory, mark the order cancelled.

  4. The same "OrderPlaced" event arrives twice at the email service. How do you avoid two emails?
    Reveal

    Make the consumer idempotent: record the event ID in a processed-events table with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the work, and skip duplicates.

  5. What is reconciliation and why do payment systems need it even when the code is correct?
    Reveal

    Comparing your records with an external source of truth (bank or processor settlement files) to find mismatches. Networks, partners, and timeouts create discrepancies no amount of local correctness can rule out.

13.1Why cross-service transactions are hard

Try it first2 minutes

Placing an order must: create the order, reserve stock (inventory service, its own DB), and charge the card (payment service and an external processor). Why can't you wrap this in one BEGIN ... COMMIT?

Reveal the answer

The three pieces live in different databases and an external system. A database transaction covers only one database. You need either a protocol that coordinates several (2PC), or a sequence of local transactions with a way to undo completed steps when a later one fails (a saga).

Idea

Each service owns its data and can only commit locally. A business transaction becomes several local transactions coordinated by messages, with explicit handling for partial failure.

Analogy

Booking a trip through separate airline, hotel, and car companies. No single agent can make all three commit atomically. You book them one by one, and if the car is unavailable you cancel the hotel and flight (often with a fee). That is a saga, and the cancellations are compensations.

13.2Two-phase commit

Try it first2 minutes

In 2PC, both participants vote YES and then the coordinator crashes before sending COMMIT. What can the participants do?

Reveal the answer

Nothing safely. They promised to commit if told to, so they cannot abort on their own, and they cannot commit without knowing the decision. They wait, holding locks, until the coordinator recovers. This blocking is 2PC's core weakness.

  • Where 2PC works well: inside one distributed database, where participants are themselves replicated and highly available (Spanner runs 2PC over Paxos groups; CockroachDB uses a similar approach). The database hides it from you.
  • Where it fits badly: across microservices, message brokers, and third-party APIs. Locks across services, coupled availability, and limited support (XA) make it rare in modern service architectures.

13.3Sagas

Try it first3 minutes

Write the saga for a ride booking: reserve driver, authorize payment, confirm ride. Give the compensation for each step. Which step needs no compensation, and why?

Reveal the answer
  1. Reserve driver; compensation: release driver.
  2. Authorize payment; compensation: void the authorization.
  3. Confirm ride; this is the last step, so if it succeeds the saga is done and nothing after it can fail. Put steps that cannot be undone (sending a confirmation, capturing money) last, after everything that can fail.
Orchestration Choreography
How A central orchestrator tells each service what to do and tracks state Each service reacts to events and emits its own
Visibility One place shows the whole flow and its state Flow is spread across services; harder to see
Coupling Orchestrator knows all steps Services know only events
Best for Complex flows, many steps, timeouts, human steps Short flows with 2-3 steps
Tools Temporal, Camunda, AWS Step Functions, a hand-built state machine Kafka topics and event handlers

Rules that make sagas work:

  • Every step is idempotent, because messages and retries repeat.
  • Compensations are semantic, not rollbacks: a refund, a cancellation notice, a release. They must also be idempotent and retried until they succeed.
  • No isolation: other users can see intermediate states (stock reserved, not yet paid). Use status fields (PENDING) as semantic locks and design the UI for them.
  • Order steps by risk: steps that are easy to undo first, irreversible steps (capture, ship, notify) last.
  • Timeouts are failures too: a step that never answers must eventually trigger compensation or a query of the remote state.
In production

Card payments follow this shape naturally: authorize (hold funds, reversible by void) during checkout, capture only when the order ships. If anything fails before capture, the compensation is a void instead of a refund: it releases the hold without moving money, which is cheaper and faster than a refund (the customer may still see a pending hold until it is voided). Authorizations expire after a network-dependent number of days, so capture before expiry or re-authorize.

13.4Transactional outbox and change data capture

Try it first2 minutes

How can a service guarantee that "order saved" and "OrderPlaced published" either both happen or neither, without 2PC?

Reveal the answer

Write the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction as the order. Commit makes both durable together. A separate relay then reads the outbox (by polling or by tailing the database log) and publishes to Kafka, retrying until it succeeds. Publishing may repeat, so consumers deduplicate.

  • Polling relay: SELECT ... FROM outbox WHERE published = false ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publish, mark published. Simple; adds polling load and some latency.
  • Change data capture (CDC): a connector such as Debezium reads the database's replication log (PostgreSQL WAL, MySQL binlog) and publishes each committed change. Low latency, no polling, preserves commit order.
  • Inbox / dedup on the consumer side: store processed event IDs with a unique constraint in the consumer's own transaction.
  • CDC beyond the outbox: stream every table change to caches (invalidation), search indexes, and warehouses, so derived stores stay in sync without dual writes in application code.

13.5Idempotency everywhere

Try it first2 minutes

List four ways to make "credit 100 to account 9 for transfer T1" safe to repeat.

Reveal the answer

(1) A unique constraint on transfer_id in the ledger table, so a second insert fails. (2) An idempotency key table storing the result of T1. (3) A conditional update: UPDATE transfers SET status = 'done' WHERE id = 'T1' AND status = 'pending', applying the credit only when 1 row changed. (4) Model the operation as setting state, not adding: record the entry for T1 with an upsert keyed by T1.

Technique How it works Example
Idempotency key Store request key and result; replay the result Idempotency-Key on payment APIs (Module 3)
Natural unique key Unique constraint on a business ID One ledger entry per (transfer_id, leg)
Processed-message table Record message IDs consumed Kafka consumer dedup
Conditional write Change only if in the expected state or version WHERE status = 'pending', WHERE version = 7
Set, do not increment Overwrite with an absolute value "balance as of event 42 = 900" instead of "+100"
Watch out

A Redis key with a TTL is a weak dedup guard: it can expire, be evicted, or be lost in a failover, and it is not atomic with the database write. Use it to reduce duplicates cheaply; use a database constraint where duplicates cause real harm.

13.6Event sourcing

Try it first2 minutes

A bank account table stores only the current balance. An auditor asks how the balance on 3 March was reached. What design answers that by construction?

Reveal the answer

Event sourcing: store every change as an immutable event (Deposited 500, Withdrew 120) in order, and derive the balance by replaying them. Any past state can be rebuilt by replaying up to that date. Double-entry ledgers in accounting work exactly this way.

  • Events are the source of truth; current state is a cached projection. Snapshots every N events keep rebuilds fast.
  • Strengths: full audit trail, time travel, rebuild new read models from history, natural fit for event-driven systems.
  • Costs: schema evolution of old events, eventual consistency of projections, more moving parts, and "delete this user's data" requests need special handling (for example, encrypting personal data per user and deleting the key).
  • Optimistic concurrency: append with an expected version per aggregate (UNIQUE (account_id, version)), so two concurrent commands cannot both apply.
  • Use it where history matters intrinsically (ledgers, order lifecycles, compliance). Do not use it for simple CRUD.

13.7CQRS

Try it first2 minutes

An order system has a normalized write schema with strict rules, but the "my orders" page needs a joined, filtered, paginated view at 50x the write rate. What can you separate?

Reveal the answer

Separate the write model (commands validated against the normalized schema) from read models built for each query (a denormalized "orders by user" table, a search index). Changes flow from the write side to the read models by events or CDC. Reads scale independently and become simple lookups, at the cost of a short lag.

  • CQRS (command query responsibility segregation) = different models for writing and reading. Often paired with event sourcing, but it does not require it: CDC from a normal database works.
  • Read-your-writes needs care: after a command, the read model may lag. Return the new state in the command response, or wait for the projection to catch up to the write's version.

13.8Reconciliation

Try it first2 minutes

Your ledger says 10,000 payments settled yesterday; the processor's settlement file lists 9,998. Name three likely causes.

Reveal the answer

Timeouts where you recorded failure but the processor actually succeeded (or the reverse), payments that settle on a different day (cutoff times, time zones), duplicates on one side, refunds or chargebacks recorded differently, and plain bugs. Reconciliation finds and classifies each mismatch so it can be fixed.

  • Compare independent records of the same facts: your ledger vs the processor's or bank's settlement files, your inventory vs the warehouse count.
  • Run it on a schedule (daily for payments), match by stable IDs, classify mismatches (missing on our side, missing on theirs, amount differs), and route them to automated fixes or a human queue.
  • Keep append-only audit records so every correction is itself recorded, never an in-place edit.
  • In interviews for payment-like systems, mentioning reconciliation is a strong signal that you know distributed systems never agree perfectly on their own.
Interview signal

Payment, order, and booking designs almost always get an "and what if this step fails halfway?" question. Answer with: idempotency keys, a saga or state machine with compensations, the outbox for events, and reconciliation as the safety net.

13.9Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Dual writes to a database and a broker in application code.
  • 2PC across microservices or third-party APIs.
  • Sagas without idempotent steps and compensations, or with irreversible steps early.
  • Assuming compensation always succeeds: it needs retries and an alert path.
  • Exactly-once claims without idempotent consumers.
  • Event sourcing for plain CRUD, paying its complexity for no benefit.
  • No reconciliation for money movement.

13.10Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Orchestration vs choreography: which would you use for a 7-step loan disbursement with a manual approval step?
    Reveal

    Orchestration: one state machine tracks progress, timeouts, retries, and the human step, and shows exactly where each loan is.

  2. What does Debezium read, and what does that give you over a polling outbox?
    Reveal

    The database's replication log (WAL or binlog). It publishes committed changes in commit order with low latency and no polling queries.

  3. Why must saga compensations be idempotent?
    Reveal

    They are retried after failures and timeouts, and the same compensation message can be delivered more than once.

  4. How does event sourcing prevent two concurrent withdrawals from both applying?
    Reveal

    Each append states the expected aggregate version; a unique constraint on (aggregate_id, version) lets only one succeed, and the other retries against the new state.

  5. Where does 2PC still make sense today?
    Reveal

    Inside a distributed database whose participants are replicated consensus groups (Spanner, CockroachDB), where blocking is rare and handled internally.

Module 14: Microservices and architecture patterns

Splitting a system into services lets teams deploy and scale independently, and adds network calls, distributed data, and operations work. This module covers when to split, how to draw boundaries, how services find and talk to each other, gateways and service meshes, and how to migrate safely.

9 lessons4 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 14.1Monolith, modular monolith, microservices
  2. 14.2Finding service boundaries
  3. 14.3How services communicate
  4. 14.4Service discovery
  5. 14.5Gateways, BFFs, and service meshes
  6. 14.6Data across services
  7. 14.7Migrating safely: the strangler fig
  8. 14.8Common mistakes
  9. 14.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. A 6-person startup asks whether to begin with 15 microservices. What do you say?
    Reveal

    Start with a modular monolith: clear internal modules, one deployable. Split out a service when a module needs independent scaling, deployment, or ownership. Microservices solve team and scale problems the startup does not have yet.

  2. Three services read and write the same database tables. Why is this a problem?
    Reveal

    They are coupled through the schema: no service can change its tables without breaking the others, and no one owns the data. It is a distributed monolith.

  3. Service A calls B, which calls C, which calls D, all synchronously, each 99.9% available. Combined availability?
    Reveal

    About 99.6% (0.999^4), and latency is the sum of all hops. Long synchronous chains are fragile.

  4. How does a service in Kubernetes find the payments service?
    Reveal

    Through DNS: payments.default.svc.cluster.local resolves to a Service virtual IP, and Kubernetes routes to healthy pods behind it.

  5. What does a service mesh sidecar do?
    Reveal

    It proxies all traffic in and out of the service, adding mTLS, retries, timeouts, load balancing, traffic shifting, and metrics without changes to application code.

14.1Monolith, modular monolith, microservices

Try it first2 minutes

Name two problems that microservices solve and two they create.

Reveal the answer

Solve: independent deployment by separate teams (no release train), independent scaling of hot parts, failure isolation, technology choice per service. Create: network latency and partial failures between services, distributed data consistency (no cross-service transactions), more infrastructure (discovery, tracing, CI/CD per service), and harder debugging.

Monolith Modular monolith Microservices
Deploy One unit One unit, strict internal modules Each service separately
Data One database One database, schema per module Database per service
Calls between parts In-process In-process through module interfaces Network (REST, gRPC, events)
Scaling Whole app Whole app Per service
Good for Small teams, early products Most teams until scale or org size demands more Many teams, independent release and scaling needs
Analogy

A food court versus one restaurant kitchen. Separate stalls can open, close, and change menus independently and one fire does not close all of them, but they need a shared payment system, trays that move between stalls, and coordination for a combo meal.

Conway's law

Systems mirror the communication structure of the organization. Service boundaries work best when they match team boundaries: one team owns a service end to end.

14.2Finding service boundaries

Try it first2 minutes

An e-commerce company plans services named UserService, DatabaseService, and ValidationService. What is wrong with these boundaries, and what would be better?

Reveal the answer

They split by technical layer, so every feature change touches all of them. Split by business capability instead: Catalog, Cart, Orders, Payments, Shipping, Customer accounts. Each owns its data and its business rules and changes mostly on its own.

  • Split by business capability (a bounded context in domain-driven design): each service owns a coherent set of business rules and the data behind them.
  • Database per service: other services get data through the owner's API or events, never by querying its tables.
  • High cohesion, low coupling: things that change together stay together. If two services must always deploy together, they are one service.
  • Signs of a distributed monolith: shared database, synchronous call chains for every request, lock-step deployments, a "common" library every service must upgrade together.

14.3How services communicate

Try it first2 minutes

Checkout needs the price (must be correct now) and should trigger loyalty points (can happen later). Sync or async for each?

Reveal the answer

Price: synchronous request (gRPC or REST) because the answer is needed to continue. Loyalty points: asynchronous event (OrderPlaced) because checkout should not wait for or fail because of the loyalty service.

  • Synchronous (REST, gRPC) when the caller needs the answer to proceed. Always set timeouts, limit retries, and add circuit breakers (Module 15).
  • Asynchronous (events, queues) for side effects, fan-out, and long work. Accept eventual consistency.
  • Keep chains short: fan out in parallel instead of in series, and cache data owned by other services where staleness is acceptable.
  • Event-carried state transfer: events include the data consumers need (OrderPlaced with items and address), so consumers do not call back for it.

14.4Service discovery

Try it first2 minutes

Payment service instances come and go with autoscaling. How does the orders service always reach a live instance?

Reveal the answer

Instances register (or are registered by the platform) in a registry with health checks. Either the caller asks the registry and load-balances itself (client-side discovery), or it calls a stable name or virtual IP and a load balancer routes to a healthy instance (server-side discovery, as in Kubernetes Services).

Client-side Server-side
Who balances Caller's library Load balancer or platform proxy
Pros No extra hop; smart balancing per call Callers stay simple; any language
Cons Library per language; registry coupling Extra hop; LB must be highly available
Examples Eureka with a client library, Consul with gRPC client balancing Kubernetes Services, AWS ALB, service mesh

14.5Gateways, BFFs, and service meshes

Try it first2 minutes

Forty services each implement mTLS, retries, and request metrics differently. Where can this logic live instead, without rewriting every service?

Reveal the answer

In a service mesh: a sidecar proxy beside each service handles mTLS, retries, timeouts, and telemetry, configured centrally by a control plane. North-south traffic (from outside) is handled by the API gateway; east-west traffic (between services) by the mesh.

  • API gateway: the front door for external clients (auth, rate limits, routing; Module 5).
  • Backend for frontend (BFF): a gateway per client type that aggregates and shapes data for that client.
  • Service mesh: sidecars (or node-level proxies) for service-to-service traffic. Strong for mTLS everywhere, canary traffic splits, and uniform metrics. Costs extra latency per hop, resource overhead, and operational complexity; adopt it when the service count justifies it.

14.6Data across services

Try it first2 minutes

The "order details" page needs order data (Orders), customer name (Customers), and shipment status (Shipping). How do you build it without a cross-service join?

Reveal the answer

Options: (1) API composition: a BFF calls all three in parallel and merges. (2) A read model: a service consumes events from all three and maintains a denormalized "order details" view (CQRS, Module 13). (3) Copy needed fields into the order at creation (customer name), accepting staleness. Use (1) for low traffic, (2) for heavy or complex reads.

  • Every piece of data has one owner; others hold copies derived from the owner's events.
  • Reports and analytics read from a warehouse fed by all services, not from service databases.
  • Cross-service invariants ("an order references a real customer") are enforced by the owning flows and sagas, not by foreign keys.

14.7Migrating safely: the strangler fig

Try it first2 minutes

You must move a 10-year-old monolith to services without a big-bang rewrite. What is the first step?

Reveal the answer

Put a routing layer (gateway or proxy) in front of the monolith so you can redirect individual routes. Then extract one well-bounded capability at a time into a new service, route its traffic there, and repeat. The monolith shrinks until it can be retired. At every step the system is working and changes can be rolled back by routing.

  • Extract the data too: a service that still reads the monolith's tables is not independent. Use CDC to sync data during the move, then switch ownership.
  • Run in parallel (shadow traffic, compare outputs) before switching critical paths.
  • Serverless functions (AWS Lambda, Cloud Functions) fit event-driven glue and spiky, short tasks: scale to zero and no servers to manage, with cold starts, execution time limits, and per-invocation cost at high volume.
In production

Most real migrations to services are slow strangler projects: a gateway routes paths, CDC keeps old and new data stores in sync during the move, and teams run old and new code paths in parallel (shadow traffic) before switching. Plan for months, not a weekend.

Interview signal

Do not open an interview with "I will use microservices". Draw the services the requirements need, show how they communicate (sync for answers, events for side effects), and mention data ownership. Boundaries with reasons beat a large box count.

14.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Microservices by default for a small team or an unproven product.
  • Shared databases between services.
  • Splitting by technical layer instead of by business capability.
  • Long synchronous call chains without timeouts and circuit breakers.
  • No distributed tracing, so a slow request across 8 services cannot be explained (Module 16).
  • Big-bang rewrites instead of incremental strangler migration.

14.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What is a bounded context?
    Reveal

    A part of the business with its own consistent model and language (Orders, Payments). It is a natural boundary for a service and its data.

  2. When should a call between services be asynchronous?
    Reveal

    When the caller does not need the result to continue: side effects, notifications, fan-out to many consumers, and slow work.

  3. What is the difference between an API gateway and a service mesh?
    Reveal

    The gateway handles north-south traffic (external clients to services): auth, rate limits, routing. The mesh handles east-west traffic (service to service): mTLS, retries, traffic shifting, telemetry.

  4. How does event-carried state transfer reduce coupling?
    Reveal

    Events carry the data consumers need, so consumers do not make synchronous callbacks to the producer and keep working when it is down.

  5. Why does the strangler fig pattern start with a routing layer?
    Reveal

    It lets you move one route at a time to new code, roll back by changing routing, and keep the system working throughout.
