Module 15: Reliability, resilience, and rate limiting

Everything fails: machines, networks, dependencies, deploys. Reliable systems expect it and contain the damage. This module covers availability math and SLOs, timeouts and retries done right, circuit breakers and bulkheads, rate limiting algorithms, load shedding, safe deployments, and disaster recovery.

10 lessons5 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 15.1Availability, SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets
  2. 15.2How systems fail
  3. 15.3Timeouts, retries, and backoff
  4. 15.4Circuit breakers, bulkheads, and fallbacks
  5. 15.5Rate limiting
  6. 15.6Load shedding and backpressure
  7. 15.7Safe deployments
  8. 15.8Disaster recovery and multi-region
  9. 15.9Common mistakes
  10. 15.10Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. 99.99% availability allows how much downtime per year?
    Reveal

    About 52.6 minutes a year (about 4.4 minutes a month).

  2. A dependency is slow, not down. Your service has no timeout on calls to it. What happens?
    Reveal

    Threads and connections wait indefinitely, pools run dry, and your service stops serving even requests that do not need the slow dependency. Slow is often worse than down.

  3. Why add random jitter to retry backoff?
    Reveal

    Without jitter, all clients that failed together retry together, creating synchronized waves of load. Jitter spreads the retries out.

  4. A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per minute. How can a client send 200 in 2 seconds?
    Reveal

    100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next. Sliding windows or token buckets fix this.

  5. What are RPO and RTO?
    Reveal

    RPO (recovery point objective): how much data you can afford to lose, as time. RTO (recovery time objective): how long you can afford to be down.

15.1Availability, SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets

Try it first2 minutes

A request passes through a load balancer (99.99%), an app tier (99.9%), and a database (99.95%), in series. What is the best availability you can promise? How would you raise it?

Reveal the answer

0.9999 x 0.999 x 0.9995 is about 99.84%. To raise it, add redundancy to the weakest tiers (more app instances across zones, a standby database with automatic failover) and remove components from the critical path.

Availability Downtime per year Per month
99% 3.65 days 7.3 hours
99.9% 8.77 hours 43.8 minutes
99.95% 4.38 hours 21.9 minutes
99.99% 52.6 minutes 4.4 minutes
99.999% 5.3 minutes 26 seconds
  • Series (all must work): multiply availabilities. Every extra dependency lowers the total.
  • Parallel (any one copy is enough): 1 - (1 - a)^n. Two independent 99% copies give 99.99%.
  • SLI (indicator): a measured number, for example the fraction of requests that succeed in under 300 ms.
  • SLO (objective): the target for the SLI, for example 99.9% over 30 days. Internal.
  • SLA (agreement): a contractual promise with penalties, set looser than the SLO.
  • Error budget: 1 - SLO. With a 99.9% SLO you may "spend" 0.1% of requests on failures. When the budget is used up, slow down releases and fix reliability; when there is budget left, ship faster.
Availability calculatorComponents in series; each can have redundant copies in parallel. Assumes independent failures and instant failover.
ComponentAvailability %CopiesTier

15.2How systems fail

Try it first2 minutes

Name four ways a dependency can fail other than "it is down".

Reveal the answer

It is slow (latency spikes), it returns errors for some requests, it returns wrong or partial data, it accepts requests but never answers (hangs), or it works for some callers but not others (a gray failure). Also: it is fine but your network path to it is not.

  • Crash failures are the easy case: health checks catch them.
  • Slow and gray failures are harder: the node looks alive but serves badly. Timeouts and outlier detection catch them.
  • Overload turns into cascading failure: one slow service makes callers hold resources, so they slow down, and their callers too.
  • Changes cause most incidents: deploys, configuration pushes, certificate expiry, schema migrations. Safe rollout matters as much as redundancy.
  • Correlated failures break redundancy assumptions: the same bug on every replica, one zone's power, a shared dependency.

15.3Timeouts, retries, and backoff

Try it first3 minutes

The gateway, the orders service, and the database client each retry failed calls 3 times. The database starts failing. How many database calls does one user click cause?

Reveal the answer

Up to 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. Retries at every layer multiply load exactly when the system is weakest, turning a brief problem into an outage. Retry at one layer (usually closest to the failure or the edge), with backoff, jitter, and a retry budget.

Rules:

  1. Every remote call has a timeout, set from the dependency's latency (for example a bit above its p99), not a default of 30 s or infinity.
  2. Propagate deadlines: if the user's request has 800 ms left, downstream calls should not wait 2 s. gRPC deadlines do this.
  3. Retry only what is safe and likely to succeed: idempotent operations (or ones with idempotency keys) and transient errors (timeouts, 503, connection reset). Do not retry 400s.
  4. Exponential backoff with jitter: wait random(0, min(cap, base x 2^attempt)) between attempts.
  5. Limit retries: a small number of attempts and a retry budget (for example, retries may add at most 10% extra load).
Retry with exponential backoff and full jitter
// TransientException: your own unchecked exception for retryable failures (timeouts, 503s)
static <T> T callWithRetry(Supplier<T> call, int maxAttempts) throws InterruptedException {
    long baseMs = 100, capMs = 5_000;
    for (int attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
        try {
            return call.get();                                   // must be idempotent
        } catch (TransientException e) {                         // timeouts, 503s: not 4xx
            if (attempt + 1 >= maxAttempts) throw e;
            long ceiling = Math.min(capMs, baseMs << attempt);   // 100, 200, 400, ...
            Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(ceiling + 1));
        }
    }
}

15.4Circuit breakers, bulkheads, and fallbacks

Try it first2 minutes

The recommendations service is down. The product page calls it on every view and waits for the timeout (1 s) each time. What two things should change?

Reveal the answer

A circuit breaker should stop calling it after a failure threshold, failing fast instead of waiting 1 s per request. And the page should degrade gracefully: render without recommendations (or with a cached or default list) instead of failing.

  • Circuit breaker: protects callers from waiting on a failing dependency and gives the dependency room to recover. Libraries: Resilience4j (Java), or the mesh (Envoy outlier detection).
  • Bulkhead: isolate resources per dependency (separate thread pools, connection pools, or instances), so a slow dependency can only exhaust its own pool, not the whole service. Named after the watertight compartments of a ship.
  • Fallbacks and graceful degradation: cached data, defaults, reduced features ("recommendations unavailable"), queued writes. Decide per feature which are critical and which are optional.
  • Fail fast on the critical path: return a clear error quickly rather than hang.

15.5Rate limiting

Try it first3 minutes

You want to allow each API key 10 requests per second on average, but also allow short bursts of up to 50. Which algorithm, and what are its two parameters?

Reveal the answer

A token bucket with refill rate 10 tokens per second and bucket size 50. Each request spends a token; an idle client accumulates up to 50 tokens for a burst; the long-run average is capped at 10 per second.

Algorithm How it works Strengths Weaknesses
Token bucket Tokens refill at rate r up to size b; each request takes one Allows bursts up to b, average r; simple state (tokens, last refill time) Bursts may be unwanted downstream
Leaky bucket Requests enter a queue that drains at a fixed rate Smooth, constant output rate Adds queueing delay; bursts wait or drop
Fixed window counter Count per calendar window (per minute) Very cheap Up to 2x the limit across a window boundary
Sliding window log Keep timestamps of recent requests; count those in the last window Exact Memory per request
Sliding window counter Weighted mix: prev_count x overlap + curr_count Close to exact, cheap Approximate
Token bucket simulatorEach request takes a token. Tokens refill at a steady rate up to the bucket size. Try a burst, then wait.

Green = allowed, red = rejected with 429. The bucket allows short bursts up to its size and a long-run rate equal to the refill rate.

Where and how to enforce limits:

  • At the edge (API gateway, CDN, WAF) for abuse and per-client quotas; inside services to protect themselves and their dependencies.
  • Key by API key, user, IP, or tenant, often several at once (per user and global).
  • Distributed counters live in Redis; do the read-check-update atomically with a Lua script, or INCR and EXPIRE key 60 NX inside one MULTI transaction; as two separate commands, a crash between them leaves a counter that never expires (Case study 2 designs this end to end).
  • Respond with 429 Too Many Requests and Retry-After; tell clients their remaining quota.
  • Decide failure behavior: if the limiter's Redis is down, fail open (allow traffic, risk overload) or fail closed (reject, risk an outage). Most public APIs fail open with a local fallback limit.

15.6Load shedding and backpressure

Try it first2 minutes

At 3x normal load, your service accepts every request, queues them, and every response takes 20 s, so all users time out. What would serve more users?

Reveal the answer

Reject excess requests early and fast (503 or 429) so the requests you accept finish within their deadline. Serving 60% of users well beats serving 100% of users badly. Shed the least important traffic first (prefetches, analytics, background sync) and keep checkout and login.

  • Load shedding: drop work when over capacity, ideally lowest priority first, before it consumes resources.
  • Bounded queues: an unbounded queue only hides overload until memory or latency explodes.
  • Adaptive concurrency limits: limit in-flight requests based on observed latency, rather than a fixed number.
  • Backpressure: slow producers down when consumers fall behind (blocking, credits, or lag-based throttling), instead of buffering forever.
  • Waiting rooms: for known spikes (ticket sales), admit users at a controlled rate (Case study 12).

15.7Safe deployments

Try it first2 minutes

A new release has a bug that fails 2% of checkouts. Which deployment strategy would have limited the blast radius, and how would you have detected it?

Reveal the answer

A canary release: send 1-5% of traffic to the new version, compare its error rate and latency with the old version, and roll back automatically when the canary is worse. Only a small share of users would have seen the bug, for minutes.

Strategy How Rollback Cost
Rolling Replace instances in batches Roll forward or back in batches Low; mixed versions run together
Blue-green Bring up a full new environment, switch traffic at once Switch back instantly Double capacity during the switch
Canary Small share of traffic first, then grow Route traffic back Needs good metrics and automation
Feature flags Ship code dark, turn features on per user or percentage Turn the flag off Flag debt; config must be managed carefully
  • Database migrations use expand and contract: add the new column or table (expand), deploy code that writes both and reads the new, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old (contract). Every step works with both code versions.
  • Configuration is code: review and canary config changes too; a bad config push has caused many large outages.

15.8Disaster recovery and multi-region

Try it first3 minutes

A payment system's region goes down. The business says: lose at most 1 second of confirmed payments, be back within 15 minutes. Which DR strategy fits, and what does the data layer need?

Reveal the answer

At least warm standby, likely active-passive with automatic failover: a second region running a scaled-down copy, with data replicated nearly synchronously (RPO about 1 s needs synchronous or very low-lag replication of the ledger). Failover must be automated and rehearsed to meet a 15-minute RTO. Active-active would need careful handling of concurrent writes to the same accounts.

  • Backups: automated, encrypted, stored in another region or account, and regularly restored in tests. An untested backup is a hope, not a backup.
  • Point-in-time recovery: base backups plus write-ahead log archives let you restore to just before a bad migration or deletion.
  • Active-passive: one region serves; the other receives replicated data and takes over on failure. Simple data model; failover takes time and may lose async-replicated writes.
  • Active-active: both regions serve. Lowest RTO; needs conflict-free data design (partition users by home region, or a globally consistent database such as Spanner, at a latency cost).
  • Practice: run failover drills (game days) and chaos experiments; recovery that is never exercised fails when needed.
In production

A practical checklist for every new dependency call in a service: timeout set from the dependency's p99, retries only for idempotent calls with backoff and jitter, a circuit breaker, a bulkhead (separate pool), a fallback, and a metric plus alert on its error rate. Most production incidents trace back to one of these missing.

Interview signal

When asked "what if X fails?", answer in three parts: how you detect it (health checks, timeouts, metrics), how the system keeps working (redundancy, failover, degradation), and how it recovers (retries, replay, reconciliation).

15.9Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • No timeouts, or library defaults of minutes.
  • Retries at every layer, without backoff, jitter, or budgets.
  • Retrying non-idempotent calls without idempotency keys.
  • Health checks that hide gray failures (always 200) or that take down the fleet when a shared dependency blips.
  • Fixed-window rate limits where bursts at boundaries matter.
  • Unbounded queues instead of load shedding.
  • Untested backups and never-rehearsed failovers.
  • Claiming 99.99% for a design with a single database and no failover.

15.10Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Two independent replicas, each 99.5% available, behind a perfect load balancer. Combined availability?
    Reveal

    1 - 0.005^2 = 99.9975%, assuming independent failures and instant failover.

  2. What is an error budget used for?
    Reveal

    To balance speed and reliability: while budget remains, teams can ship and take risks; when it is spent, they prioritize reliability work over features.

  3. What does the half-open state of a circuit breaker do?
    Reveal

    After the cooldown, it lets a limited number of test calls through. Success closes the breaker; failure opens it again.

  4. Token bucket vs leaky bucket: which smooths output to a constant rate?
    Reveal

    Leaky bucket. Token bucket allows bursts up to the bucket size.

  5. Why is "expand and contract" needed for schema changes during rolling deploys?
    Reveal

    Old and new code run at the same time, so every intermediate schema must work with both versions; expand first, contract only after all code uses the new shape.

Module 16: Observability and security

You cannot run what you cannot see, and you cannot trust what you have not secured. This module covers metrics, logs, and traces, why percentiles matter more than averages, alerting on symptoms, and the security building blocks a design must name: authentication, authorization, tokens, OAuth, mTLS, encryption, and secrets.

9 lessons5 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 16.1Metrics, logs, and traces
  2. 16.2Percentiles and tail latency
  3. 16.3Alerting and on-call
  4. 16.4Authentication and authorization
  5. 16.5OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
  6. 16.6Service-to-service security
  7. 16.7Protecting data
  8. 16.8Common mistakes
  9. 16.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Average latency is 80 ms, but users complain. What metric should you look at?
    Reveal

    High percentiles (p95, p99). The average hides the slow tail that a real share of users hit.

  2. A request touches 8 services and is slow. Which tool tells you where the time went?
    Reveal

    Distributed tracing: one trace ID across all services, with a timed span per operation.

  3. 401 vs 403?
    Reveal

    401 Unauthorized means not authenticated (no or invalid credentials). 403 Forbidden means authenticated but not allowed to do this.

  4. A JWT has been stolen. Why is that worse than a stolen session ID, and what limits the damage?
    Reveal

    A JWT is valid until it expires and services verify it without a lookup, so you cannot simply delete it. Keep access tokens short-lived (minutes), use refresh tokens that can be revoked, and keep a denylist for emergencies.

  5. Where should a database password live?
    Reveal

    In a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager), injected at runtime with access control and rotation. Never in code, images, or plain config files.

16.1Metrics, logs, and traces

Try it first2 minutes

For each question, pick metrics, logs, or traces: (a) Is the error rate up right now? (b) Why did order 4471 fail? (c) Which service added 300 ms to checkout?

Reveal the answer

(a) Metrics: cheap aggregated numbers over time, ideal for dashboards and alerts. (b) Logs: detailed events for a specific request, found by order ID or request ID. (c) Traces: the timing of each hop for one request.

Signal What it is Answers Watch out
Metrics Numbers aggregated over time (counters, gauges, histograms) Is something wrong? How much? Trends High-cardinality labels (user ID) explode cost
Logs Timestamped records of events What exactly happened to this request? Volume and cost; unstructured text is hard to query
Traces A tree of timed spans for one request across services Where did the time go? Which dependency failed? Usually sampled; needs context propagation
  • RED for services: Rate (requests/s), Errors, Duration (latency distribution).
  • USE for resources: Utilization, Saturation (queueing), Errors.
  • Structured logs (JSON) with a request ID / trace ID on every line, propagated through every hop, including message headers.
  • OpenTelemetry is the standard way to emit all three signals; backends include Prometheus and Grafana, Datadog, Jaeger, and Cloud Monitoring.

16.2Percentiles and tail latency

Try it first2 minutes

A page calls 100 backend shards in parallel and waits for all. Each shard is slow (above its p99) 1% of the time. What fraction of page loads is slow?

Reveal the answer

1 - 0.99^100, about 63%. With fan-out, a backend's rare slow case becomes the page's common case. That is why large systems track p99 and p99.9 and use techniques like hedged requests.

  • Report percentiles, not averages: p50 (typical), p95, p99 (tail), p99.9 for high-volume paths. Compute them from histograms; averaging percentiles across servers is mathematically wrong.
  • Tail causes: garbage collection pauses, queueing under load, cache misses, noisy neighbors, retries, cold starts.
  • Tail fixes: reduce fan-out, set tight timeouts, hedged requests (send a second copy to another replica if the first has not answered by the p95 time, use whichever returns first), and keep utilization below the point where queues grow.

16.3Alerting and on-call

Try it first2 minutes

An alert fires whenever any server's CPU exceeds 80%. It wakes the on-call engineer 5 times a week, and users are usually fine. What should you alert on instead?

Reveal the answer

Symptoms users feel: error rate and latency against the SLO (for example, "error budget burning 10x faster than allowed over the last hour"). CPU belongs on a dashboard for diagnosis. Every page should be urgent, actionable, and tied to user impact.

  • Page on symptoms (SLO burn rate, error rate, latency, queue lag past a threshold); ticket on causes (disk filling slowly, certificate expiring in 14 days).
  • Every alert has a runbook: what it means, how to check, how to mitigate.
  • Dashboards per service: RED metrics, dependencies, saturation, recent deploys.
  • Blameless postmortems after incidents: timeline, root causes, and action items that remove the failure class.
In production

On-call for a data pipeline adds signals beyond request metrics: consumer lag, records per minute against the expected baseline, age of the newest processed record (freshness), dead-letter queue size, and reconciliation mismatches. "Zero errors" can still mean "zero records processed".

16.4Authentication and authorization

Try it first2 minutes

User 7 calls GET /orders/9912. Order 9912 belongs to user 8. Authentication succeeded. What check is missing, and what is this bug called?

Reveal the answer

Authorization: checking that the authenticated user is allowed to read this specific resource (owner or permitted role). Skipping it is an insecure direct object reference (IDOR), one of the most common API vulnerabilities. Check ownership on every object access, server-side.

  • Authentication (AuthN): who are you? Passwords plus MFA, SSO, OAuth/OIDC, API keys, client certificates.
  • Authorization (AuthZ): what may you do? RBAC (roles such as admin, support), ABAC (attributes: department, region, time), relationship-based (owner, shared-with; Google Zanzibar style). Enforce on the server for every request and every object.
  • Least privilege for users, services, and database accounts.
Server-side session Self-contained token (JWT)
Client holds Random session ID in a cookie Signed token with claims (user, roles, expiry)
Per-request cost Lookup in a session store (Redis) Verify signature locally
Revocation Delete the session: immediate Wait for expiry, or keep a denylist
Fits Web apps, one domain APIs, mobile, many services verifying independently

JWT rules: verify signature, exp, iss, and aud; prefer asymmetric signing (RS256 or ES256) so services verify with a public key; keep access tokens short-lived; never put secrets in the payload (it is only encoded, not encrypted); verify against an allow-list of algorithms (reject alg: none and HS/RS confusion); store browser tokens in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies rather than local storage, and since browsers send cookies automatically, protect state-changing requests against CSRF.

16.5OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect

Try it first2 minutes

A budgeting app wants to read your bank transactions. Why should you never give it your bank password, and what does OAuth give instead?

Reveal the answer

A password grants everything, forever, and you cannot revoke it from one app without changing it everywhere. OAuth gives the app a limited, revocable access token for specific scopes (read transactions only), issued by the bank's authorization server after you consent. The app never sees your password.

  • OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization: an app gets an access token with scopes to call an API on a user's behalf.
  • OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds authentication on top: an ID token (a JWT) that says who the user is. "Sign in with Google" is OIDC.
  • Flows: authorization code with PKCE for web, mobile, and single-page apps; client credentials for service-to-service calls with no user. The old implicit flow is deprecated.

16.6Service-to-service security

Try it first2 minutes

An attacker gets onto your internal network. In a "trusted internal network" design, what can they do, and what design prevents it?

Reveal the answer

They can call any internal service, since services accept requests from anywhere inside. Zero-trust design prevents it: every service authenticates every caller (mTLS with service identities, or signed service tokens) and authorizes it (orders may call payments; analytics may not), regardless of network location.

  • mTLS: both sides present certificates, so each service knows the caller's identity and traffic is encrypted. A service mesh issues and rotates certificates automatically.
  • Service tokens: client-credentials OAuth tokens or signed JWTs with the calling service's identity and scopes.
  • Request signing (HMAC of method, path, body, and timestamp with a shared secret): common for partner and bank integrations and for webhooks; the timestamp and a nonce stop replays.
  • Network policies still help as a second layer: deny by default, allow known paths.

16.7Protecting data

Try it first2 minutes

You must store card numbers to charge customers monthly. How do you minimize the risk and the compliance scope?

Reveal the answer

Do not store them yourself if possible: use the payment processor's vault and keep only its token. If you must, isolate a small tokenization service that stores encrypted card numbers (keys in an HSM or KMS), returns tokens to every other system, and is the only component in PCI DSS scope.

  • In transit: TLS everywhere, including internal traffic for sensitive data.
  • At rest: disk and database encryption, plus field-level encryption for the most sensitive fields.
  • Envelope encryption: data is encrypted with a data key; the data key is encrypted with a master key held in KMS or an HSM. Rotating the master key does not require re-encrypting all data.
  • Secrets management: Vault or a cloud secrets manager, short-lived credentials, automatic rotation, audit of every access.
  • PII minimization: collect less, keep it shorter, mask it in logs, restrict who can see it, and support deletion requests.
  • Tokenization: replace sensitive values (card numbers) with tokens; only the vault can map them back.
  • Audit logs: append-only records of who accessed or changed sensitive data.
Note

Design-level defenses interviewers like to hear: CDN and WAF in front for DDoS and common attacks; rate limits per user and IP; parameterized queries against injection; per-object authorization against IDOR; idempotency keys and timestamps against replays; least-privilege IAM roles instead of long-lived keys.

Interview signal

Close every design with one or two sentences on observability (the key metric and alert) and security (how callers authenticate and what data is protected). It takes 30 seconds and is a common gap in otherwise good answers.

Go deeper

Web security basics: CORS, CSRF, XSS, SSRF

  • CORS: browsers block a page from reading responses from another origin unless the server allows it with Access-Control-Allow-Origin. It protects users, not your API; it is not authentication. Never combine a wildcard origin with credentials.
  • CSRF: another site makes the browser send a request to your site with the user's cookies. Defend with SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens on state-changing requests, and Origin checks. APIs that take tokens in an Authorization header are not exposed this way.
  • XSS: attacker-supplied script runs inside your page. Escape all output by context, set a Content-Security-Policy, and keep session cookies HttpOnly so scripts cannot read them.
  • SSRF: your server fetches a URL the attacker controls (webhooks, link previews, image fetchers, crawlers) and is pointed at internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254). Allow-list destinations, resolve DNS and block private and link-local ranges before connecting, route fetches through an egress proxy, and require the token-based metadata service (IMDSv2 on AWS).

16.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Averages instead of percentiles in dashboards and SLOs.
  • No trace or request ID propagated across services and queues.
  • Alerting on causes (CPU, memory) instead of user-facing symptoms.
  • Authenticating but not authorizing each object (IDOR).
  • Long-lived JWTs with no revocation path; secrets in JWT payloads.
  • Trusting the internal network instead of authenticating service calls.
  • Secrets in code or config files, and sensitive data in logs.

16.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What are RED and USE?
    Reveal

    RED (rate, errors, duration) for request-driven services; USE (utilization, saturation, errors) for resources like CPU, disks, and pools.

  2. What is a hedged request?
    Reveal

    Sending a duplicate request to another replica if the first has not answered within a short delay (for example the p95), and using whichever answers first. It trims tail latency for a small amount of extra load.

  3. OAuth vs OIDC in one sentence each.
    Reveal

    OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization: an app gets a scoped token to call an API on a user's behalf. OIDC adds authentication: an ID token that states who the user is.

  4. Why is PKCE used even by apps that cannot keep a client secret?
    Reveal

    It binds the authorization code to a secret verifier created by the app for that login, so a stolen code cannot be exchanged for tokens by anyone else.

  5. What does envelope encryption make cheap?
    Reveal

    Key rotation and access control: the master key stays in KMS, only small data keys are re-wrapped, and every decrypt of a data key is authorized and audited by KMS.

Module 17: Building blocks toolkit

Many case studies hinge on one specialized component: unique IDs, a Bloom filter, a geospatial index, a search or vector index, a leaderboard, a delayed-job store. This module is the toolkit: what each block does, how it works inside, and when to reach for it.

10 lessons6 figures7 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 17.1Unique ID generation
  2. 17.2Probabilistic data structures
  3. 17.3Geospatial indexing
  4. 17.4Search and inverted indexes
  5. 17.5Counters, leaderboards, and top-K
  6. 17.6Delayed jobs and scheduling
  7. 17.7Push, pull, and fan-out
  8. 17.8Vector search and LLM-era building blocks
  9. 17.9Common mistakes
  10. 17.10Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Why not use a database auto-increment ID as the public order ID in a sharded system?
    Reveal

    Each shard would generate its own sequence (collisions), a single global sequence is a bottleneck, and sequential IDs leak business volume. Use Snowflake-style or UUIDv7 IDs.

  2. A web crawler must check whether it has seen a URL among 10 billion. Exact set too big for memory. What structure?
    Reveal

    A Bloom filter: a few bits per URL, no false negatives, a small false positive rate (skipping a few unseen URLs is acceptable).

  3. Count unique daily visitors across 500M events with a few KB of memory?
    Reveal

    HyperLogLog: about 12 KB per counter in Redis with under 1% standard error.

  4. "Find restaurants within 2 km" on 50M places. What index?
    Reveal

    A geospatial index: geohash prefixes in a B-tree, a quadtree, S2 or H3 cells, or a database with spatial indexes (PostGIS, Elasticsearch geo queries).

  5. Real-time leaderboard of 10M players: top 100 and any player's rank. What do you use?
    Reveal

    A Redis sorted set: ZADD to update scores, ZRANGE key 0 99 REV for the top 100, ZREVRANK for a player's rank, each O(log n).

17.1Unique ID generation

Try it first3 minutes

You need IDs that are unique across 200 servers, roughly sortable by time, fit in 64 bits, and need no network call per ID. Design the bits.

Reveal the answer

Snowflake: 1 unused sign bit, 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch (about 69 years), 10 bits of machine ID (1,024 machines), 12 bits of per-millisecond sequence (4,096 IDs per ms per machine). Each machine generates IDs locally; uniqueness comes from the machine ID; sorting by ID approximately sorts by time.

Option Size Sortable Coordination Notes
DB auto-increment 64 bit Yes Single DB Bottleneck and single point of failure; leaks counts
UUIDv4 128 bit No None Random; scatters inserts across a B-tree index
UUIDv7 128 bit Yes (ms) None Time-ordered prefix plus random bits (RFC 9562, 2024); index-friendly; PostgreSQL 18 has a built-in uuidv7()
Snowflake 64 bit Yes (ms) Machine ID assignment Compact; watch clock moving backwards
Ticket server / ranges 64 bit Roughly A central counter hands out blocks (1,000 IDs at a time) Simple; small gaps when a server restarts
Watch out

Snowflake trusts the clock. If NTP moves time backwards, a generator can repeat IDs; implementations wait until the clock passes the last timestamp, or refuse to generate.

17.2Probabilistic data structures

Try it first2 minutes

A Bloom filter says "maybe present" for a key. Can you trust it? What if it says "not present"?

Reveal the answer

"Not present" is always correct (no false negatives). "Maybe present" can be wrong (a false positive), so check the real store when it matters. That makes Bloom filters ideal as a cheap guard in front of expensive lookups.

Structure Answers Memory Error Typical use
Bloom filter Is x in the set? About 10 bits per item for 1% false positives False positives only Skip disk lookups (LSM SSTables), crawler seen-URLs, block known-bad items, cache penetration guard
HyperLogLog How many distinct items? About 12 KB per counter (Redis) About 0.8% standard error Unique visitors, distinct queries
Count-min sketch About how often did x occur? Small fixed grid of counters Overestimates only Heavy hitters, top-K trending, rate of an IP
  • A standard Bloom filter cannot delete items (clearing a bit could erase others); counting Bloom filters or cuckoo filters support deletes.
  • Count-min sketch: d hash functions each increment one counter in its own row; the estimate is the minimum across rows. Pair it with a min-heap to keep the current top K.

17.3Geospatial indexing

Try it first2 minutes

Why can't you answer "places within 2 km" with a normal B-tree index on (lat, lng)?

Reveal the answer

A B-tree sorts by one dimension first. An index on (lat, lng) can narrow latitude, but every place in that latitude band, around the whole globe, still matches. You need an index that keeps points close in both dimensions close in the index: geohash strings, quadtrees, space-filling curves (S2), or R-trees.

Approach How Strengths Weaknesses
Geohash Base32 string of interleaved lat/lng bits; prefix = cell Works with any key-value or B-tree store; easy sharding by prefix Fixed cell sizes; edge effects need neighbor queries
Quadtree Recursive split of dense cells Adapts to density Usually in memory; must be rebuilt or updated
S2 / H3 Hierarchical cells on a sphere (squares / hexagons) Even cells, good coverings, used at Google and Uber More complex library
R-tree (PostGIS) Bounding-box tree Arbitrary shapes, exact queries in SQL Single-database scale

For moving objects (drivers updating every few seconds), keep current positions in memory, keyed by cell (for example Redis geo sets or an in-memory grid per city), not in a disk index that is rewritten constantly. Case study 11 builds this.

17.4Search and inverted indexes

Try it first2 minutes

Why is WHERE description LIKE '%refund%' slow on 100M rows, and what does a search engine do instead?

Reveal the answer

A leading wildcard cannot use a B-tree index, so the database scans every row. A search engine builds an inverted index at write time: each term maps to the list of documents containing it, so a query looks up a few posting lists and intersects them.

  • Elasticsearch / OpenSearch: an index is split into primary shards (fixed at creation) with replicas; queries scatter to shards and gather the top results; relevance uses BM25 by default.
  • Near real-time: new documents become searchable after a refresh (1 s by default), not instantly.
  • Not the source of truth: write to the database first, then feed the search index through CDC or events; rebuild the index from the database when mappings change.
  • Analyzers decide tokenization, lowercasing, stemming, and synonyms; they matter more for quality than hardware.

17.5Counters, leaderboards, and top-K

Try it first2 minutes

How do you show "views: 1.2M" on a viral video receiving 50,000 views per second without overloading one database row?

Reveal the answer

Do not update one row per view. Count in memory or in sharded Redis counters (video:42:views#0..#15), flush aggregated increments to the database every few seconds, and read the displayed number from a cache. Exact real-time precision is not needed for a view count.

  • Counters: Redis INCR (atomic), sharded counters for hot keys, periodic flush to durable storage. Approximate is usually fine for display.
  • Leaderboards: Redis sorted sets (ZADD, ZINCRBY, ZRANGE ... REV, ZREVRANK). For hundreds of millions of players, shard by score range or keep exact ranks only for the top tier and approximate the rest.
  • Top-K / trending: exact counting per key in a stream processor for moderate cardinality; count-min sketch plus a heap for huge cardinality; windowed (last hour) using stream windows (Module 12, Case study 15).

17.6Delayed jobs and scheduling

Try it first2 minutes

Send a reminder exactly 24 hours after sign-up for 10 million users a day. How do you store and trigger these without scanning a huge table every second?

Reveal the answer

Store each job keyed by its due time: a Redis sorted set scored by due timestamp (workers pop entries with score <= now), or a database table indexed by (due_at, status) and partitioned into time buckets that workers claim with SKIP LOCKED. Workers only look at the current bucket. Jobs must be idempotent, because a worker can crash after sending.

  • Delay queues: some brokers support short delays (SQS delay up to 15 minutes; RabbitMQ per-message TTL plus a dead-letter exchange); longer or exact delays need a scheduler store.
  • Time-bucketed tables scale to billions of scheduled tasks; Case study 14 designs a distributed job scheduler with leases and retries.

17.7Push, pull, and fan-out

Try it first2 minutes

A user with 50M followers posts. Writing the post into 50M follower feeds takes minutes. What alternative serves their followers?

Reveal the answer

Do not fan out on write for that user. Store the post once; when a follower opens their feed, merge in posts from the few celebrities they follow at read time (fan-out on read). Normal users still use fan-out on write. This hybrid is the standard answer (Case study 4).

Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull)
Work happens When content is created When content is read
Read latency Fast: precomputed Slower: gather and merge
Write cost Proportional to followers Constant
Problem case Celebrities Users who follow many active accounts

Presence (online status) is a related pattern: clients send heartbeats every N seconds; a key with a TTL (online:user7, expiring after 2N) marks them online; changes are pushed only to friends who are currently connected.

In production

Many of these blocks are one command away in existing infrastructure: Redis has sorted sets, HyperLogLog, Bloom filters (module), and geo commands; PostgreSQL has PostGIS and partial indexes; Elasticsearch handles text and geo queries. Reach for the existing tool before building a custom index.

Interview signal

Use these blocks by name with their trade-off: "a Bloom filter to skip known URLs, accepting a 1% false positive rate", "Snowflake IDs so posts sort by time without a central counter". Naming the error or cost is what shows depth.

17.8Vector search and LLM-era building blocks

Try it first2 minutes

A support portal must match "my card was charged twice" to the help article "Duplicate transactions", which shares no words with it. Why does keyword search fail, and what replaces it?

Reveal the answer

Keyword search (BM25 over an inverted index) needs shared terms. Semantic search turns queries and documents into vectors with an embedding model, so similar meanings land close together, and finds the nearest vectors. Production systems usually combine both (hybrid search).

  • Embeddings: a model maps text or images to vectors of hundreds to a few thousand numbers; similarity is cosine or dot product. Changing the model means re-embedding everything, so version indexes.
  • Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes: exact search compares against every vector. HNSW (a layered proximity graph) is fast with high recall but memory-hungry; IVF clusters vectors and searches only nearby clusters, often with compression (product quantization). Both trade a little recall for large speedups.
  • Where vectors live: pgvector inside PostgreSQL for small and medium corpora; OpenSearch or Elasticsearch k-NN alongside text search; dedicated vector databases (Milvus, Qdrant, Pinecone) or managed services at large scale.
  • Hybrid ranking: run BM25 and vector search, merge the lists (for example reciprocal rank fusion), optionally rerank the top results with a stronger model. Apply access-control filters during retrieval so users never see chunks they may not read.
  • Serving LLM features: rate limits and quotas counted in tokens, not requests; streaming responses over SSE; tight timeouts with fallbacks; caching repeated prompts; and cost tracking per tenant. Keep the index fresh from the source of truth through CDC, like any search index.

17.9Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Auto-increment IDs across shards, or random UUIDv4 as a clustered primary key on a hot table.
  • Treating a Bloom filter "maybe" as "yes".
  • Exact distinct counts or exact view counts where approximate answers are fine and far cheaper.
  • Lat/lng B-tree indexes for radius search.
  • Search index as the source of truth.
  • Scanning a whole jobs table to find due work.
  • Fan-out on write for celebrity accounts.

17.10Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. How many IDs per millisecond can one Snowflake worker generate, and what happens beyond that?
    Reveal

    4,096 (12 sequence bits). After that it waits for the next millisecond.

  2. Why does a geohash search query neighboring cells?
    Reveal

    Points close to the user can lie across a cell boundary and have a different prefix; checking the 8 neighbors covers them.

  3. Which probabilistic structure would you use for "top 10 hashtags in the last hour" at Twitter scale?
    Reveal

    A count-min sketch per window to estimate counts, with a min-heap of the current top K, or exact counting in a stream processor if the key space is manageable.

  4. How does a Redis sorted set give a player's rank quickly?
    Reveal

    It is ordered by score (a skip list plus a hash table), so ZREVRANK finds the position in O(log n).

  5. Why must search indexes be fed from the database rather than written directly by the app alongside the DB?
    Reveal

    Two separate writes can diverge on failure (dual write). Feeding from the database's change stream keeps the index eventually consistent with the source of truth and rebuildable.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Case study 1Starter35 min

Case study 1: URL shortener

Turn long URLs into short codes and redirect fast. A classic first design: tiny writes, huge read volume, and one real puzzle, generating short unique codes at scale.

Uses: M3 APIs, M6 caching, M17 IDs
Your status

On this page

  1. C1.1Requirements
  2. C1.2Estimates
  3. C1.3API
  4. C1.4Data model
  5. C1.5High-level design
  6. C1.6Deep dives
  7. C1.7Failures and bottlenecks
  8. C1.8What a strong answer shows
  9. C1.9Follow-up questions
Try it first35 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design it yourself first: requirements with numbers, estimates, API, data model, a diagram of the write and read paths, and two deep dives. Then compare section by section.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: a 7-character base62 code and why 7 is enough; a code generation scheme that cannot collide (counter ranges or a key service) or handles collisions (hash plus retry); a cache in front of a key-value store for redirects; 301 vs 302 and its effect on analytics; click analytics sent asynchronously; expiry, custom aliases, and abuse protection.

C1.1Requirements

Functional

  • Create a short URL for a long URL; optional custom alias and expiry.
  • Redirect a short URL to its long URL.
  • Optional: click counts per URL.
  • Out of scope: user accounts UI, link editing, QR codes.

Non-functional

  • 100M new URLs per day; reads outnumber writes about 100 to 1.
  • Redirect latency under 50 ms at p99 (excluding the user's network).
  • 99.99% availability for redirects; creation can be slightly less available.
  • Codes never collide and are not guessable in sequence; links last 5 years by default.

C1.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Write QPS 100M / 86,400 about 1,200/s, about 3,500/s at peak
Read QPS 1,200 x 100 about 120,000/s, about 350,000/s at peak
URLs over 5 years 100M x 365 x 5 about 180 billion
Storage 180B x 500 bytes about 90 TB before replication
Code length 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion 7 base62 characters are enough

What it means: reads dominate, so the redirect path must be served mostly from cache. 90 TB and simple key lookups point to a horizontally scalable key-value store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) or sharded SQL keyed by code.

C1.3API

Endpoints
POST /v1/urls
  { "long_url": "https://...", "custom_alias": "sale24", "expires_at": "2027-01-01" }
  -> 201 { "code": "aZ3k9Qx", "short_url": "https://sho.rt/aZ3k9Qx" }
  -> 409 if the alias is taken, 400 for an invalid URL, 429 if rate limited

GET /{code}
  -> 302 Location: https://...     (or 301, see deep dives)
  -> 404 unknown code, 410 expired

C1.4Data model

Field Type Notes
code string, primary key 7 characters; the partition key
long_url string up to about 2 KB
owner_id ID, nullable for rate limits and management
created_at, expires_at timestamps expires_at can drive a store-level TTL

One access pattern dominates: get by code. A key-value store partitioned by code spreads load evenly with no hot shards except viral links, which the cache absorbs.

C1.5High-level design

  • Shorten service takes the next ID from a block it leased, encodes it in base62, and writes code -> long_url with a conditional insert.
  • Redirect service reads the cache, falls back to the store on a miss, fills the cache, and returns the redirect. It emits a click event asynchronously.
  • Separate read and write services so the 100x larger read path scales and deploys on its own.

C1.6Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    How do you generate the code?

    Compare hashing the URL, a counter in base62, and a pre-generated key service.

    Write your answer, then reveal
    Approach How Pros Cons
    Hash + truncate First 7 chars of base62(SHA-256(long URL)) Same URL gets same code; stateless Collisions: must check and retry with a salt; extra read per write
    Counter + base62 Unique number from a counter, encoded in base62 Never collides; no read before write Needs distributed counter; sequential codes are guessable
    Key generation service Pre-generate random unused codes; servers take batches Random, no collisions, fast Extra service and storage; keys in a batch lost on a crash (acceptable)

    A solid choice: each shorten server leases a block of IDs (for example 1M) from a small strongly consistent store, so there is no per-request coordination. To avoid guessable sequential codes, pass the number through a reversible scramble (a fixed bijective permutation or format-preserving encryption) that maps the range [0, 62^7) onto itself, so codes stay 7 characters (a full 64-bit number can need 11 base62 characters).

  2. 2
    301 or 302?

    What changes for users, caches, and analytics?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    301 Moved Permanently lets browsers and proxies cache the redirect by default, so repeat clicks may never reach you: less load, but you lose click counts and cannot reliably change or expire the target. 302 Found (or 307) is not cached by default, so every click hits your service: accurate analytics and control, more load. In practice the Cache-Control header decides caching as much as the code does: either code can work with Cache-Control: private, max-age=... (Bitly, for example, uses 301). 302 or 307 is the safe default when the target can change.

  3. 3
    How do you serve 350K redirects per second at p99 under 50 ms?

    Which layers absorb the reads?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A Redis cluster in front of the store with LRU eviction; hot links have hit ratios near 100%. Size the cache from links clicked per day, not from all 180B links: even 100M active links x 500 bytes is about 50 GB, which a small Redis cluster holds. Redirect servers can also keep a small in-process cache for the very hottest codes. The store handles only misses, as single-key lookups.

  4. 4
    How do you count clicks without slowing redirects?

    Where do click events go?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The redirect service publishes a small event (code, time, referrer, country) to Kafka without waiting on it, and a stream job aggregates counts per code per minute into an analytics store. Losing a tiny fraction of events in a crash is acceptable for analytics; the redirect itself must never fail because analytics is down.

  5. 5
    Custom aliases and duplicate long URLs

    How do you prevent two users from claiming the same alias? Should the same long URL return the same code?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Write with a conditional put (insert only if absent); the loser gets 409. Use a separate namespace or minimum length for aliases so they never collide with generated codes. For duplicates, most services create a new code per request (different owners, expiries, and analytics); deduplicating needs an index on a hash of the long URL and leaks whether someone else shortened it.

  6. 6
    Expiry and abuse

    How do you remove expired links and stop abuse?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Store expires_at; the store's TTL feature deletes rows, and the redirect service checks expiry on read (return 410) in case deletion lags. Rate-limit creation per user and IP, check long URLs against malware and phishing lists asynchronously (disable the code if flagged), and never use sequential codes that allow enumerating everyone's links.

C1.7Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
A link goes viral One key gets most traffic Cache hit near 100%; in-process cache; CDN caching with a short TTL
Cache cluster down All reads hit the store Store sized for it with headroom, or rate-limited fallback; replicas for the cache
ID range store down New blocks cannot be leased Servers hold large blocks, so creation continues for hours
Analytics pipeline down Lost or delayed counts Redirects unaffected; Kafka retains events for replay
Region outage Redirects fail Multi-region read replicas of the store and caches; GeoDNS

C1.8What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): correct estimates and code length, a collision-free generation scheme with its trade-offs, cache in front of a partitioned key-value store, 301 vs 302 explained, async analytics. L5 adds: multi-region active-active reads, hot-key handling, abuse and security (scanning, enumeration), data retention and cost, and a clear story for what happens when each component fails.

C1.9Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. How many characters do you need for 1 trillion URLs?
    Reveal

    62^7 is about 3.5 trillion, so 7 base62 characters. 6 characters give about 57 billion, not enough.

  2. Why not use the database's auto-increment ID?
    Reveal

    A single sequence is a write bottleneck and single point of failure, and sequential codes expose volume and allow enumeration. Leased ranges plus scrambling keep uniqueness without those problems.

  3. A viral link's cache entry expires and 50,000 requests miss at once. What protects the URL store?
    Reveal

    Request coalescing (single-flight) so one request reloads the key while the others wait, refreshing hot keys before they expire, and jittered TTLs so many keys do not expire together (Module 6).

  4. How would you support editing the destination of a link?
    Reveal

    Use 302 so clients do not cache the old target, update the row, and delete the cache entry (cache-aside delete on write).

  5. How do you make redirects fast for users in India and the US?
    Reveal

    Deploy redirect services and caches in both regions, replicate the URL store to both (reads are local; writes can go to a home region or a multi-region store), and use GeoDNS to route users to the nearest region.

Case study 2Starter35 min

Case study 2: Distributed rate limiter

Limit how many requests each client can make, across dozens of gateway instances, adding only a millisecond or two. The interesting parts are the algorithm, atomic shared state, placement, and what happens when the limiter itself fails.

Uses: M15 rate limiting, M6 Redis
Your status

On this page

  1. C2.1Requirements
  2. C2.2Estimates
  3. C2.3Where it runs
  4. C2.4Algorithm and atomic state
  5. C2.5Deep dives
  6. C2.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C2.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C2.8Follow-up questions
Try it first35 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a rate limiter for a public API: requirements, algorithm choice, where it runs, how instances share state, the response to clients, and failure behavior.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: rules per key (API key, user, IP) and per window; token bucket or sliding window with reasons; enforcement in the gateway; shared state in Redis updated atomically with a Lua script; 429 with Retry-After and quota headers; fail-open with a local fallback; rule configuration pushed to gateways; and a note on multi-region accuracy.

C2.1Requirements

Functional

  • Limit requests per client key per rule, for example 100 per minute per API key, 10 per second per IP for login.
  • Several rules can apply to one request (per second and per day; per user and global).
  • Rejected requests get 429 Too Many Requests with retry information.
  • Rules change without redeploying.

Non-functional

  • 1M requests/s across all gateways; 10M active keys.
  • Adds under 2 ms at p99.
  • The limiter must not take the API down: if it fails, traffic flows (fail open) with a rough local limit.
  • Approximate accuracy is acceptable (a few percent over the limit briefly).

C2.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Limiter checks One per rule per request 1-3M Redis operations/s
State per key Tokens + timestamp in a hash, about 50-100 bytes 10M keys x 2 rules x 100 B = about 2 GB
Redis cluster About 100K-plus ops/s per shard 10-30 shards with replicas

C2.3Where it runs

Placement Pros Cons
Client side No server cost Untrusted; clients can ignore it
API gateway / middleware One place for all services; rejects before backends spend work Gateway needs shared state
Sidecar / service mesh Per-service limits without code Configuration spread out
Inside each service Protects that service's own resources Duplicated logic

Put user-facing quotas in the gateway; let individual services also protect themselves (concurrency limits, load shedding).

C2.4Algorithm and atomic state

Token bucket per key: allows short bursts up to the bucket size and an average rate equal to the refill rate (Module 15 compares the alternatives). The read-refill-take-write sequence must be atomic, or two gateways can both see the last token and both allow. A Lua script runs atomically in Redis:

Token bucket in Redis (one round trip, atomic)
-- KEYS[1] = bucket key, ARGV = capacity, refill per second, cost
local cap, rate, cost = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[3])
local t = redis.call('TIME')                          -- server clock: no client skew
local now = tonumber(t[1]) + tonumber(t[2]) / 1e6
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or cap
local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + math.max(0, now - ts) * rate)  -- refill; clamp if clock moved back
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then tokens = tokens - cost; allowed = 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap / rate) * 2)   -- idle keys disappear
return { allowed, math.floor(tokens) }

For a simple fixed window, INCR key plus EXPIRE key 60 works only if both run atomically (one Lua script, or INCR plus EXPIRE key 60 NX inside MULTI on Redis 7+); otherwise a crash between them leaves a counter that never expires. A sliding window counter keeps two window counters and weights the previous one.

C2.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Why not keep counters in each gateway's memory?

    What goes wrong with 40 gateway instances?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Each instance sees only its share of traffic, so a client spread across 40 instances gets up to 40x the limit. Options: shared counters in Redis (accurate, one network hop), routing each key to a fixed gateway by consistent hashing (local counters work, but uneven load), or local counters with a per-instance share of the limit (limit / N, inaccurate when traffic is uneven). Shared Redis is the usual answer; local counters work as a fallback.

  2. 2
    Redis is down or slow. What does the gateway do?

    Fail open or fail closed?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Set a tight timeout (a few ms) on the limiter call. On failure, most public APIs fail open so a limiter outage does not become an API outage, but switch to a local in-memory limiter with a conservative per-instance limit to keep some protection. Security-critical limits (login attempts, OTP sends) may fail closed instead. Alert in both cases.

  3. 3
    How do you stop one huge customer's key from overloading one Redis shard?

    Think hot keys.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The key's bucket lives on one shard, but each request is one cheap script call, so even 50K/s for one key is usually fine. Beyond that: check a local short-lived "this key is over limit" flag before calling Redis (rejected clients cost nothing), or split the key's limit across N sub-buckets on different shards.

  4. 4
    Global limits across regions

    A customer's limit is 1,000/s worldwide and they call from 3 regions.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Exact global counting needs cross-region round trips on every request, which is too slow. Common answers: give each region a share of the limit (static or adjusted every few seconds from usage), or count locally and sync totals asynchronously, accepting brief overshoot. Say that strict global limits trade latency for accuracy.

  5. 5
    What does the client see?

    Design the response.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After (seconds), plus quota headers such as X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset (an IETF draft standardizes RateLimit headers). Document limits; clients should back off with jitter.

  6. 6
    How are rules managed?

    Where do they live and how do gateways learn about changes?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Rules (key type, limit, window, burst, scope) live in a config store or database, owned by a small admin service. Gateways cache them in memory and refresh on a push (watch on etcd, a pub/sub message) or poll every few seconds. Rule changes are versioned and can be rolled out gradually.

C2.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Redis shard failure Limiter calls for its keys fail Replicas with automatic failover; fail open to local limits meanwhile
Redis latency spike Every request slows Tight timeout, fail open, local over-limit cache
Bad rule pushed Legitimate traffic rejected Versioned rules, gradual rollout, quick rollback, dry-run mode that logs instead of rejecting
Clock differences between gateways Inconsistent refill Use Redis server time inside the script
Many users behind one IP (carrier NAT, offices) Legitimate users blocked together Limit by API key or user first; keep IP limits generous; for IPv6, limit by /64 prefix since one user can rotate addresses

C2.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): the algorithm and its burst behavior, atomic updates with Lua, gateway placement, correct 429 response, fail-open decision with reasons. L5 adds: multi-region limits, hot-key protection, rule management and safe rollout, a dry-run mode, and limits per tenant tier as a product feature.

C2.8Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why is GET count; if count < limit then INCR wrong across gateways?
    Reveal

    Two gateways can read the same count and both increment past the limit. The check and update must be one atomic operation (INCR then compare, or a Lua script).

  2. Token bucket or sliding window log for a login endpoint allowing 5 attempts per 15 minutes per account?
    Reveal

    A sliding window (log or counter): the limit is about attempts in any 15-minute span, and bursts are exactly what you want to block. Volume is low, so the log's memory cost is fine.

  3. How do you limit concurrent requests rather than requests per second?
    Reveal

    A counter of in-flight requests per key: increment on start, decrement on finish (with a TTL or lease so crashed requests do not leak), reject when at the maximum.

  4. How would you test the limiter before enforcing a new rule?
    Reveal

    Shadow or dry-run mode: evaluate the rule and log or emit metrics on what would have been rejected, then enforce once the numbers look right.

Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design put(key, value) and get(key) for a store holding 100 TB with 500K ops/s that must stay writable when nodes fail. Cover partitioning, replication, consistency, failure handling, and the storage engine on each node.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: consistent hashing with virtual nodes; N replicas on distinct nodes and zones; tunable N, R, W quorums; versioning and conflict resolution (vector clocks or last-write-wins); gossip-based membership and failure detection; hinted handoff for short outages and Merkle-tree anti-entropy for long ones; read repair; and an LSM-tree storage engine with commit log, memtable, SSTables, and Bloom filters.

C3.1Requirements

Functional: put(key, value), get(key), delete(key). Values up to about 1 MB, typically a few KB.

Non-functional

  • 100 TB of data, 500K operations/s, growing.
  • Always writable: accept writes during node failures and partitions (AP), with tunable consistency per request.
  • Single-digit millisecond latency at p99 within a region.
  • Add and remove nodes without downtime; no single point of failure.

C3.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Raw data with 3 replicas 100 TB x 3 300 TB
Nodes for storage 300 TB / about 4 TB usable per node about 75-100 nodes
Load per node 500K x 3 replicas / 100 nodes about 15K ops/s per node, comfortable for LSM storage

C3.3API and data model

Interface
get(key)                -> list of (value, version)   # several values if concurrent writes conflicted
put(key, value, ctx)    -> ok                          # ctx = version the client last read
delete(key, ctx)        -> ok                          # writes a tombstone
consistency per call:  ONE | QUORUM | ALL

The store treats values as opaque bytes. A version (vector clock, or a timestamp for last-write-wins) travels with each value.

C3.4High-level design

  • Partitioning: consistent hashing with virtual nodes (Module 10). Each node announces its tokens; any node can compute where a key lives.
  • Replication: the preference list for a key is the next N distinct physical nodes clockwise, placed in different racks or zones.
  • Coordinator: the node a client contacts (or a partition-aware client) forwards to the replicas and waits for W acks or R replies.
  • No leader per key: any replica accepts writes, which keeps writes available during failures.

C3.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Consistency choices

    Pick N, R, W for (a) a shopping cart that must always accept writes and (b) a user profile that should rarely be stale.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    N = 3 for both. (a) W = 1, R = 1, or W = 2 with sloppy quorums: writes almost never fail; conflicts are merged later. (b) W = 2, R = 2 (QUORUM): R + W > N means reads overlap the latest write unless concurrent writes or sloppy quorums intervene. The API lets each request choose.

  2. 2
    Conflicting writes

    Two clients write the same key on different replicas during a partition. What does the store return later?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    With last-write-wins (Cassandra), the higher timestamp wins and the other write is silently lost; simple but depends on clocks. With vector clocks (Dynamo, Riak), the store detects that neither version descends from the other and returns both ("siblings"); the application merges them (union of carts) and writes back the merged value with a new clock.

  3. 3
    Detecting failures

    How do nodes learn that a node is down, without a central master?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Gossip: every second each node exchanges membership and heartbeat counters with a few random peers, so state spreads through the cluster in a few rounds. A node whose heartbeat stops advancing is suspected down (Cassandra uses an adaptive accrual failure detector). Suspicion only affects routing; data stays assigned until an operator or policy removes the node permanently.

  4. 4
    Temporary failures

    Replica D is down for 2 minutes. How do writes for its keys still reach W = 2?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff: the coordinator writes to the next healthy node on the ring (F) instead, with a hint "this belongs to D". When D returns, F sends the hinted writes to D and deletes them. Writes stay available; the overlap guarantee is weaker during the outage.

  5. 5
    Permanent divergence

    A replica was down for a day or lost writes. How do replicas converge without copying everything?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Anti-entropy with Merkle trees: each replica keeps a hash tree over its key ranges; two replicas compare roots and descend only into subtrees whose hashes differ, then exchange just those keys. Read repair fixes stale replicas noticed during reads.

  6. 6
    Storage engine

    What does each node do with a write?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Append to a commit log (durability), insert into an in-memory memtable, acknowledge. When the memtable fills, flush it as an immutable sorted SSTable; background compaction merges SSTables and drops overwritten values and expired tombstones. Reads check the memtable, then SSTables newest first, skipping files with per-file Bloom filters.

  7. 7
    Deletes

    Why can't a delete just remove the key from one replica?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A replica that missed the delete would later "resurrect" the value through repair. Deletes write a tombstone that replicates like a value and is removed only after a grace period longer than any expected outage.

  8. 8
    Adding a node

    How does a new node join without downtime?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    It takes tokens on the ring, and existing replicas stream the affected ranges to it in the background (throttled). While streaming runs, writes go to the old owners and the joining node, but reads stay on the old owners, since the new node does not have all the data yet; when streaming completes, ownership switches.

C3.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Node down briefly Its replicas miss writes Sloppy quorum, hinted handoff, read repair
Node lost Replication factor drops for its ranges Rebuild from other replicas; anti-entropy
Zone outage Up to one replica per key lost if placed well Place replicas across zones
Hot key One replica set overloaded Client-side caching, key splitting, more replicas for reads
Compaction backlog Read latency rises, disk fills Throttle writes, tune compaction strategy, add nodes

C3.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): consistent hashing with virtual nodes, replication on distinct nodes, R + W > N and what it means, conflict handling, hinted handoff, and an LSM write path. L5 adds: precise trade-offs of sloppy quorums, tombstones and resurrection, gossip and failure detection details, compaction strategies, multi-datacenter replication, and operational concerns like streaming and rebalancing.

C3.8Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why use virtual nodes?
    Reveal

    They balance data across nodes, spread a failed node's load across many peers, and let bigger machines take more tokens.

  2. How is this different from a single-leader database like PostgreSQL with replicas?
    Reveal

    Any replica accepts writes, there is no failover step, and writes stay available in partitions. The cost: conflicts, weaker consistency, and no multi-key transactions.

  3. How would you support range queries?
    Reveal

    Hash partitioning destroys key order. Use compound keys (partition key hashed, clustering keys sorted inside the partition) for ranges within a partition, or range partitioning with dynamic splitting (Bigtable-style) for global ranges.

  4. Why might QUORUM reads still return stale data?
    Reveal

    A concurrent write may be in progress, a sloppy quorum may have stored the write on stand-in nodes, or a failed write may have reached fewer than W replicas but not been rolled back.

Case study 4: News feed

Show each user a feed of recent posts from people they follow, in under 200 ms, for hundreds of millions of users. The core decision is when to do the work of assembling feeds: when a post is written, or when a feed is read.

Uses: M6 caching, M12 queues, M17 fan-out
Your status

On this page

  1. C4.1Requirements
  2. C4.2Estimates
  3. C4.3API
  4. C4.4Data model
  5. C4.5High-level design
  6. C4.6Deep dives
  7. C4.7Failures and bottlenecks
  8. C4.8What a strong answer shows
  9. C4.9Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design the home feed for a social app: posting, following, and reading a paginated feed. Include estimates, the fan-out strategy, storage for posts and feeds, and how celebrities are handled.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: fan-out on write into per-user feed lists in a cache, fan-out on read for celebrity accounts (hybrid), a post store and follow graph store, hydration of post IDs into full posts from caches, cursor pagination, async fan-out workers via Kafka, feeds only for active users, and how deletes, privacy, and new follows behave.

C4.1Requirements

Functional

  • Publish a post (text, images).
  • Follow and unfollow users.
  • Read a home feed of posts from followed users, newest first (ranking is an extension), paginated.
  • Out of scope: comments, ads, the ranking model itself.

Non-functional

  • 500M daily active users; feed load under 200 ms at p99.
  • A new post appears in followers' feeds within about 5 seconds (eventual consistency is fine).
  • Highly available reads; the author sees their own post immediately.

C4.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Posts 500M x 0.2 per day = 100M/day about 1,200/s
Feed reads 500M x 10 per day = 5B/day about 58K/s, about 150K/s at peak
Fan-out writes 100M posts x 200 average followers 20B feed inserts/day, about 230K/s
Feed cache 500M users x 500 post IDs x 8 bytes about 2 TB; keep only active users

Reads are 50x posts, so precomputing feeds pays off. But the fan-out volume is large and skewed: a post by an account with 50M followers would be 50M inserts.

C4.3API

Endpoints
POST /v1/posts                 { "text": "...", "media_ids": [...] }      -> 201 { "post_id": ... }
PUT  /v1/users/{id}/followers/me                                            -> 204  (follow, idempotent)
GET  /v1/feed?cursor=...&limit=20   -> 200 { "posts": [...], "next_cursor": "..." }

C4.4Data model

Store Key Contents
Posts (sharded by post_id) post_id (Snowflake, time-ordered) author, text, media keys, created_at
Follow graph (follower_id, followee_id), stored twice: by follower and by followee follow time; counts cached separately
Feed cache (Redis) feed:{user_id} list of the latest ~500 post IDs
Post / user caches post:{id}, user:{id} hydrated objects for rendering

Time-ordered post IDs mean sorting by ID sorts by time, which makes merging and cursors simple.

C4.5High-level design

C4.6Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Push, pull, or hybrid?

    Compare fan-out on write and fan-out on read, then choose.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Fan-out on write (push): on each post, insert its ID into every follower's feed list. Reads are fast (one list read). Writes cost one insert per follower: fine for typical users, terrible for celebrities. Fan-out on read (pull): on each feed read, fetch recent posts of everyone the user follows and merge. Writes are cheap; reads are slow and expensive. Hybrid: push for normal authors; for authors above a follower threshold (say 100K), skip fan-out and merge their recent posts at read time. Each reader follows only a few celebrities, so the read-time merge stays small.

  2. 2
    Feed storage

    Where do feed lists live, and for whom?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Redis lists or sorted sets keyed by user, capped at a few hundred IDs (LPUSH + LTRIM). Only for users active in the last N days: inactive users get no fan-out, and their feed is rebuilt by pull when they return. The feed cache is a derived structure; losing it means rebuilding, not data loss.

  3. 3
    Hydration

    The feed has 20 post IDs. How do you return full posts fast?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Batch-fetch posts and authors from caches (MGET), fall back to stores for misses, and fill the caches. Counts (likes, comments) come from counter caches. Hydration happens at read time so edits, deletes, and profile changes show up without rewriting feeds.

  4. 4
    Pagination

    How does "load more" work while new posts keep arriving?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Cursor pagination by post ID: the next page asks for IDs lower than the last one seen. New posts at the top do not shift pages. "New posts available" at the top is a separate request for IDs greater than the newest shown.

  5. 5
    The author sees their own post

    Fan-out is asynchronous. How does the author see their post at once?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Insert the post into the author's own feed synchronously during publish, or have the client show it optimistically and merge on read.

  6. 6
    Deletes, blocks, and privacy

    A post is deleted after fan-out to 10M feeds. Do you remove it everywhere?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    No. Mark it deleted in the post store; hydration drops deleted or no-longer-visible posts (blocked authors, changed privacy) at read time. Lazy cleanup avoids millions of writes. Deleting a whole account is different: privacy laws (GDPR, India's DPDP Act) require removing the user's data from the post store, caches, search indexes, analytics archives, and eventually backups. Track every derived store, run a deletion workflow across them, and for archives and backups encrypt each user's data with its own key and delete the key (crypto-shredding).

  7. 7
    New follows and unfollows

    What happens to the feed right after following someone?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Backfill: insert the followee's few most recent post IDs into the follower's feed (async). Unfollow: filter at read time and let old entries age out.

  8. 8
    Ranking

    How would ranking change the design?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Feed assembly gathers a larger candidate set (from the feed list plus celebrity pulls), scores candidates with a ranking model using features from a feature store, and caches the ranked result briefly. The storage design stays; a ranking stage is added to the read path.

C4.7Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Celebrity post Massive fan-out Hybrid: pull celebrities at read time
Fan-out backlog (Kafka lag) Posts appear late Scale workers on lag; prioritize active followers
Feed cache node loss Some feeds missing Rebuild on read by pull; replicas
Hot post (viral) Post cache key overloaded or a stampede when it expires In-process caching, key replication, request coalescing, early refresh
Follow graph hot shard A celebrity's follower list is huge Shard follower lists by (followee, bucket); stream it in pages

C4.8What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): estimates showing read-heaviness and fan-out cost, the hybrid strategy with a threshold, IDs in feeds plus hydration, cursor pagination, async fan-out. L5 adds: active-user optimization, celebrity edge cases (a celebrity following many celebrities), ranking pipeline, cost of the feed cache, and multi-region feed generation.

C4.9Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why store post IDs in feeds instead of full posts?
    Reveal

    IDs are small (8 bytes), so feeds fit in memory; edits and deletes show up through hydration without rewriting millions of feeds.

  2. A user follows 5,000 accounts. Which strategy hurts them?
    Reveal

    Fan-out on read: merging 5,000 accounts per read is slow. Push handles them well, since their feed is precomputed.

  3. How would you build a "Trending now" section?
    Reveal

    A stream job counts engagement per post over sliding windows and keeps a top-K, cached and refreshed every minute (Case study 15).

  4. How do you keep fan-out from delaying important posts?
    Reveal

    Separate queues or priorities (close friends, recent interactions first), and fan out to recently active followers before inactive ones.
