Case study 5: Chat system

Deliver messages between users in real time, in order, without losing any, across phones and laptops that go offline. The hard parts are persistent connections at scale, per-conversation ordering, delivery acknowledgments, and sync after reconnect.

Uses: M2 WebSockets, M12 ordering, M8 wide-column
Your status

On this page

  1. C5.1Requirements
  2. C5.2Estimates
  3. C5.3API
  4. C5.4Data model
  5. C5.5High-level design
  6. C5.6Deep dives
  7. C5.7Failures and bottlenecks
  8. C5.8What a strong answer shows
  9. C5.9Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design one-to-one and group chat with online presence, sent/delivered/read receipts, offline delivery, and multi-device sync.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: WebSocket gateways plus a session registry; messages persisted before acknowledging; per-conversation sequence numbers for ordering; client-generated IDs for dedup on retry; a wide-column message store partitioned by conversation; routing to the recipient's gateway through pub/sub or Kafka; push notifications for offline users; sync from the last seen sequence on reconnect; presence through heartbeats with TTLs; group fan-out strategy.

C5.1Requirements

Functional

  • One-to-one and group chats (groups up to a few hundred members).
  • Text messages; media via object storage (Module 7).
  • Sent, delivered, and read receipts; online and last-seen presence.
  • Offline users get push notifications and receive messages on reconnect; history syncs across devices.

Non-functional

  • 500M daily active users, up to 100M connected at once.
  • Delivery under about 200 ms when both users are online in the same region.
  • Never lose an acknowledged message; preserve order within a conversation.

C5.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Messages 500M x 50 per day = 25B/day about 300K/s, about 1M/s at peak
Storage 25B x 200 bytes about 5 TB/day, about 1.8 PB/year before replication
Connections 100M concurrent / about 100K per gateway about 1,000 gateway servers

Write-heavy, append-only, read mostly as "latest messages of a conversation": a wide-column store partitioned by conversation fits (Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB).

C5.3API

Over the WebSocket (JSON or protobuf frames)
client -> server  send      { client_msg_id, conversation_id, body }
server -> client  ack       { client_msg_id, message_id, seq }               # "sent"
server -> client  message   { conversation_id, seq, sender, body, sent_at }
client -> server  delivered { conversation_id, up_to_seq }
client -> server  read      { conversation_id, up_to_seq }

HTTP:  GET /v1/conversations/{id}/messages?after_seq=...&limit=50   (sync and history)

C5.4Data model

Message store (CQL)
CREATE TABLE messages (
  conversation_id bigint,
  bucket          int,           -- seq / 10000: caps partition size, computable from a cursor
  seq             bigint,        -- per-conversation sequence, increasing
  message_id      bigint,        -- global ID (Snowflake)
  sender_id       bigint,
  body            blob,          -- ciphertext if end-to-end encrypted
  sent_at         timestamp,
  PRIMARY KEY ((conversation_id, bucket), seq)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (seq DESC);

Other stores: conversation membership, per-user per-device read cursors ((user, device, conversation) -> last_seq), and the session registry in Redis (user -> [gateway, device]).

C5.5High-level design

C5.6Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Ordering

    Two messages sent close together arrive at different chat servers. How do all members see the same order?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Give each message a sequence number per conversation, assigned by the single owner of that conversation (route all messages of a conversation to one partition or consistent-hash owner), which assigns seq and persists messages in seq order. Clients sort by seq and advance their cursor only over contiguous numbers: if 5 is missing while 6 has arrived, they refetch the gap instead of skipping it, and give up on a gap only after a timeout. Wall-clock timestamps are only for display.

  2. 2
    Never lose, never duplicate

    The network drops Alice's ack and her app resends. What prevents a duplicate?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The client generates client_msg_id once per message and reuses it on retry. The server keeps a dedup record (per conversation) and returns the original message_id and seq instead of storing again. Acknowledge "sent" only after the message is durably stored.

  3. 3
    Delivery and receipts

    How do the three ticks work?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Sent: the server stored it. Delivered: the recipient's device acknowledged receiving up_to_seq. Read: the recipient opened the conversation up to seq. Receipts are messages too, routed back to the sender's devices and stored as cursors.

  4. 4
    Offline and multi-device

    Bob's laptop was offline for 3 hours; his phone was online. What happens when the laptop reconnects?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Each device keeps its own cursor (last seq per conversation). On reconnect it asks for messages after its cursor for each active conversation and receives them from the store, then switches to live delivery. While Bob had no online device, a push notification (APNs/FCM) was sent.

  5. 5
    Group chats

    How do you deliver a message to a 300-member group?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Store the message once in the conversation's partition, then fan out delivery: look up members and route to each online member's gateway, push to offline ones. For very large channels (thousands of members), do not push every message: members fetch on open, and only mentions trigger notifications.

  6. 6
    Presence

    How do you show "online" for 500M users without huge write load?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Clients send heartbeats (every 30 s) over their connection; the gateway refreshes online:{user} with a TTL of about 60 s. Status changes are published only to friends who are currently viewing the user (subscribe on open), not to everyone. Last-seen is written lazily.

  7. 7
    Gateway failure

    A gateway with 100K connections crashes. What happens?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Clients reconnect (with jittered backoff) through the load balancer to other gateways and re-register in the session registry. Messages sent meanwhile are stored; reconnecting clients sync from their cursors. No message lives only in a gateway.

  8. 8
    End-to-end encryption

    How does it change the design?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Clients encrypt with keys the server never sees (Signal protocol); the server stores and routes ciphertext. Server-side search and moderation of content become impossible, and multi-device needs per-device keys.

C5.7Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Gateway crash 100K clients disconnect Reconnect with jitter; sync from cursors
Hot group One partition receives a burst Rate limits per conversation; batch fan-out
Recipient's gateway unknown or stale Message not delivered live Stored anyway; push notification; sync on reconnect
Store partition grows huge (old busy group) Slow reads Already bounded: the partition key includes bucket = seq / 10000, so sync from a cursor knows which buckets to read
Push provider throttling Delayed notifications Queue with retries, collapse multiple notifications

C5.8What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): WebSocket gateways with a session registry, persist-then-ack, per-conversation sequence numbers, client message IDs for dedup, wide-column storage keyed by conversation, offline push and cursor-based sync. L5 adds: group fan-out strategy by size, presence at scale, gateway draining and reconnect storms, multi-region routing, end-to-end encryption implications, and storage tiering.

C5.9Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why not use timestamps for message order?
    Reveal

    Clocks differ between devices and servers, and two messages can share a timestamp. A per-conversation sequence assigned by one owner gives a single agreed order.

  2. Why acknowledge only after storing the message?
    Reveal

    If the server acked first and crashed, the sender would believe the message was sent while it is lost. Persist, then ack.

  3. How would you design message search?
    Reveal

    Without end-to-end encryption: index messages in Elasticsearch partitioned by user or conversation, fed from the store's change stream. With end-to-end encryption: search on the device over locally stored history.

  4. Users in India chat with users in the US. Where is the conversation stored?
    Reveal

    In one home region per conversation (often the creator's), so ordering has one owner; gateways in each region forward to it. Reads can be served from replicas; cross-region latency affects only delivery time.

Case study 6: Notification system

Send push, SMS, email, and in-app notifications on behalf of every service in the company, reliably, without spamming users, and without letting a marketing blast delay a one-time password.

Uses: M12 queues and retries, M15 rate limiting, M13 idempotency
Your status

On this page

  1. C6.1Requirements
  2. C6.2Estimates
  3. C6.3API
  4. C6.4High-level design
  5. C6.5Deep dives
  6. C6.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C6.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C6.8Follow-up questions
Try it first40 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a notification platform that other services call. Cover channels, priorities, user preferences, templates, retries, dedup, provider failures, and delivery tracking.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: one API with idempotency keys; preference and template lookup; separate queues per channel and priority; workers that call third-party providers with retries, backoff, and failover; dedup so retries never double-send; per-user and per-provider rate limits; quiet hours and time zones; device token management; delivery status from provider callbacks; bulk campaigns fanned out in throttled batches.

C6.1Requirements

Functional

  • Services send notifications to users through push (iOS, Android), SMS, email, and in-app.
  • Transactional (OTP, payment alerts) and bulk (marketing campaigns, digests); scheduled sends.
  • Respect user preferences: channel opt-outs, categories, quiet hours.
  • Templates with localization; delivery tracking (sent, delivered, opened).

Non-functional

  • 1B notifications/day, bursts of 10M+ from campaigns.
  • OTPs and security alerts delivered within seconds even during a campaign.
  • No duplicate sends from retries; no lost transactional messages.
  • Survive a provider outage (an SMS vendor going down).

C6.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Average rate 1B / 86,400 about 12K/s
Campaign burst 10M in 10 minutes about 17K/s on top of normal traffic
Status records 1B x 200 bytes 200 GB/day; keep 30-90 days hot

C6.3API

Endpoint
POST /v1/notifications
Idempotency-Key: 6f1c...                       # retries never double-send
{
  "user_id": 7, "category": "payment_alert", "priority": "high",
  "channels": ["push", "sms"], "template": "txn_debit",
  "params": {"amount": "1,250.00", "merchant": "Cafe"}, "send_at": null
}
-> 202 { "notification_id": "..." }

C6.4High-level design

Flow: validate and dedup by idempotency key, look up preferences and contact info (device tokens, phone, email), render the template per locale, then enqueue one message per channel into the right priority queue. Channel workers call providers, retry failures, and record status; providers report delivery through callbacks.

C6.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Priorities

    A 50M-user campaign is queued when a user requests an OTP. How does the OTP go out in seconds?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Separate queues (topics) and worker pools per priority and channel: sms-high is never behind sms-bulk. Bulk sends are throttled to a budget so they cannot exhaust shared provider quotas. Transactional traffic gets reserved capacity.

  2. 2
    Dedup and exactly-once feeling

    Workers retry after a timeout from the email provider. How do you avoid two identical emails?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Delivery is at-least-once, so dedup at each step: the API stores the idempotency key; each channel message has a stable ID (notification_id + channel); the worker checks and records "sent" in a dedup store before and after the provider call; providers that accept idempotency keys get one. A rare duplicate after an ambiguous timeout is accepted for low-risk channels; for OTPs the code itself makes duplicates harmless.

  3. 3
    Provider failures

    The primary SMS vendor returns errors for 20 minutes. What happens?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Workers retry with backoff a few times, a circuit breaker opens on the vendor, and traffic fails over to a secondary vendor. Messages that still fail go to a dead-letter queue. Track per-provider success rate and latency to route automatically.

  4. 4
    Preferences, quiet hours, and fatigue

    How do you avoid spamming users?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Check preferences per category and channel at send time (they may change after scheduling). Defer non-urgent messages during quiet hours in the user's time zone. Rate-limit per user per category (for example at most 3 marketing pushes a day) and collapse repeats ("5 new messages" instead of 5 pushes).

  5. 5
    Device tokens

    Push needs device tokens. How do you keep them valid?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Apps register tokens on login and refresh; store user -> [device tokens]. When APNs or FCM reports a token as invalid or unregistered, delete it. Send to all active devices, or only the most recent one, by category.

  6. 6
    Bulk campaigns

    How do you send 50M notifications without a spike that breaks everything?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A campaign service splits the audience into batches (by user ID ranges), enqueues them gradually under a rate limit, and tracks progress so it can pause, resume, or cancel. Rendering happens per batch.

  7. 7
    Tracking

    How do you know a notification was delivered or opened?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Providers send delivery callbacks (webhooks); emails carry tracking pixels and links; apps report opens. All update a status log keyed by notification ID, feeding analytics and retries.

C6.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Provider outage Channel stops Retries, circuit breaker, failover vendor, DLQ
Campaign burst Queues fill, quotas used up Separate priorities, throttled bulk sends
Preference service down Cannot decide whether to send Cached preferences; fail closed for marketing, open for security alerts
Duplicate events from producers Repeated sends Idempotency keys at the API

C6.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): queue per channel and priority, idempotency and dedup, retries with backoff and DLQ, preferences and rate limits per user, provider callbacks. L5 adds: multi-provider routing on live metrics, campaign orchestration and throttling, time-zone-aware scheduling, compliance (unsubscribe, consent records), and cost controls per channel.

C6.8Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why not call providers directly from each service?
    Reveal

    Every service would reimplement retries, preferences, templates, rate limits, and provider failover, inconsistently. A platform centralizes them and protects users from spam.

  2. Can you guarantee exactly-once delivery of an SMS?
    Reveal

    No. Provider calls can time out after sending. You get at-least-once with dedup, which makes duplicates rare, and design messages so a duplicate is harmless.

  3. How would you schedule a notification for 9 AM in each user's time zone?
    Reveal

    Store the send time per user in UTC computed from their time zone, in a time-bucketed scheduler (Case study 14), which enqueues when due.

  4. In-app notifications: how are they stored and delivered?
    Reveal

    Write each to a per-user inbox table (newest first, with read flags); push a real-time event over the app's WebSocket if connected; the app fetches the inbox on open.

Case study 7Core40 min

Case study 7: Search autocomplete

Return the top suggestions for every keystroke in tens of milliseconds. The trick is to do the expensive work (counting and ranking queries) offline and serve precomputed answers from memory and caches.

Uses: M6 caching, M12 batch vs stream, M10 sharding
Your status

On this page

  1. C7.1Requirements
  2. C7.2Estimates
  3. C7.3High-level design
  4. C7.4Deep dives
  5. C7.5Failures and bottlenecks
  6. C7.6What a strong answer shows
  7. C7.7Follow-up questions
Try it first40 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design typeahead for a search box: suggestions for each prefix ranked by popularity, refreshed from recent searches. Cover the data structure, serving path, build path, sharding, caching, and freshness.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: a trie (or prefix table) with the top-k suggestions precomputed at each node; serving from memory behind browser and CDN caches; debouncing in the client; an offline (or streaming) pipeline that aggregates query logs into counts, builds the trie, and ships snapshots; sharding by prefix with attention to skew; atomic swaps of new versions; filtering offensive suggestions; and an optional trending blend.

C7.1Requirements

Functional: as the user types, return the top 10 completions for the current prefix, ranked by search frequency; suggestions refresh at least daily (hourly for trending); filter unsafe terms.

Non-functional: 100M daily users; responses within 100 ms end to end, so the server side should take 10-20 ms; highly available; slightly stale results are fine.

C7.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Prefix requests 100M users x 10 searches x 6 requests each (debounced) 6B/day, about 70K/s, about 200K/s at peak
Distinct queries kept Long tail cut at a minimum count about 100M queries
Trie size Nodes for 100M queries (shared prefixes) plus top-10 references per node tens of GB: fits in memory across a few shards with replicas

C7.3High-level design

C7.4Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Data structure

    A plain trie finds all completions of "hol" by walking its subtree. Why is that too slow, and what fixes it?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Popular prefixes ("a", "ho") have millions of descendants; scanning and sorting them per keystroke is far too slow. Store the top-k completions at every node during the build; a query walks at most the prefix length and returns the cached list. The cost is memory (k references per node), bounded by capping prefix length (for example 20 characters). An equivalent alternative is a prefix table in a key-value store: prefix -> top 10, generated offline.

  2. 2
    Building the data

    How do raw searches become rankings?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Search events stream into Kafka and land in storage. A batch job (hourly or daily) aggregates counts per query over a window, with decay so old popularity fades, drops rare and blocked queries, then builds the trie with top-k per node and writes a versioned snapshot to object storage. A streaming job can maintain short-window counts for trending queries and blend them in.

  3. 3
    Updating servers

    How do servers switch to the new trie without errors?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Each server loads the new snapshot into memory alongside the old one, then swaps a pointer atomically; or bring up new instances with the new version and shift traffic (blue-green). Never mutate the serving trie in place under load.

  4. 4
    Sharding

    The trie is too big or too hot for one server. How do you split it?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    By prefix range (a-f, g-m, ...) with replicas per shard. Prefix popularity is skewed ("s" and "c" are far more common than "x"), so split by measured load, not by letters evenly, and keep a small routing map. Every shard has several replicas for read throughput and availability.

  5. 5
    Caching

    Where else can you save work?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Clients debounce keystrokes (wait about 100-150 ms) and cache results per prefix for the session. Responses for short, common prefixes are identical for everyone, so the CDN or an edge cache can serve them with a TTL of minutes. Most traffic never reaches the service.

  6. 6
    Personalization and safety

    How do you add a user's own recent searches and keep offensive suggestions out?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Fetch the user's recent queries matching the prefix (client side or a small per-user store) and merge them with the global list. Apply a blocklist when building (so blocked terms never enter the trie) and as a fast filter at serve time for emergencies.

C7.5Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Build pipeline fails Suggestions grow stale Keep serving the last good snapshot; alert
Bad snapshot (corrupt, offensive) Wrong suggestions everywhere Validate before publish; roll back to previous version
Hot prefix shard Latency rises Split the range, add replicas, rely on CDN caching
Breaking news query Not in the daily build Streaming trending layer with short windows

C7.6What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): top-k at each trie node, offline aggregation and build, in-memory serving with replicas, client debounce and caching, versioned snapshots. L5 adds: freshness blending with a streaming layer, load-based sharding for skew, multi-language handling, typo tolerance, and abuse resistance (people trying to push queries into suggestions).

C7.7Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why not query the search engine (Elasticsearch prefix queries) directly per keystroke?
    Reveal

    It works at small scale, but ranking by global query popularity per keystroke at 200K/s is expensive; precomputed top-k per prefix is far cheaper and faster.

  2. How do you keep someone from manipulating suggestions by searching a phrase repeatedly?
    Reveal

    Count unique users rather than raw searches, rate-limit per user and IP, require a minimum spread of users, and review fast-rising terms.

  3. How would you support "did you mean" for typos?
    Reveal

    Fuzzy matching on the client query (edit distance over the trie or n-gram indexes) with a separate, smaller index; return corrections when the exact prefix has few results.

  4. How big is k, and why not store all completions?
    Reveal

    Usually 5-10, what the UI shows. Storing everything at every node would multiply memory by the subtree sizes.

Case study 8: Web crawler

Download a billion pages a month, politely, without fetching the same page twice or getting stuck in traps. A crawler is a feedback loop: every page fetched produces more URLs to fetch.

Uses: M17 Bloom filters, M12 queues, M10 partitioning
Your status

On this page

  1. C8.1Requirements
  2. C8.2Estimates
  3. C8.3High-level design
  4. C8.4Deep dives
  5. C8.5Failures and bottlenecks
  6. C8.6What a strong answer shows
  7. C8.7Follow-up questions
Try it first40 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a crawler for a search engine: from seed URLs, fetch pages, extract links, and keep going. Cover the URL frontier, politeness, dedup of URLs and content, storage, distribution across machines, and recrawling.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: a frontier with priority queues and per-host queues; politeness (one connection per host, crawl delay, robots.txt); URL normalization and a URL-seen check (Bloom filter plus store); content dedup (checksums and SimHash for near duplicates); DNS caching; storing raw pages in object storage; partitioning work by host so politeness stays local; trap protection; and recrawl scheduling by change rate.

C8.1Requirements

Functional: start from seeds; fetch HTML pages; extract and enqueue new links; store page content for indexing; recrawl pages over time; obey robots.txt.

Non-functional: 1B pages per month; polite to every site; robust to malformed pages and traps; scalable by adding machines; extensible to new content types.

C8.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Fetch rate 1B / (30 x 86,400) about 400 pages/s, plan for 800-1,000
Storage 1B x 500 KB average about 500 TB per month of raw pages (compress, tier)
URLs seen Tens of billions over time Bloom filter of about 10 bits each: tens of GB, sharded

C8.3High-level design

C8.4Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    The URL frontier

    How do you decide what to fetch next while staying polite?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Two layers. Front queues by priority (PageRank-like importance, freshness need); a selector takes from high priority more often. Back queues: one queue per host, each mapped to one worker thread, plus a min-heap of "next time this host may be fetched". A worker takes the host whose time has come, fetches one URL, and sets the next allowed time (crawl delay). This guarantees at most one in-flight request per host.

  2. 2
    Politeness and robots.txt

    What exactly do you respect?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Fetch and cache each host's robots.txt (refresh daily) and skip disallowed paths; honor crawl delays; limit concurrency per host and per IP (many hosts share one server); identify the crawler in the User-Agent; back off on 429 and 503.

  3. 3
    URL dedup

    How do you avoid fetching the same URL twice among tens of billions?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Normalize first (lowercase host, remove default ports, fragments, tracking parameters, sort query parameters). Then check a Bloom filter sharded by URL hash: "definitely new" goes on; "maybe seen" is either skipped (accepting a tiny loss) or confirmed against a persistent URL store.

  4. 4
    Content dedup

    Different URLs often serve the same page. How do you detect it?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Exact duplicates: a checksum (SHA-256 of normalized content) in a seen-content store. Near duplicates (same article with different ads or dates): SimHash fingerprints, where similar documents have fingerprints differing in few bits. Skip storing and extracting links from duplicates.

  5. 5
    Distribution

    How do you spread work over 100 machines without breaking politeness?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Partition by host (hash of hostname): one machine owns all of a host's URLs, so per-host queues and delays stay local. Extracted links for other hosts are sent to their owners. Consistent hashing lets machines join and leave.

  6. 6
    Traps and junk

    How do you avoid infinite calendars and session-ID URLs?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Limit URL length and path depth, cap pages per host per crawl cycle, detect repeating path segments, drop known session parameters, and lower the priority of hosts that produce many near-duplicates.

  7. 7
    DNS and fetching

    Why is DNS a bottleneck, and what else slows fetching?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Each new host needs a lookup, and synchronous resolvers block threads. Run a local caching resolver with asynchronous lookups. Use non-blocking I/O for fetches, timeouts, size limits, and redirect limits.

  8. 8
    Recrawling

    How often do you revisit a page?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Estimate each page's change rate from history (did the checksum change since last time?) and its importance; schedule high-change, important pages (news front pages) often and static pages rarely. Use conditional requests (If-Modified-Since, ETags) to save bandwidth.

C8.5Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Worker crash Its in-flight URLs lost Frontier stored durably; leases with timeouts re-queue URLs
Slow or hostile site Threads stuck Timeouts, size limits, per-host budgets
Frontier grows unbounded Memory exhaustion Keep queues on disk, hold only heads in memory; drop low priority
JavaScript-only pages Empty content Separate rendering pool with headless browsers, used selectively

C8.6What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): frontier with per-host queues and politeness, URL normalization and Bloom-filter dedup, content checksums, host-based partitioning, raw storage in object store. L5 adds: prioritization and recrawl policy, SimHash near-dup detection, trap handling, rendering JavaScript selectively, and freshness versus coverage trade-offs.

C8.7Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. BFS or DFS over the link graph?
    Reveal

    Roughly BFS with priorities: DFS dives into one site and violates politeness; prioritized BFS spreads across hosts and reaches important pages earlier.

  2. Why partition by host and not by URL hash?
    Reveal

    Politeness is per host. If a host's URLs were spread over many machines, they would need to coordinate their request rate to that host.

  3. What happens to a Bloom filter false positive?
    Reveal

    A new URL is wrongly treated as seen and skipped. At a 1% rate this is an accepted loss; important URLs can be double-checked against the exact store.

  4. How would you crawl only pages that changed?
    Reveal

    Conditional GETs with ETag or Last-Modified, sitemaps with lastmod dates, and adaptive recrawl intervals from observed change history.

Case study 9: Video streaming platform

Let creators upload videos and let millions watch them smoothly on any connection. Most of the design is about bytes: getting big uploads in reliably, transcoding them in parallel, and serving segments from CDN caches near viewers.

Uses: M7 CDN and object storage, M12 queues, M15 reliability
Your status

On this page

  1. C9.1Requirements
  2. C9.2Estimates
  3. C9.3High-level design
  4. C9.4Deep dives
  5. C9.5Failures and bottlenecks
  6. C9.6What a strong answer shows
  7. C9.7Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a YouTube-like service: upload, processing, playback with adaptive quality, and view counts. Estimate storage and bandwidth and explain where each byte lives.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: resumable direct uploads to object storage; a processing pipeline triggered by events that splits video into chunks and transcodes them in parallel into multiple resolutions and bitrates; packaging into HLS or DASH segments with manifests; thumbnails; metadata and status in a database; playback via signed manifests and CDN-served segments; adaptive bitrate in the player; and asynchronous view counting.

C9.1Requirements

Functional: upload videos (up to a few GB); process them into streamable formats; watch with automatic quality; see title, description, view counts. Out of scope: comments, recommendations, live streaming (follow-up).

Non-functional: 100M daily viewers; playback starts within about 2 seconds and rarely stalls; uploads survive network drops; durable storage; cost-efficient bandwidth.

C9.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Uploads 500K videos/day x 300 MB average 150 TB/day raw
Processed copies About 4-6 renditions, together similar to or larger than the raw size Another 150-300 TB/day
Views 100M users x 5 videos 500M views/day, about 6K starts/s
Bandwidth If 10M people watch at once at about 3 Mbps about 30 Tbps: only a CDN can deliver this

C9.3High-level design

C9.4Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Upload

    A 2 GB upload over mobile data fails at 70%. How does the design handle it?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Resumable, chunked uploads straight to object storage (S3 multipart or GCS resumable): the client uploads parts with presigned URLs and retries only failed parts. The API creates a video record (status = uploading) first and finalizes it when all parts are in. App servers never stream the bytes.

  2. 2
    Transcoding pipeline

    How do you turn one upload into streamable renditions quickly?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    An upload event creates a job. A coordinator splits the video into chunks (by GOP or scene boundaries), fans the chunks out to many transcoder workers that encode each chunk into each target resolution and bitrate (codecs such as H.264, VP9, AV1), then merges and packages them into HLS or DASH segments of a few seconds with manifests. Thumbnails and audio tracks are separate tasks. Model it as a DAG of tasks with retries per task; workers are stateless and scale on queue depth (often spot instances).

  3. 3
    Playback

    What happens when a viewer presses play?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The watch API checks permissions and returns metadata plus a manifest URL (signed if needed). The player downloads the manifest (list of renditions and segment URLs), starts with a low or medium quality segment to start fast, measures throughput, and switches quality per segment. All segments come from the CDN.

  4. 4
    CDN strategy

    Popular videos are watched millions of times; most videos are watched rarely. How do you serve both cheaply?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Popular content stays hot in edge caches (pre-position new releases from big creators). The long tail is served from regional caches or the origin with an origin shield so misses are collapsed. Very large platforms place cache appliances inside ISP networks (Netflix Open Connect) to cut transit costs.

  5. 5
    View counts

    How do you count 500M views a day without hammering the database?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Players send view events to an ingestion endpoint into Kafka; a stream job deduplicates (same user and video within a window), filters bots, and aggregates counts per video per minute; counts are stored and cached. Displayed counts lag by seconds or minutes, which is fine.

  6. 6
    Storage cost

    Video storage grows by hundreds of TB per day. How do you control cost?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Keep the original plus a set of renditions; generate rare renditions on demand; move old, rarely watched videos (and their originals) to colder storage tiers; delete failed or abandoned uploads with lifecycle rules.

  7. 7
    Live streaming

    What changes for live?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Ingest a live stream (RTMP or SRT) at a nearby ingest server, transcode in real time, and publish segments continuously with a rolling manifest. Latency is set by segment length and buffering; low-latency HLS or DASH uses partial segments. There is no time to transcode in parallel chunks after the fact.

C9.5Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Transcoder crash Chunk not processed Task retries; idempotent outputs keyed by video, chunk, rendition
Upload spike Processing backlog Queue absorbs it; autoscale workers; prioritize short or popular videos
CDN miss storm on a viral video Origin overloaded Origin shield, request collapsing, pre-warming
Viewer bandwidth drops Stalls Adaptive bitrate, buffer targets, short segments

C9.6What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): storage and bandwidth estimates that force a CDN, direct resumable uploads, an event-driven parallel transcoding pipeline, segments and manifests with adaptive bitrate, and async view counting. L5 adds: CDN economics and tiering, codec choices versus device support, DRM and signed URLs, live streaming latency trade-offs, and cost controls.

C9.7Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why split video into segments of a few seconds?
    Reveal

    Each segment is a cacheable file, the player can switch quality at every segment boundary, and seeking jumps to the right segment without downloading the rest.

  2. How do you prevent people from hotlinking or downloading private videos?
    Reveal

    Signed, expiring URLs or cookies for manifests and segments, checked by the CDN; DRM for premium content.

  3. Where are video metadata and video bytes stored?
    Reveal

    Metadata (title, owner, status, rendition list) in a database; bytes (originals and segments) in object storage, delivered via the CDN.

  4. How do you make playback start faster?
    Reveal

    Start with a lower bitrate, keep the first segment small, preconnect to the CDN, and prefetch the beginning of likely next videos.

Case study 10: File storage and sync

Keep a folder in sync across laptops and phones, like Dropbox or Google Drive. Splitting files into content-addressed blocks makes uploads incremental and deduplicated; a change journal with cursors makes sync reliable; conflicts are handled explicitly.

Uses: M7 object storage, M8 data modeling, M2 long polling
Your status

On this page

  1. C10.1Requirements
  2. C10.2Estimates
  3. C10.3High-level design
  4. C10.4Deep dives
  5. C10.5Failures and bottlenecks
  6. C10.6What a strong answer shows
  7. C10.7Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design file upload, download, automatic sync across devices, sharing, and version history. Large files must not be re-uploaded fully after a small change.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: chunking files into blocks named by their hash; uploading only missing blocks directly to object storage; a metadata service (strongly consistent, sharded by user or namespace) that stores file versions as lists of block hashes; a per-namespace change journal; devices syncing from a cursor and getting notified by long polling or WebSocket; conflict handling with conflicted copies; sharing via ACLs; versions and deletion retention.

C10.1Requirements

Functional: upload and download files; automatic sync of a folder across a user's devices; offline edits that sync later; share files and folders; version history and restore.

Non-functional: 50M daily users; files up to tens of GB; never lose data; sync within seconds when online; use little bandwidth for small edits.

C10.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Stored data 500M users x 10 GB average used about 5 EB before dedup and compression
File changes 50M users x 20 changes/day 1B/day, about 12K metadata commits/s
Block size 4 MB blocks a 1 GB file = 256 blocks

The metadata (who has which files and versions) is small but must be strongly consistent. The bytes are huge but immutable once written, which makes them easy to store and cache.

C10.3High-level design

C10.4Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Upload protocol

    How does the client upload a modified 1 GB file efficiently and safely?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The client splits the file into blocks and hashes each (SHA-256). It asks the metadata service which hashes are missing, uploads only those blocks (directly to the block store via presigned URLs, in parallel, resumable), then commits a new file version: path, size, and the ordered list of block hashes. The commit is the atomic moment the new version exists. The commit checks and pins every block it references in the same transaction, and garbage collection deletes only blocks that have been unreferenced for longer than a grace period, so a block the server just reported as present cannot vanish before the commit.

  2. 2
    Metadata model

    What tables does the metadata service need?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Namespaces (a user's root or a shared folder), file entries (namespace, path, latest version), versions (file, version number, block list, author, time), block references (hash to location and reference count), and a journal per namespace: an ordered log of changes with a sequence number. It needs transactions and is sharded by namespace, so a relational database (sharded MySQL or PostgreSQL) fits.

  3. 3
    Sync

    How does the phone learn about changes and catch up after being offline?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Each device stores a cursor: the last journal sequence it applied for each namespace. It keeps a long-poll or WebSocket open to the notification service, which signals "namespace changed". The device then asks for changes after its cursor, downloads missing blocks, applies them, and advances the cursor. After days offline the same call returns everything missed.

  4. 4
    Conflicts

    Two devices edit the same file offline and both sync. What happens?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Each commit says which version it was based on. The first commit wins and becomes the latest version; the second commit's base is now stale, so the server rejects it as a conflict, and the client saves its version as "file (conflicted copy from Laptop)". Automatic merging is not attempted for arbitrary files (documents with real-time co-editing use a different design, Case study 16).

  5. 5
    Dedup and its risks

    Should identical blocks be shared across all users?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Global dedup saves the most space but lets a user test whether someone else has a specific file (upload a block and see if it was "already there"), a privacy leak. Many services dedup per user or per organization only. Encrypted storage per user also limits cross-user dedup.

  6. 6
    Sharing and permissions

    How do shared folders work?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A shared folder is its own namespace with an ACL (owner, editors, viewers); each member mounts it in their tree. Permission checks happen in the metadata service on every operation; downloads use short-lived signed URLs so the block store does not need to know ACLs.

  7. 7
    Deletes and history

    How do version history and deletion work with shared blocks?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Deleting a file creates a tombstone version; older versions remain restorable for a retention period. Blocks are reference-counted (or found by mark-and-sweep over live versions) and deleted only when no version anywhere references them.

C10.5Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Upload interrupted Partial blocks Blocks are independent and resumable; commit only after all are present
Metadata shard hot (a huge shared folder) Slow commits Split namespaces, rate-limit, cache listings
Notification server loss Devices miss "changed" signals Clients poll on reconnect and periodically; the journal is the source of truth
Corrupted block Bad file Verify hash on upload and download; store redundantly

C10.6What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): separating metadata from bytes, hash-named blocks with incremental upload, a commit step, a change journal with device cursors, long-poll or WebSocket notifications, and conflicted copies. L5 adds: content-defined chunking, dedup privacy trade-offs, garbage collection of blocks, sharing semantics, cold storage tiering, and client-side encryption.

C10.7Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why name blocks by their content hash?
    Reveal

    The name proves the content (integrity check), identical content gets the same name (dedup), and the client can ask "which of these do you already have?" before uploading.

  2. Why must metadata be strongly consistent when blocks need not be?
    Reveal

    Two devices must agree on which version is latest and detect conflicts. Blocks are immutable: once written under a hash they never change, so there is nothing to disagree about.

  3. How do you list a folder with 100,000 files quickly?
    Reveal

    Store entries indexed by (namespace, parent path), paginate with cursors, and let clients use their synced local index instead of listing from the server.

  4. How does the client know which local files changed?
    Reveal

    A file system watcher (OS events) plus periodic scans comparing size, modification time, and hashes against its local index.

Case study 11Core45 min

Case study 11: Nearby search and ride matching

Two location problems in one: finding places near a user (mostly static data, read-heavy), and matching riders with moving drivers whose positions change every few seconds (write-heavy, real time, and a driver must never get two trips).

Uses: M17 geospatial, M10 sharding, M11 locks
Your status

On this page

  1. C11.1Requirements
  2. C11.2Estimates
  3. C11.3Static places: nearby search
  4. C11.4High-level design for rides
  5. C11.5Deep dives
  6. C11.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C11.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C11.8Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design (a) "restaurants near me" and (b) ride matching: drivers report location every 4 seconds, riders request a ride, the system offers it to a nearby driver and assigns exactly one.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: for static places, a geohash or quadtree index (or PostGIS) with caching and a neighbor-cell search; for drivers, an in-memory geo index keyed by cells and sharded by city, updated from a location stream without touching disk per update; matching by estimated time of arrival (ETA), not straight-line distance; offers with timeouts; an atomic state change so a driver is assigned once; a trip state machine; and recovery when an index node fails.

C11.1Requirements

Functional

  • Places: find businesses within a radius of a point, with filters; business data changes rarely.
  • Rides: drivers send location every 4 s while online; a rider requests a ride; the system finds nearby available drivers, offers the trip, assigns one; both see live positions during the trip.

Non-functional

  • 1M drivers online at peak; matching within a few seconds; nearby search under 100 ms.
  • A driver is never assigned two trips at once; a trip is never assigned to two drivers.
  • High availability: a location index failure must not stop rides for long.

C11.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Location updates 1M drivers / 4 s 250K writes/s
Location record driver ID, lat, lng, time, status about 50-100 bytes; 1M drivers = 100 MB in memory
Ride requests 20M rides/day about 230/s, peaks of a few thousand
Places 200M businesses static index fits on a few machines; reads cached

250K writes/s of tiny, constantly overwritten data says: keep current positions in memory, not in a disk-based database row per update.

C11.3Static places: nearby search

Store businesses in a database (source of truth) and build a geospatial index: a geohash column with a B-tree index (query the user's cell plus 8 neighbors, then filter by exact distance), a quadtree in memory, or PostGIS / Elasticsearch geo queries. Choose geohash precision so the cell plus its 8 neighbors covers the radius: 5 characters (cells about 4.9 km) for a 1 km radius, 6 characters (about 1.2 x 0.6 km) for about 0.5 km. Popular areas are cached; business detail pages are cached separately. Updates are rare, so rebuilding the index nightly or updating it asynchronously is fine.

C11.4High-level design for rides

C11.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Geo index for moving drivers

    How do you store 1M positions updated every 4 s and query "available drivers near this point"?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    In memory, partitioned by city or region (each shard owns a set of cells). Map each driver to a cell (geohash, S2, or H3) and keep cell -> set of available drivers plus driver -> (position, cell, time). An update overwrites the position and moves the driver between cells only when the cell changes. A query reads the rider's cell and neighbors. Redis geo sets or a custom in-memory service both work. Redis expires whole keys, not members of a set, so store each driver's last-seen time and prune stale members on a timer (or use per-time-bucket keys with a TTL); a driver who stops reporting disappears within seconds.

  2. 2
    Matching

    Is the closest driver by straight-line distance the best choice?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    No. A driver 500 m away across a river can be 15 minutes away. Get candidates from the geo index, compute ETAs with a routing service (road graph, traffic), and rank by ETA plus factors like driver rating or acceptance rate. Large systems batch requests every second or two and solve assignment jointly to reduce total wait.

  3. 3
    Exactly one assignment

    Two matchers offer different riders to the same driver at the same moment. How do you prevent double assignment?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The driver's state lives in a store with an atomic conditional update: available -> offered(trip) succeeds for only one trip (compare-and-set on a version, or a lease in Redis with fencing). The trip moves searching -> driver_assigned the same way. Offers time out (about 10-15 s) and return the driver to available.

  4. 4
    Offer flow

    The chosen driver ignores the offer. What happens?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The offer expires, the driver goes back to available (perhaps with a cooldown), and matching moves to the next candidate. The rider sees "finding a driver" throughout. All steps are recorded on the trip state machine so a crash resumes correctly.

  5. 5
    Index node failure

    The shard holding Mumbai's index crashes. How fast do you recover?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Positions are soft state: a replacement node (or replica) rebuilds within one update interval because every driver reports again in 4 s. Replicas or a standby can take over immediately. Trip and driver assignment state lives in a durable store, not in the index.

  6. 6
    Live tracking during a trip

    How do rider and driver see each other's location?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Driver updates already flow in; the trip service publishes the driver's position to the rider's connection (WebSocket via a gateway) every few seconds. Positions are also written to the location stream for ETA updates, history, and fraud checks.

  7. 7
    Hot spots

    Thousands of riders request at a stadium after a concert. What breaks?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    One cell's shard becomes hot and supply runs out. Split hot cells finer, batch matching in the area, and use surge pricing or queueing to balance demand and supply.

C11.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Index shard crash No matches in that area for seconds Replica takeover; rebuild from next updates
Driver app disconnects Stale position Expire positions after N missed updates; mark unavailable
Routing service slow Matching slows Cached ETA estimates per cell pair; fall back to distance
City-level spike Hot shard Finer cells, more shards per city, batching

C11.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): separate static-place search from moving-driver tracking, in-memory cell-based index sharded by region, atomic driver assignment with timeouts, trip state machine, estimates that justify memory over disk. L5 adds: ETA-based and batched matching, hot-spot handling, multi-region design, supply and demand balancing, and how location data feeds pricing and fraud systems.

C11.8Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why not write every location update to PostgreSQL?
    Reveal

    250K writes/s of rows that are overwritten every 4 seconds would waste disk and I/O for data that is only useful for a few seconds. Keep current positions in memory; stream history asynchronously to cheaper storage.

  2. Geohash or quadtree for drivers?
    Reveal

    Fixed cells (geohash, S2, H3) are simpler for constantly moving points because updating a position is a cell lookup. Quadtrees adapt to density but must rebalance as points move.

  3. How do you find drivers near a cell boundary?
    Reveal

    Query the rider's cell and its neighbors (or a ring of H3 cells), then filter by real distance or ETA.

  4. What consistency does the driver state need?
    Reveal

    Strong, for the assignment step: a conditional update so only one trip wins. Positions can be eventually consistent.

Case study 12Core45 min

Case study 12: Ticket booking

Millions of fans arrive at 10:00 for 50,000 seats. Two problems collide: a huge spike that must not take the site down, and seats that must never be sold twice. The design answers both with admission control in front and atomic seat holds behind.

Uses: M8 locking, M15 load shedding, M13 sagas
Your status

On this page

  1. C12.1Requirements
  2. C12.2Estimates
  3. C12.3API and data model
  4. C12.4High-level design
  5. C12.5Deep dives
  6. C12.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C12.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C12.8Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design booking for concerts or movie seats: browse events, see the seat map, hold seats while paying, and confirm. Handle a launch spike of millions of users.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: static event pages on a CDN; a virtual waiting room that admits users at a controlled rate; a seat map served from a cache (may be slightly stale); seat holds via an atomic conditional update in the database (or Redis holds confirmed in the database) with an expiry; payment with idempotency inside the hold window; confirmation that checks the hold is still valid; a sweeper for expired holds; and bot and fairness controls.

C12.1Requirements

Functional: browse events; view the seat map with availability; select and hold seats for about 10 minutes; pay; receive tickets; release unpaid holds.

Non-functional: launch spikes of 10M users for 50K seats; no seat sold twice; the site stays up under the spike; fair access; holds expire reliably.

C12.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Launch traffic 10M users refreshing millions of requests/s at the edge for a few minutes
Bookable rate 50K seats in, say, 15 minutes about 55 bookings/s: tiny for the database
Seat rows 50K seats per event small: one database partition per event

The database is not the bottleneck; the crowd is. Admit people at the rate the booking flow can serve, and make each booking atomic.

C12.3API and data model

Endpoints
GET  /v1/events/{id}/seats                       -> seat map (cached, refreshed every few seconds)
POST /v1/events/{id}/holds  {"seats": ["A12","A13"]}  -> 201 {"hold_id", "expires_at"} or 409 if taken
POST /v1/holds/{hold_id}/purchase  Idempotency-Key: ... -> 201 {"order_id"} or 410 if the hold expired
Seat table and the hold statement
CREATE TABLE seats (
  event_id   bigint, seat_id text,
  status     text NOT NULL,            -- AVAILABLE | HELD | BOOKED
  hold_id    uuid, hold_expires_at timestamptz, order_id bigint,
  PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_id)
);

-- Hold two seats atomically: succeed only if every seat is free (or its hold expired)
UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', hold_id = :hold, hold_expires_at = now() + interval '10 minutes'
WHERE event_id = :event AND seat_id IN ('A12', 'A13')
  AND (status = 'AVAILABLE' OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < now()));
-- If rows updated != 2, roll back the transaction and return 409.

C12.4High-level design

C12.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    No double booking

    Two users click the same seat at the same millisecond. What guarantees only one hold succeeds?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The hold is a single conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE' in a transaction: the database row lock serializes the two updates, the second sees the seat already held and updates 0 rows. Alternatives: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT on the seat rows, or a Redis SET seat NX PX 600000 hold followed by the database update as the final authority. Never read availability and then write in separate steps without a guard.

  2. 2
    Hold expiry

    The user closes the tab during payment. How do the seats come back?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Holds carry hold_expires_at. The hold query already treats expired holds as available (lazy expiry), so no seat stays stuck even if the sweeper is late. A background sweeper also resets expired holds to AVAILABLE to keep the seat map accurate.

  3. 3
    Payment inside the hold

    Payment succeeds 1 second after the hold expired and someone else took the seat. What now?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Confirmation is a conditional update HELD -> BOOKED WHERE hold_id = :hold (and not expired). If it fails, the order fails and the payment is voided or refunded automatically (a compensation, Module 13). Better: authorize payment first, confirm the seat, then capture; a failed confirmation just voids the authorization.

  4. 4
    The spike

    10M users arrive at once. How does the system survive?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Serve all static content (event page, seat map shell) from the CDN. Put a virtual waiting room in front of the booking flow: users get a position in a queue (a signed token with an admission time) and are admitted at a rate the booking service can handle. Pre-scale stateless services before launch. Rate-limit per user and IP, and shed excess traffic with a clear "you are in line" page rather than errors.

  5. 5
    Seat map freshness

    The seat map is read by everyone constantly. Do you query the database each time?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    No. Cache the map per event (Redis or the CDN) and refresh every second or two from the database, or update it from seat change events. A stale map only means a user may pick a seat that just went; the hold step returns 409 and they pick again.

  6. 6
    Fairness and bots

    How do you stop bots from grabbing all tickets?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Waiting-room randomization at start time, CAPTCHA or device checks at admission, per-account and per-payment-card ticket limits, verified fan programs, and anomaly detection on purchase patterns.

  7. 7
    General admission

    Some events have no seat numbers, just 20,000 standing tickets. What changes?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Use a counter per ticket category: UPDATE inventory SET held = held + :n WHERE event = :e AND sold + held + :n <= capacity, plus one row per hold (hold_id, qty, expires_at). A counter cannot expire holds lazily, so a sweeper releases expired holds and decrements held; otherwise abandoned holds would shrink sellable stock forever. The same conditional pattern prevents overselling. For extreme rates, pre-split inventory into buckets (shards) and decrement them in parallel.

C12.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Thundering herd at launch Everything overloads CDN, waiting room, pre-scaling, load shedding
Hot event partition Lock contention on popular seats Short transactions; holds keep locks brief; queue admission
Payment provider slow Holds expire during payment Extend hold once while payment is in progress; idempotent retries
Sweeper down Map shows stale holds Lazy expiry in queries keeps correctness

C12.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): atomic conditional seat holds with expiry, payment within the hold and failure compensation, a cached seat map, a waiting room and CDN for the spike. L5 adds: fairness and anti-bot strategy, inventory sharding for general admission, hold extension rules, end-to-end failure handling with the payment provider, and capacity planning for the launch.

C12.8Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why not lock seats with a long database transaction while the user pays?
    Reveal

    Payment takes minutes; holding row locks that long blocks other transactions and connections. Use a short transaction to set a HELD status with an expiry instead.

  2. Optimistic or pessimistic locking for seats?
    Reveal

    The conditional update is an optimistic, atomic check-and-set; it fits because each attempt is a single short statement. FOR UPDATE NOWAIT is the pessimistic version that fails fast instead of waiting.

  3. How would you design this for a cinema chain with thousands of small shows?
    Reveal

    The same model, partitioned by show; contention is low, so the waiting room is unnecessary except for blockbuster openings.

  4. How do you handle a user double-clicking "Buy"?
    Reveal

    An idempotency key on the purchase request, plus the conditional HELD -> BOOKED update, so the second request returns the same order.

C13
Case study 13Stretch50 min

Case study 13: Payment system

Accept payments for merchants, move money correctly, and prove it. Scale is modest compared with feeds or chat; correctness is everything. The design centers on idempotency, a payment state machine, a double-entry ledger, safe handling of ambiguous processor responses, and reconciliation.

Uses: M13 sagas and outbox, M3 idempotency keys, M8 transactions
Your status

On this page

  1. C13.1Requirements
  2. C13.2Estimates
  3. C13.3API
  4. C13.4High-level design
  5. C13.5Deep dives
  6. C13.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C13.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C13.8Follow-up questions
Try it first50 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a Stripe-like payments platform: merchants create payments through an API; you charge cards through processors; merchants get webhooks; refunds and payouts happen later. No double charges, no lost money, full audit trail.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: idempotency keys end to end (merchant to you, you to processor); a payment state machine stored in a relational database with conditional transitions; authorize and capture; the outbox pattern to publish events; signed, retried webhooks; a double-entry ledger with immutable entries; handling processor timeouts by querying status and reconciling; daily reconciliation with settlement files; tokenization to limit PCI scope; integer minor units for money; and a risk check before authorization.

C13.1Requirements

Functional

  • Merchants create payments (card, UPI, wallets) and refunds through an API.
  • Authorize and capture (immediately or later); void uncaptured authorizations.
  • Notify merchants of outcomes (webhooks); pay out merchant balances on a schedule.
  • Full history: every money movement recorded and explainable.

Non-functional

  • Never charge twice for one intended payment; never lose a confirmed payment.
  • 99.99% API availability; payment latency is dominated by processors (hundreds of ms to seconds).
  • Volume: 10M payments/day (about 120/s average, peaks of a few thousand per second during sales).
  • Compliance: PCI DSS for card data, audit trails, data residency where required.

C13.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Payments 10M/day about 120/s, plan for 3,000/s peaks
Ledger entries About 3-6 per payment (customer, merchant, fees, refunds) 30-60M rows/day
Storage 60M x 300 bytes about 18 GB/day; years of history fit in a sharded relational store

The numbers fit relational databases comfortably; choose them for transactions and constraints, and shard by merchant or account when needed.

C13.3API

Endpoints
POST /v1/payments
Idempotency-Key: 8b4f...                       # required; same key = same payment
{ "amount": 125000, "currency": "INR", "payment_method": "pm_tok_...", "capture": "manual" }
-> 201 { "id": "pay_77", "status": "authorized" }   (or "requires_action" for 3-D Secure)

POST /v1/payments/pay_77/capture   Idempotency-Key: ...   -> 200 { "status": "captured" }
POST /v1/refunds { "payment": "pay_77", "amount": 125000 }  Idempotency-Key: ...
Webhook to merchant: payment.succeeded, payment.failed, refund.succeeded (signed)

Amounts are integers in minor units (paise, cents), never floating point.

C13.4High-level design

C13.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Idempotency end to end

    The merchant's request times out and they retry. The processor call from your side times out too. How do you guarantee one charge?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The merchant's Idempotency-Key is claimed atomically in your database before any work (Module 3), together with a fingerprint of the request; a retry with the same key and parameters returns the stored outcome or waits for the in-flight attempt, while the same key with different parameters is rejected. Keys are kept for a defined window (Stripe documents at least 24 hours); after that, a reused key counts as a new request. Your call to the processor carries your own idempotency key derived from the payment attempt ID (a retry of the same attempt reuses it; a new attempt with a different card gets a new one), so your retries cannot create a second charge there either.

  2. 2
    State machine

    What states does a payment go through, and how are transitions protected?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    created -> requires_action (3-D Secure) -> authorized -> captured -> settled, with pending_confirmation (outcome unknown), failed, voided, refunded (and partially refunded) branches. Each transition is a conditional update (UPDATE payments SET status = 'captured' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'authorized'), and the allowed transitions are enforced in code and ideally by a database check. An event is written to the outbox in the same transaction.

  3. 3
    Ambiguous outcomes

    The processor call times out. Did the authorization happen?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Treat it as unknown, not failed. Mark the payment pending_confirmation, then query the processor's status API with your idempotency key (with backoff), or retry the same request (safe because it is idempotent). Late webhooks from the processor also resolve it. Anything still unknown is caught by reconciliation. Never report failure to the merchant while the outcome is unknown.

  4. 4
    The ledger

    Why double-entry, and what are its rules?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Every money movement is recorded as entries on at least two accounts so that total debits equal total credits (for example: processor receivable, merchant payable, fee revenue). Entries are append-only and immutable; corrections are new reversing entries. Balances are derived by summing (with cached running balances). This makes errors visible (unbalanced transactions are rejected) and gives a complete audit trail.

  5. 5
    Events and webhooks

    How do merchants and internal systems reliably learn about outcomes?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The state change and an outbox row commit together; a relay publishes to Kafka (Module 13). A webhook service delivers to merchant endpoints with an HMAC signature and timestamp, retries with backoff for days, and exposes an events API so merchants can fetch anything they missed. Merchants must handle duplicates.

  6. 6
    Refunds

    Two partial refunds for the same payment arrive at the same moment with different idempotency keys. What stops refunding more than was captured?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Idempotency keys only stop duplicates of the same request. Guard the amount itself with a conditional update in the refund transaction: UPDATE payments SET refunded = refunded + :amt WHERE id = :id AND refunded + :amt <= captured; if 0 rows change, reject the refund. Then post the refund's ledger entries in the same transaction.

  7. 7
    Reconciliation

    Your records and the processor's settlement file disagree on 3 payments. What process finds and fixes this?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A daily job loads processor settlement files and matches them to your ledger by processor reference and amount. Mismatches are classified (missing on our side, missing on theirs, amount differs, status differs) and either auto-corrected (for example, marking a timed-out payment as succeeded and posting entries) or sent to an operations queue. Payouts to merchants are computed only from reconciled balances.

  8. 8
    Card data and PCI

    How do you keep most of the system out of PCI scope?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Card numbers go from the customer's browser straight to a tokenization service (hosted fields or an SDK), which stores them encrypted (keys in an HSM or KMS) and returns a token. Everything else, including merchant servers and your payment service, handles only tokens. The vault is small, isolated, and audited.

  9. 9
    Scaling and availability

    How does this grow to 10x and survive a region failure?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Shard payments and ledger by merchant or account (keeping a payment's entries on one shard so transactions stay local). Run synchronous replication within the region and a warm standby or active-passive setup across regions with tight RPO. Data residency rules can constrain this: India's RBI requires payment data to be stored in India, so cross-region disaster recovery needs two Indian regions. Processor connectors are stateless and fail over between processors where the business allows (routing by success rate and cost).

C13.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Processor timeout Unknown outcome Pending state, status queries, idempotent retries, reconciliation
Processor outage Payments fail Circuit breaker, route to a secondary processor, clear errors to merchants
Duplicate merchant requests Double charge risk Idempotency keys with atomic claim
Webhook endpoint down Merchant misses events Retries for days, events API, dashboard
Bug posts wrong entries Balances wrong Ledger invariants checked per transaction; reversing entries; reconciliation alerts
Authorization expires before capture Capture fails Track the network's authorization validity window; capture or re-authorize before it lapses
Customer disputes a charge (chargeback) Funds pulled back weeks later Dispute state machine, evidence submission, ledger entries for the reversal and fees

C13.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): idempotency keys with atomic claims, a state machine with conditional transitions, authorize vs capture, outbox plus webhooks, careful handling of timeouts as unknown, integer money. L5 adds: double-entry ledger design and invariants, reconciliation as a first-class component, PCI scope reduction through tokenization, multi-processor routing, and regional resilience with explicit RPO.

C13.8Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why not use floats for amounts?
    Reveal

    Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift. Use integers in minor units (or exact decimal types) and store the currency with every amount.

  2. Why authorize first and capture later?
    Reveal

    Authorization holds funds without moving them; if the order cannot be fulfilled, a void releases the hold at no cost. Capture happens when goods ship or the service is delivered.

  3. Could you use an eventually consistent NoSQL store for the ledger?
    Reveal

    It is possible with careful design, but you lose multi-row transactions and constraints that make balanced entries and state transitions simple. A relational database (or distributed SQL) is the natural fit.

  4. How do you test that the ledger is always balanced?
    Reveal

    Enforce per-transaction balance in the write path, run continuous invariant checks (sum of all entries is zero; account balances match entry sums), and alert on any violation.

  5. C14.5Deep dives
  6. C14.6Failures and bottlenecks

  8. C14.8Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a scheduler service: clients register one-time and recurring (cron) jobs that call an HTTP endpoint or run a task. Jobs must fire within about a second of their time, survive node failures, retry on failure, and keep run history.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: a jobs table keyed by next run time and partitioned (time buckets and shards); scheduler nodes that each own shards through leases from a coordination service; polling only "due soon" jobs of owned shards; claiming each run with a conditional update or a unique (job_id, scheduled_time) key; enqueueing runs to a queue for workers; at-least-once execution with idempotency keys passed to the job; retries with backoff; heartbeats for long jobs; computing the next cron time in the job's time zone; and spreading load at popular times like midnight.

C14.1Requirements

Functional: create, update, cancel jobs; one-time (run_at) and recurring (cron expression with time zone); payload or callback URL; retries with a policy; run history and status.

Non-functional: 100M scheduled jobs, 10M runs per day with peaks at round hours; trigger accuracy about 1 s; no lost runs; duplicate triggers extremely rare and harmless; horizontally scalable; no single point of failure.

C14.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Average runs 10M / 86,400 about 120/s
Peak at 00:00 Many cron jobs at midnight, say 2M in the first minute about 33K/s for a minute: needs smoothing
Jobs table 100M x 1 KB about 100 GB, sharded

C14.3Data model

Table Key Fields
jobs job_id owner, schedule (cron, tz) or run_at, payload, retry policy, next_run_at, status
due_index (shard, time_bucket, next_run_at, job_id) lets a scheduler read "my shard, next minute" cheaply
runs (job_id, scheduled_time) unique attempt count, status, worker, started/finished, error

C14.4High-level design

C14.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Finding due jobs

    Why not SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE next_run_at <= now() every second?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    On 100M rows, from many nodes, every second, that query fights over the same index and duplicates work. Instead, split jobs into shards (hash of job_id) and time buckets (minute of next_run_at). Each scheduler node reads only its shards' next bucket a little ahead of time, loads due jobs into an in-memory timer (a priority queue or timing wheel), and fires them on time. Jobs created or rescheduled for the near future (say run_at = now + 5 s), after their bucket was already loaded, must not be missed: the API also notifies the owning node to add them to its timer, and nodes rescan the current bucket periodically as a safety net.

  2. 2
    One trigger per run

    Two scheduler nodes both think they own shard 7 after a network blip. How do you avoid double triggers?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Shard ownership is a lease in a coordination service (etcd or ZooKeeper) with an epoch number. The node then claims the run and records it in one database transaction: insert into runs with unique (job_id, scheduled_time) and status PENDING, and advance the job's next_run_at with a conditional update from the expected old value (the epoch acts as a fencing token). Only one claim succeeds. Enqueueing happens after the commit through an outbox relay or a sweeper that picks up PENDING runs older than a few seconds, so a crash between claim and enqueue cannot lose the run; workers dedup on (job_id, scheduled_time).

  3. 3
    Execution guarantees

    A worker crashes halfway through a job. What happens, and what must job authors do?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Delivery is at-least-once: the run message's visibility timeout or lease expires and another worker retries it. So jobs receive an idempotency key (job_id + scheduled_time) and must make their effects idempotent. Long jobs send heartbeats to extend their lease; missing heartbeats mark them failed and eligible for retry.

  4. 4
    Recurring jobs

    When do you compute the next run time of a cron job, and what about time zones?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Right after claiming a run, compute the next fire time from the cron expression in the job's time zone (handling daylight saving gaps and repeats by documented rules), convert to UTC, and update next_run_at in the same transaction as the claim. That way a crash cannot skip or duplicate the next occurrence.

  5. 5
    Midnight spikes

    Millions of jobs are scheduled at 00:00. How do you protect the system and the endpoints they call?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Add small jitter where the job allows it (spread over the first minute), rate-limit per tenant and per target endpoint, prefetch due jobs a little early, and let the queue absorb the burst while workers scale on queue depth.

  6. 6
    Retries and failures

    A job's endpoint returns 500. What is the retry policy?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Exponential backoff with jitter up to a maximum number of attempts or time window, recorded per attempt in runs; then mark it failed, alert the owner, and optionally move it to a dead-letter list for manual replay. Most 4xx errors are permanent and fail immediately, except 408 (timeout) and 429 (rate limited), which are retried, honoring Retry-After.

C14.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Scheduler node dies Its shards stop firing Lease expires in seconds; another node takes the shards, re-enqueues PENDING runs, and catches up on missed due jobs
Coordination service unavailable No new leases Existing leases keep running until expiry; nodes stop firing when unsure (safety over liveness)
Clock skew between nodes Early or late firing NTP; fire based on database or coordinator time; small lookahead
Worker backlog Jobs run late Autoscale workers on queue lag; priority queues per tier

C14.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): time-bucketed, sharded storage of due jobs; leases for shard ownership; atomic claim per run; at-least-once execution with idempotency keys; retries with backoff; next-run computation done atomically. L5 adds: fencing tokens, timing wheels, multi-tenant fairness and rate limits, daylight-saving semantics, catch-up policy after outages (run missed jobs or skip), and operational visibility.

C14.8Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why not just use one leader that schedules everything?
    Reveal

    It works up to a point and is simpler, but one node becomes the throughput limit and its failover pauses all scheduling. Sharding with leases spreads load and limits the blast radius of a failure.

  2. What is a timing wheel?
    Reveal

    A circular array of buckets, one per time slot (for example per second); jobs are placed in the slot for their fire time, and a pointer advances each tick and fires that slot. Insert and fire are O(1).

  3. Exactly-once execution of an external HTTP call?
    Reveal

    Not achievable in general: a call can succeed and the acknowledgment be lost. Use at-least-once triggering with an idempotency key the endpoint honors.

  4. What should happen to runs missed during a 2-hour outage?
    Reveal

    It depends on the job: some must run once to catch up (billing), some should run every missed occurrence, and some should skip to the next scheduled time (a cache refresh). Make it a per-job policy.
