Case study 15Stretch45 min

Case study 15: Ad click aggregation and top-K trending

Count a billion ad clicks a day per ad per minute, fast enough for dashboards and exact enough for billing, and keep a live top-K of the most clicked ads. This is the canonical stream processing design: windows, event time, dedup, hot keys, and exactly-once counts.

Uses: M12 stream processing, M17 count-min sketch, M13 reconciliation
Your status

On this page

  1. C15.1Requirements
  2. C15.2Estimates
  3. C15.3High-level design
  4. C15.4Deep dives
  5. C15.5Failures and bottlenecks
  6. C15.6What a strong answer shows
  7. C15.7Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a system that ingests ad click events, shows advertisers clicks per ad per minute with a few minutes of delay, answers "top 100 ads in the last hour", and produces billing numbers that must be correct.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: durable ingestion into Kafka keyed by ad ID; a stream processor with event-time tumbling windows and watermarks; dedup by click ID; exactly-once state and output (checkpoints plus idempotent upserts keyed by ad and window); handling hot ads with two-stage aggregation; top-K per window from per-partition heaps; an OLAP store for queries; raw events archived; and a batch recompute that reconciles billing.

C15.1Requirements

Functional: record clicks; aggregate clicks per ad per minute (with dimensions such as country); query time ranges; top-K most clicked ads over the last N minutes; filter invalid clicks.

Non-functional: 1B clicks/day, peaks of 50K/s; aggregates available within a few minutes; billing numbers exact; tolerate late events (mobile devices offline) and duplicates; no data loss.

C15.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Average ingest 1B / 86,400 about 12K/s; peaks 50K/s
Raw storage 1B x 200 bytes about 200 GB/day
Aggregates A row exists only for an (ad, minute) with at least one click at most 1B rows/day, and many hold a single click; roll up to hours early

C15.3High-level design

C15.4Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Windows and late events

    A click happened at 10:01:30 but arrives at 10:04. Which minute does it count in, and when is the 10:01 window final?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Count it in 10:01 by event time. A watermark tracks how far event time has progressed (for example, max event time seen minus 2 minutes). The 10:01 window fires when the watermark passes 10:02. Events that arrive later, but before the watermark passes 10:02 plus the allowed lateness, re-fire the window with a corrected count (the upsert overwrites it). Events after that go to a late-events side output for the batch recompute.

  2. 2
    Duplicates and fraud

    The same click can be logged twice (client retries) and bots click ads. How do you filter?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Each click carries a unique click ID (generated server-side at the redirect); the stream job keeps recently seen IDs in keyed state with a TTL and drops repeats. Invalid traffic rules (same user and ad within seconds, known bot signatures, data center IPs) run in the stream job or a separate fraud pipeline that marks clicks invalid before billing.

  3. 3
    Exactly-once counts

    A stream worker crashes after counting some events. How do you avoid double or missing counts?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The stream processor (Flink) checkpoints its operator state together with Kafka offsets; after a crash it rewinds to the last checkpoint and reprocesses, producing the same state. Output is made idempotent by upserting keyed rows (ad_id, window_start) -> count, so re-emitted results overwrite instead of adding. Alternatively, use transactional sinks committed with checkpoints.

  4. 4
    Hot ads

    One ad gets 30% of all clicks during a big campaign, so one partition is overloaded. What do you do?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Two-stage aggregation: first aggregate by (ad_id, random salt 0-9) across many workers, then combine the 10 partial counts per ad in a second, much smaller stage. The same trick works for any skewed key.

  5. 5
    Top-K

    How do you compute the top 100 ads per hour from per-minute counts?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Because the stream is partitioned by ad ID, each ad's count for a window is complete in one partition. Each partition keeps a min-heap of its top 100 for the window; a final step merges the partition heaps into a global top 100, which is exact. For extremely high-cardinality keys (all search terms), use a count-min sketch plus heap to approximate.

  6. 6
    Billing accuracy

    Streaming numbers may be slightly off. How is billing made exact?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Archive every raw event to object storage. A daily batch job recomputes counts from the raw data with the final fraud labels and late events included, compares with the streaming results, and the batch output is what is billed. Differences above a threshold raise alerts. This is the Lambda pattern: fast approximate path plus exact batch path.

  7. 7
    Serving queries

    Advertisers filter by ad, campaign, country, and time range. Where do the aggregates live?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A columnar OLAP store (ClickHouse, Apache Druid, Apache Pinot, or BigQuery) with rows keyed by ad and minute plus dimension columns, pre-rolled up to hours and days for long ranges. A query service adds authorization and caching.

C15.5Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Stream job failure Aggregates pause Restart from checkpoint; Kafka retains raw events
Kafka partition hot Lag on a hot ad Adding partitions does not split one key: salt the producer key for known hot ads, or partition randomly and key by ad inside the stream job
Late events beyond lateness Streaming undercounts Side output to batch path; billing from batch
OLAP store overloaded Slow dashboards Rollups, caching, query limits per advertiser

C15.6What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): Kafka plus stream processor with tumbling windows, event time and watermarks, dedup by click ID, idempotent upserts, OLAP store for queries, and a top-K that is correct because of the partitioning. L5 adds: exactly-once mechanics (checkpoints, transactional sinks), skew handling, a reconciliation path for billing, fraud integration, and cost and retention of raw and aggregated data.

C15.7Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why partition the raw click topic by ad ID?
    Reveal

    All clicks for an ad land in one partition, so its window counts are computed in one place without cross-partition merging (except for salted hot ads).

  2. Tumbling or sliding windows for "clicks in the last hour, updated every minute"?
    Reveal

    Sliding (hopping) windows of one hour advancing every minute, or tumbling one-minute counts summed over the last 60 at query time, which is cheaper to store.

  3. Why not write each click directly to the database and use COUNT(*)?
    Reveal

    At 50K writes/s plus heavy aggregate queries, the database would be overwhelmed; pre-aggregation reduces 1B events to far fewer rows and makes queries cheap.

  4. How would you show a near real-time "top trending" list to users?
    Reveal

    Sliding-window counts with a heap per partition, merged and cached every few seconds, served from the cache.

Case study 16Stretch45 min

Case study 16: Collaborative document editor

Several people type into the same document at the same time and all of them end up with the same text, instantly. The design rests on giving each document one place that orders edits, and on an algorithm (OT or CRDT) that merges concurrent edits correctly.

Uses: M11 ordering, M2 WebSockets, M9 multi-leader conflicts
Your status

On this page

  1. C16.1Requirements
  2. C16.2Estimates
  3. C16.3High-level design
  4. C16.4Deep dives
  5. C16.5Failures and bottlenecks
  6. C16.6What a strong answer shows
  7. C16.7Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design Google Docs-style real-time co-editing: concurrent edits, live cursors, history, offline edits, and many documents.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: clients send small operations (insert, delete) over WebSockets; one session server owns each active document (found through a directory with leases) and assigns each operation a revision number; operational transformation (or CRDTs) to merge concurrent operations; an append-only operation log plus periodic snapshots; broadcasting transformed operations to collaborators; ephemeral cursors and presence; reconnect and offline sync from the last acknowledged revision; failover of the session owner; and permissions.

C16.1Requirements

Functional: open and edit a shared document; see others' edits within a fraction of a second; see their cursors; version history; work offline briefly and sync; share with permissions.

Non-functional: edits appear to collaborators in under 200 ms; no edit is ever lost; all replicas converge to the same text; millions of documents, typically fewer than 10 simultaneous editors per document (up to about 100).

C16.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Active documents 5M documents open at peak spread across hundreds of session servers
Operations 5M docs x 1 op/s average while typing about 5M ops/s overall, small per document
Op size about 50-100 bytes logs grow; snapshots bound replay time

Load per document is tiny; the challenge is correctness of concurrent edits and routing every editor of a document to the same place.

C16.3High-level design

C16.4Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Why not send the whole document or lock paragraphs?

    What goes wrong with simpler approaches?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Sending full documents loses concurrent edits (last write wins). Locking paragraphs blocks collaborators and still needs merging for edits near boundaries. Sending small operations and merging them keeps everyone editing freely.

  2. 2
    Operational transformation

    Alice and Bob both edit revision 5. How does the server produce one consistent order?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The session server is the single sequencer: it applies operations in arrival order and gives each a revision. An incoming operation based on an older revision is transformed against all operations applied since (shifting positions for inserts and deletes that happened before it), then applied and broadcast. Clients do the same for their own unacknowledged local operations, so every replica converges. Google Docs uses OT with a central server.

  3. 3
    CRDTs

    How do CRDTs differ, and when are they better?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    CRDTs give every character a unique, ordered identifier so concurrent inserts and deletes commute: any order of applying them gives the same result, with no central transform step. They suit offline-first and peer-to-peer editing (Yjs, Automerge). Costs: per-character metadata and tombstones that grow memory, and more complex garbage collection. OT needs a central sequencer but keeps documents compact.

  4. 4
    Routing and ownership

    How do all editors of one document reach the same session server, and what if it dies?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A directory maps document IDs to session servers using consistent hashing or explicit leases in a coordination service. On failure, the lease expires, another server takes ownership, loads the latest snapshot plus subsequent operations from the log, and clients reconnect and resend unacknowledged operations (idempotent by client operation IDs).

  5. 5
    Persistence

    How do you store a document that receives thousands of small edits?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Append every operation to an operation log keyed by (doc_id, revision) before acknowledging, and write a snapshot every N operations or minutes. Loading a document is "latest snapshot + operations after it". History and "restore version" come from snapshots and the log.

  6. 6
    Cursors and presence

    Should cursor positions be stored?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    No. Cursors and selections are ephemeral: broadcast them through the session server at a limited rate, transform them against operations like any position, and drop them when a user disconnects.

  7. 7
    Offline edits

    A user edits on a plane for an hour. How do their edits merge?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The client keeps its local operations based on the last revision it saw. On reconnect it sends them; the server transforms them against everything that happened meanwhile (OT), or the CRDT state merges automatically. Large divergences can produce surprising but consistent results, so some products show a review of merged changes.

C16.5Failures and bottlenecks

Failure or bottleneck Effect Mitigation
Session server crash Editing pauses briefly Lease takeover, reload snapshot + log, clients resend pending ops
Very popular document (1,000 viewers) Broadcast fan-out Separate read-only viewers onto a fan-out tier; limit editors
Log grows without bound Slow loads Snapshots and compaction
Network flaps Duplicate operations Client operation IDs make resends idempotent

C16.6What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

L4 (SDE2): operations over WebSockets, one owner per document that sequences operations, a correct explanation of why concurrent edits need transformation, operation log plus snapshots, reconnect with resend. L5 adds: OT vs CRDT trade-offs in depth, ownership failover with leases and fencing, offline merge behavior, presence at scale, and permission changes during a live session.

C16.7Follow-up questions

Self-checkFollow-ups interviewers ask
  1. Why does a single session server per document simplify correctness?
    Reveal

    It provides one total order of operations (revision numbers), so transformation only has to handle operations against a known history, and every client converges to the server's sequence.

  2. Does a single owner per document limit scale?
    Reveal

    Not in practice: each document has few editors and little traffic, and millions of documents are spread across many servers.

  3. How would you implement "suggestion mode" or comments anchored to text?
    Reveal

    As additional operations or annotations with anchors expressed in positions that are transformed like cursors, so they move with the text.

  4. What changes for a spreadsheet instead of a text document?
    Reveal

    Operations target cells and ranges (set value, insert row); conflicts are per cell and simpler, but formulas and row and column insertions need transformation of references.

Numbers

Rule of thumb Value
Seconds per day 86,400, about 10^5
1M requests/day about 12/s; 1B/day is about 12K/s
Peak / average 2-3x normally; 10x+ for launches
Memory reference / SSD random read / DC round trip / cross-continent round trip ~100 ns / ~20-100 us / ~0.5 ms / ~150 ms
Redis / SQL primary / stateless server ~100K ops/s / thousands to low tens of thousands queries/s / 1K-10K req/s
Base62 codes 62^6 is about 57 billion; 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion
Snowflake 41-bit ms time, 10-bit machine, 12-bit sequence (4,096 per ms)

Details: Module 4.

Availability

Nines Per year Per month
99.9% 8.77 h 43.8 min
99.95% 4.38 h 21.9 min
99.99% 52.6 min 4.4 min
99.999% 5.3 min 26 s

Series: multiply. Parallel copies: 1 - (1 - a)^n. RPO = data you can lose; RTO = time to recover. Module 15.

Which database?

Need Choose Example
Transactions, joins, constraints, moderate scale Relational PostgreSQL, MySQL
SQL with horizontal write scale, global Distributed SQL Spanner, CockroachDB
Lookup by key at huge scale Key-value DynamoDB, Redis
Flexible documents read as a whole Document MongoDB
Huge append-heavy writes, time-ordered per key Wide-column (LSM) Cassandra, Bigtable, HBase
Full-text search, facets Search index Elasticsearch, OpenSearch
Metrics over time Time-series Prometheus, InfluxDB, TimescaleDB
Analytics over billions of rows Columnar warehouse BigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHouse
Multi-hop relationships Graph Neo4j

Module 8.

Caching patterns

Pattern Write path Risk
Cache-aside (default) Write DB, delete cache key Stale-set race; bound with TTL
Write-through Write cache and DB together Slower writes
Write-behind Write cache, flush to DB later Data loss on cache failure
Write-around Write DB only First read misses

Failure modes: stampede (single-flight, early refresh), avalanche (TTL jitter), penetration (negative cache, Bloom filter), hot key (local cache, key replication). Module 6.

Replication, partitioning, consistency

Topic Remember
Sync vs async replication Sync: no loss, slower, blocks on slow replica. Async: fast, can lose recent writes on failover
Lag anomalies Read-your-writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix
Quorum R + W > N gives overlap; N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 is common
Partition key High cardinality, even load, matches the main query
Consistent hashing Adding a node moves about 1/N of keys; virtual nodes balance load
CAP During a partition choose consistency (refuse) or availability (answer, maybe stale)
PACELC Else: latency vs consistency, paid on every request
Consensus 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f failures; majority commits (Raft)
Locks Lease + fencing token, or a database constraint

Modules 9-11.

Messaging

Kafka RabbitMQ SQS
Model Partitioned log, replay Broker queues, routing Managed queue
Ordering Per partition (by key) Per queue FIFO per message group
Best for Event backbone, streams, many consumers Task routing, priorities Simple background jobs

Delivery is at-least-once; make consumers idempotent. Retries with backoff, then a DLQ. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count; Kafka share groups (4.2+) do not, but lose per-key order. Module 12.

Cross-service correctness

Problem Pattern
Write DB and publish event atomically Transactional outbox, or CDC
Multi-service business transaction Saga (orchestration or choreography) with compensations
Retries must not repeat effects Idempotency keys, unique constraints, conditional updates
Separate read and write needs CQRS with projections
Full history required Event sourcing
Records must match a partner Reconciliation

Module 13.

Real-time and APIs

Need Use
Rare updates, delay fine Polling
Server pushes only Server-sent events
Two-way, frequent WebSocket (with connection registry and pub/sub)
Internal high-volume calls gRPC
Public API REST with cursor pagination, idempotency keys, 429 + Retry-After
Rich client with varied data GraphQL or a BFF

Modules 2-3.

Rate limiting

Algorithm One line
Token bucket Bursts up to b, average r; the usual default
Leaky bucket Constant output rate; smooths
Fixed window Cheap; allows 2x at boundaries
Sliding log Exact; memory per request
Sliding counter Weighted approximation; cheap and close

Atomic in Redis with Lua; fail open with a local fallback. Module 15, Case study 2.

Trade-off phrases worth saying

  • "Reads outnumber writes 100 to 1, so I'll put a cache in front and accept up to 60 seconds of staleness for this data."
  • "This must never double-charge, so the write path uses an idempotency key with a unique constraint, and events go out through an outbox."
  • "I'll partition by user_id because every main query includes it; the risk is very large users, which I'll handle by splitting their data into buckets."
  • "During a network partition, booking chooses consistency: we reject rather than risk selling a seat twice. Browsing chooses availability and serves cached data."
  • "I'm keeping this synchronous because the caller needs the answer; everything else goes on a queue."
  • "One PostgreSQL primary handles this load today; I'd plan the shard key now and shard when we pass about X writes per second."

Interview framework

A system design round rewards a clear process as much as a good design. This page gives a time plan for 45 minutes, what to say in each phase, how to choose deep dives, what L4 and L5 interviewers listen for, and the red flags to avoid.

On this page

  1. The 45-minute plan
  2. What to say in each phase
  3. What interviewers look for
  4. Drawing on a whiteboard
  5. Red flags
  6. How to practice

The 45-minute plan

Minutes Phase Output Watch out
0-5 Requirements 3-5 functional requirements, numeric non-functional ones, out of scope Do not draw yet
5-10 Estimates QPS (average, peak), storage, bandwidth, read/write ratio, and what they imply Round hard; state the implication
10-15 API and data model 3-5 endpoints; main entities, keys, and the store for each Keep it short
15-30 High-level design Diagram of the main flows; walk one request end to end Start simple, then evolve
30-42 Deep dives 2-3 hardest problems: bottlenecks, consistency, failures Let the interviewer steer; propose if they do not
42-45 Wrap-up Trade-offs, what you would do next, monitoring Summarize; do not start new topics

What to say in each phase

Requirements

  • "Let me confirm scope: users can do A, B, C. I'll leave out D and E unless you want them."
  • "Roughly how many users and requests? Read-heavy or write-heavy? Global or one region?"
  • "What matters most: latency, availability, or strict correctness? Is it fine if X is a few seconds stale?"

Estimates

  • Write the formula, round, and conclude: "About 120K reads per second, so the read path needs a cache; 90 TB over five years, so one database node is not enough."

High-level design

  • Draw clients, entry point (LB or gateway), services, data stores, caches, queues. Number the flows.
  • Walk through one write and one read: "The client calls..., the service writes..., then publishes..."
  • Name each technology with its reason: "Redis here because reads are key lookups and we accept 60 s staleness."

Deep dives

Pick from what the numbers and requirements make hard:

  1. The bottleneck your estimates exposed (hot keys, write volume, fan-out, bandwidth).
  2. The correctness risk (double booking, double charge, lost messages, ordering).
  3. A failure (a node, a dependency, a region, a spike) and how the design degrades.

For each: state the problem, give two options, choose one with its trade-off, and say how you would know it works (a metric).

Wrap-up

  • "The main trade-offs are... With more time I would add... I'd monitor..."

What interviewers look for

Interview signal

SDE-2 / L4 (Google SWE III, Meta E4, Amazon SDE2): a working, reasonably scaled design; correct use of standard building blocks; estimates that drive decisions; clear trade-offs; sensible data model and partition key; handles 1-2 deep dives well with guidance. You may need prompting for the hardest failure modes, but you respond to it well.

L5 adds: drives the interview without prompting, finds the hard problems unasked, goes deep on several (consistency, failure, scaling limits), discusses operations (monitoring, rollout, migration, cost), and compares alternatives quantitatively.

Dimension Weak Solid (L4) Strong (L5)
Requirements Starts drawing Clarifies scope and numbers Uncovers hidden requirements (consistency per feature, compliance)
Design Buzzwords, missing flows Coherent components, clear data flow Elegant, minimal, evolves with scale
Data No model or wrong store Fitting store, keys, partitioning Access-pattern-driven model, hot spots handled
Trade-offs None stated Names main trade-offs Quantifies them, picks per requirement
Failures Ignored Handles obvious failures Systematic: what fails, detection, recovery, degradation
Communication Silent or rambling Structured, checks in Leads, adapts to interviewer cues

Drawing on a whiteboard

  • One shape per kind of component (see the legend); label every box with its role, not only a product name.
  • Solid arrows for synchronous calls, dashed for async messages; number the steps of a flow.
  • Write key decisions next to the component: "partition key: user_id", "TTL 60 s", "W = 2".
  • Leave space to the right for the evolution; do not erase, extend.

Red flags

Common mistakes

  • Designing before clarifying scope and scale.
  • Numbers that change nothing: estimates without conclusions.
  • Technology lists ("Kafka, Redis, Cassandra") without reasons.
  • Single points of failure in a design that claims high availability.
  • Ignoring the data model and partitioning.
  • Strong consistency everywhere or nowhere, instead of per feature.
  • Going silent for long stretches; think out loud.
  • Arguing with the interviewer's constraint instead of adapting the design.

How to practice

  1. Do each case study cold with a 45-minute timer, speaking out loud (record yourself).
  2. Compare with the handbook; write down what you missed in one line each.
  3. Redo it from memory when the tracker brings it back.
  4. From week 6 of the roadmap, do a mock with a peer every two weeks, alternating interviewer and candidate.
  5. Before each real interview, skim the cheat sheets and redo two case studies quickly (20 minutes each, diagram only).

Glossary

Every term used in the handbook, in one line each, with a link to where it is explained. Search finds these too.

A
ACID
Atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability: the guarantees of database transactions. Read more
Active-active
Several regions serve traffic at the same time; needs a conflict strategy for writes. Read more
Adaptive bitrate
The video player switches quality per segment based on measured bandwidth. Read more
Anti-entropy
Background process that finds and repairs differences between replicas, often with Merkle trees. Read more
API gateway
Single entry point that handles auth, rate limits, and routing to services. Read more
At-least-once
Delivery that may repeat messages but never loses them; consumers must be idempotent. Read more
At-most-once
Delivery that never repeats but may lose messages. Read more
Availability
Fraction of time a system answers requests successfully. Read more
B
B-tree
Sorted, balanced tree index used by relational databases; good for lookups and ranges. Read more
Backpressure
Slowing producers when consumers cannot keep up, instead of buffering forever. Read more
BFF (backend for frontend)
A gateway tailored to one client type that aggregates and shapes data. Read more
Bloom filter
Compact set that answers "definitely not" or "probably yes". Read more
Blue-green deploy
Run a full new environment and switch all traffic at once; switch back to roll back. Read more
Bulkhead
Isolating resources per dependency so one failure cannot exhaust everything. Read more
C
Cache-aside
App reads cache, loads from DB on miss, and deletes the cache key on write. Read more
Canary release
Send a small share of traffic to a new version and compare before rolling out. Read more
CAP theorem
During a network partition a system must choose consistency or availability. Read more
CDC (change data capture)
Streaming a database's committed changes from its log to other systems. Read more
CDN
Network of edge caches that serve content close to users. Read more
Circuit breaker
Stops calling a failing dependency for a while, then tests it again. Read more
Consistent hashing
Mapping keys and nodes onto a ring so adding a node moves only about 1/N of keys. Read more
Consumer group
Set of consumers sharing a Kafka topic's partitions; in a classic group each partition goes to one member. Read more
Consumer lag
How far a consumer is behind the newest message. Read more
Count-min sketch
Small structure estimating item frequencies; only overestimates. Read more
CQRS
Separate models for writes (commands) and reads (queries). Read more
CRDT
Data type whose concurrent updates always merge to the same result. Read more
D
Dead-letter queue (DLQ)
Where messages go after repeated processing failures, for inspection and replay. Read more
Denormalization
Storing copies of data to make reads faster, at the cost of harder updates. Read more
DNS
System that maps names to IP addresses, with caching by TTL. Read more
Double-entry ledger
Recording every money movement as balanced debits and credits. Read more
Dual write
Writing to two systems without a shared transaction; can leave them inconsistent. Read more
Durability
Confirmed data survives crashes and failures. Read more
E
Envelope encryption
Data keys encrypt data; a master key in KMS encrypts the data keys. Read more
Error budget
The failure allowance implied by an SLO, used to balance speed and reliability. Read more
Event sourcing
Storing every change as an event and deriving current state by replay. Read more
Eventual consistency
Replicas converge if writes stop; reads may be stale meanwhile. Read more
Exactly-once (effectively)
At-least-once delivery plus idempotent or transactional processing. Read more
F
Failover
Promoting a replica to replace a failed leader. Read more
Fan-out on write / read
Precompute feeds when posting, or assemble them when reading. Read more
Fencing token
Increasing number checked by storage to reject a stale lock holder or leader. Read more
G
Geohash
Base32 string encoding of a location; shared prefixes mean nearby cells. Read more
gRPC
RPC framework using Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2. Read more
H
Hedged request
Sending a duplicate request after a delay and using the faster answer. Read more
Hinted handoff
A stand-in node holds writes for a down replica and delivers them later. Read more
Horizontal scaling
Adding more machines rather than bigger ones. Read more
Hot key
A key receiving a disproportionate share of traffic. Read more
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
Multiplexed HTTP over TCP, and over QUIC (UDP) without TCP head-of-line blocking. Read more
HyperLogLog
Structure that estimates distinct counts with a few KB of memory. Read more
I
Idempotency key
Client-chosen ID that lets the server return the original result for retries. Read more
Idempotent
An operation that has the same effect whether done once or many times. Read more
Inverted index
Map from each term to the documents containing it; powers search. Read more
Isolation level
How much concurrent transactions can see of each other; read committed to serializable. Read more
J
JWT
Signed token carrying claims, verified without a lookup; hard to revoke early. Read more
K
Kafka
Distributed, partitioned, replicated log used as an event backbone. Read more
L
L4 / L7 load balancer
Balances TCP connections by address, or HTTP requests by content. Read more
Last write wins (LWW)
Conflict rule that keeps the value with the latest timestamp, dropping others. Read more
Latency vs throughput
Time per request versus requests per second; batching trades one for the other. Read more
Leader election
Choosing one node to coordinate, typically through consensus and leases. Read more
Lease
Time-limited ownership that must be renewed; expires if the holder dies. Read more
Linearizability
Strongest consistency: the system behaves like a single up-to-date copy. Read more
Little's Law
Items in a system = arrival rate x time in system; sizes pools and consumer counts. Read more
Load shedding
Rejecting excess work early so accepted work still succeeds. Read more
Long polling
Server holds a request open until data arrives or a timeout. Read more
LSM tree
Write-optimized storage: memtable, sorted files, background compaction. Read more
M
Merkle tree
Tree of hashes used to find differing ranges between replicas cheaply. Read more
Microservices
Independently deployable services, each owning its data. Read more
mTLS
TLS where both sides present certificates, authenticating service to service. Read more
Multi-leader replication
Several nodes accept writes and replicate to each other; conflicts must be resolved. Read more
O
OAuth 2.0
Delegated authorization: an app gets a scoped token to act for a user. Read more
Object storage
Durable, cheap storage of files by key over HTTP (S3, GCS). Read more
OIDC
Identity layer on OAuth 2.0 that adds an ID token for login. Read more
Operational transformation (OT)
Adjusting concurrent edit operations so all replicas converge. Read more
Optimistic locking
Detect conflicts with a version check at write time and retry. Read more
Outbox pattern
Writing an event row in the same transaction as the data, then relaying it. Read more
P
PACELC
If partitioned, availability or consistency; else, latency or consistency. Read more
Partition key
The field that decides which shard or partition holds a record. Read more
Percentile (p99)
Value below which 99% of measurements fall; used for latency. Read more
Pessimistic locking
Lock rows before changing them (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE). Read more
Presigned URL
Time-limited URL granting one operation on one object. Read more
Q
Quadtree
Tree that splits space into four cells wherever points are dense. Read more
Quorum
Minimum replicas that must respond; R + W > N gives overlap. Read more
R
Raft
Consensus protocol based on leader election and majority log replication. Read more
RAG
Retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve relevant chunks, then let an LLM answer from them. Read more
Rate limiting
Restricting how many requests a client may make per time window. Read more
Read repair
Fixing a stale replica noticed during a read. Read more
Read-your-writes
A user always sees their own recent writes. Read more
Reconciliation
Comparing your records with an external source to find and fix mismatches. Read more
Replication lag
Delay before a follower reflects the leader's writes. Read more
Reverse proxy
Server in front of servers: TLS termination, routing, caching. Read more
RPO / RTO
How much data you can lose / how long recovery may take. Read more
S
Saga
Sequence of local transactions with compensations, replacing a distributed transaction. Read more
Schema registry
Service that stores event schemas and rejects incompatible changes. Read more
Server-sent events (SSE)
One-way server-to-client event stream over HTTP. Read more
Service discovery
How a caller finds healthy instances of a service. Read more
Service mesh
Sidecar proxies plus a control plane for service-to-service traffic. Read more
Sharding
Splitting data across nodes by a partition key. Read more
Share group
Kafka (4.2+) group with queue semantics: many consumers per partition, per-record acks, no per-key order. Read more
SLI / SLO / SLA
Measured indicator / internal target / contractual promise. Read more
Sloppy quorum
Counting stand-in nodes toward W during failures; keeps writes available. Read more
Snowflake ID
64-bit time-ordered ID: timestamp, machine ID, sequence. Read more
Split brain
Two nodes both acting as leader after a partition. Read more
SSRF
Tricking a server into fetching internal URLs; block private ranges and allow-list destinations. Read more
Stampede (thundering herd)
Many requests rebuilding the same expired cache key at once. Read more
Stateless service
Service that keeps no per-client state between requests. Read more
Sticky session
Load balancer keeps a client on one server. Read more
Strangler fig
Migrating a monolith piece by piece behind a routing layer. Read more
T
TCP / UDP
Reliable ordered byte stream / connectionless datagrams. Read more
Token bucket
Rate limiter allowing bursts up to a bucket size and an average refill rate. Read more
Two-phase commit (2PC)
Atomic commit across participants via prepare and commit; blocks if the coordinator fails. Read more
U
UUIDv7
128-bit ID with a millisecond timestamp prefix; sortable and index-friendly. Read more
V
Vector clock
Per-node counters that detect whether events are ordered or concurrent. Read more
Vector search
Finding items whose embedding vectors are nearest to a query vector, using ANN indexes such as HNSW. Read more
Virtual nodes
Many ring positions per physical node to balance consistent hashing. Read more
W
Watermark
Stream processing marker saying events up to time T have likely arrived. Read more
WebSocket
Full-duplex connection upgraded from HTTP. Read more
Write skew
Two transactions read the same data and write different rows, breaking a rule together. Read more
Write-ahead log (WAL)
Log written before data pages so changes survive crashes. Read more

Roadmap and revision

A 13-week plan at two HLD sessions a week (about 5 hours), with case studies starting in week 4 and mocks from week 8. Stretch it to 18-20 weeks if you alternate HLD with LLD sessions.

On this page

  1. Weekly plan
  2. Revision rules
  3. Mock interviews
  4. Using the handbook at work

Weekly plan

Each session is about 2-2.5 hours. Start every session by clearing the revision queue on the home page (15-20 minutes).

Week Session 1 Session 2
1 M1 Systems and requirements M2 Networking
2 M3 API design M4 Estimation + decode drills
3 M5 Scaling and LB M6 Caching
4 M7 CDN and object storage C1 URL shortener + C2 Rate limiter
5 M8 Databases (part 1: ACID, isolation, locking) M8 (part 2: indexes, engines, NoSQL, choosing)
6 M9 Replication M10 Sharding
7 M11 Consistency, CAP, consensus C3 Key-value store
8 M12 Queues and streams M13 Transactions; first mock
9 M14 Microservices + C4 News feed C5 Chat + C6 Notifications
10 M15 Reliability M16 Observability and security; mock
11 C12 Tickets + C13 Payments M17 Toolkit + C7 Autocomplete
12 C8 Crawler + C11 Nearby and rides C9 Video + C10 File sync
13 C14 Scheduler + C15 Ad clicks C16 Co-editing; 60-minute mock

After week 13: one or two practice prompts from the tracker per week, plus the revision queue, until your interviews.

Revision rules

  • Spaced review: set a status after every case study and practice prompt. The queue brings designs back after 1, 2, 4, 10, or 30 days.
  • Redesign, do not reread: on review, close the page, set a 20-30 minute timer, and draw the design from scratch. Then compare.
  • One-line misses: keep a running list of what you forgot ("forgot hot keys", "no idempotency on retry"). Read it before every mock.
  • Mastery checklists: revisit them at the end of each phase; untick anything that is no longer true.

Mock interviews

When Format Focus
Week 8 45 min with a peer, a Starter or Core prompt Process: requirements, estimates, a clean diagram
Week 10 45 min, a Core prompt you have not done Deep dives and failure handling
Week 13 60 min, a Stretch prompt Driving the interview, trade-offs, L5-style depth
Then Every 1-2 weeks Rotate prompts from the tracker

Score each mock with the rubric on the interview framework page and note the weakest dimension; that decides the next week's revision.

Using the handbook at work

  • Before writing a design doc, run the decode method on the problem and use the cheat sheets as a checklist.
  • During design reviews, use each module's "Common mistakes" box as review questions.
  • During incidents and postmortems, revisit Module 15 and Module 16: most incidents map to a missing timeout, retry policy, idempotency guard, or alert.

Design practice tracker

All 16 case studies and 20 more practice prompts in one list. Set a status after each attempt; due designs come back in the revision queue. Practice prompts reuse the case studies and modules listed under each.

Your designs

How to use practice prompts

Practice prompts have no write-up of their own. Each one combines ideas from the case studies and modules listed under it. Attempt it with a 45-minute timer, then reread the linked material to check your design, and set your status honestly.

Status When to choose it
Could not design it You could not get a coherent architecture without help
Designed with hints You needed to look something up for the core design
Designed independently Full design, estimates, and two deep dives on your own
Needs revision You did it before, but a redo went badly
Can teach it Done twice, weeks apart, and you can answer every follow-up

Backup

Back up or move your progress

Progress saves to your account automatically. Use this only to move progress by hand, for example from a private window.
